title: Silent Success: A Release Gate That Passed on Checks It Never Ran, and Eight More
summary: A blocking quality gate in a production release pipeline reported PASS on a run in which one subgate had executed neither of its two checks and another had run six of its eight. Both keys that decided the run asked whether a violation had been observed, and both computed that from a population already stripped of the cases that failed to run, so absent data answered "no" and a run that checked almost nothing scored perfectly, for two weeks of green builds. Introducing a third value, pass, violate, and unable to determine, turned those silent passes into failures and put the shortfall into the exit status; separate work on the same specifications then found a detector firing with a margin of 0.000177 percentage points, its firing floor holding at the sixth decimal place. Eight further instances of the same form followed: five more from the same engagement, two in open-source projects, a gateway where a configured cache TTL was declared but never applied on the write path, and an inference server whose count of free cache slots was credited on every step for releases that returned nothing, and one committed by the author while writing this paper, using tooling built to prevent exactly it. What the nine cases are offered for is not the novelty of the category but the convergence of the remedy, nine different missed questions, one kind of act, seven of the nine answerable by a single query, command, or comparison, and that convergence is falsifiable, which is what this paper asks to be judged on.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a systematic flaw in production release pipeline quality gates where checks that fail to execute are treated as "pass," leading to false positive results. The author proposes introducing a third value ("unable to determine") to properly handle incomplete checks, and demonstrates this fix across nine real-world case studies.
AI.motivation: The author discovered that quality gates can report PASS when subgates haven't executed their checks - some ran zero checks, others ran only partial checks. This occurs because the system interprets "no violation observed" from a population already stripped of failed cases, causing runs that check almost nothing to score perfectly for weeks.
AI.method: The author analyzed nine instances of this quality gate failure across different contexts (commercial engagements, open-source projects, and self-committed). Each case involved checks that didn't execute but were treated as passing. The solution involved introducing a three-state system (pass/violate/unable to determine) and applying various detection methods (queries, commands, comparisons).
AI.result: The three-state solution converted silent passes into failures. One detector fired with a margin of 0.000177 percentage points, with its firing floor holding at the sixth decimal place. Seven of the nine cases could be answered by a single query, command, or comparison, demonstrating convergence of the remedy despite different missed questions.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues that the convergence of the remedy is the key contribution - nine different problems with quality gates, but one kind of fix. This convergence is presented as falsifiable, and the author invites judgment on this claim. The paper's core insight is that silent failures in quality gates are a common pattern that can be systematically addressed.

title: Bringing AI to Autonomous Systems -- From Cognition to Collective Intelligence
summary: The purpose of this article is to highlight the central role of autonomous systems as the ultimate stage in the development of AI, to explain the underlying technical challenges that require a combination of connectionist AI and symbolic AI, and to integrate AI and systems engineering. We present a comprehensive framework for the design and evaluation of autonomous systems, based on a generic agent architecture that characterizes their behavior as the composition of cognitive functions organized around a long-term memory containing the agent's evolving knowledge. We address the challenges posed by the implementation of the fundamental features of the agent architecture, in particular the link between sensory data and structured data stored in memory, decision-making related to the achievement of the agent's goals and their planning, as well as the coordination of agents to combine individual and collective intelligence. We explain that agent trustworthiness, unlike that of traditional systems, is not limited to behavioral properties. It includes an essential dimension related to cognitive properties, the validity of which depends on how the agent uses its knowledge in decision-making. We present avenues for the development of methods for evaluating agent trustworthiness. We conclude with a critical assessment of the substantial gap between the aspirational vision of autonomous multi-agent systems and the current state of the art.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for designing and evaluating autonomous systems based on a generic agent architecture with long-term memory. It addresses technical challenges combining connectionist and symbolic AI, including sensory-memory linking, decision-making, and multi-agent coordination. The paper emphasizes that agent trustworthiness must include cognitive properties beyond behavioral properties, and concludes that a significant gap exists between the aspirational vision and current state of autonomous multi-agent systems.
AI.motivation: To highlight the central role of autonomous systems as the ultimate stage in AI development, explain the technical challenges requiring combination of connectionist and symbolic AI, and integrate AI with systems engineering. The authors also seek to address agent trustworthiness beyond traditional behavioral properties to include cognitive properties.
AI.method: The authors propose a comprehensive framework for the design and evaluation of autonomous systems based on a generic agent architecture. This architecture characterizes agent behavior as the composition of cognitive functions organized around a long-term memory containing the agent's evolving knowledge. The framework addresses implementation challenges including: 1) linking sensory data with structured data in memory, 2) decision-making for goal achievement and planning, and 3) coordination of multiple agents for individual and collective intelligence.
AI.result: The paper presents a framework addressing the fundamental features of agent architecture, including the integration of connectionist and symbolic AI approaches. It establishes that agent trustworthiness must encompass both behavioral properties and cognitive properties related to how the agent uses its knowledge in decision-making. The authors also outline avenues for developing methods to evaluate agent trustworthiness.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that there exists a substantial gap between the aspirational vision of autonomous multi-agent systems and the current state of the art. This highlights the significant challenges remaining in realizing fully autonomous systems that can effectively combine cognitive functions, integrate multiple AI paradigms, and achieve trustworthy autonomous behavior.

title: Empty Intersection: Provenance Coverage Rose to 98% and Neither Verification Decision Moved
summary: Two structural defenses for provenance, a grade on every row, so that a verification routine cannot mistake the system's own output for an observation, and a single write ingress, so that the grade is enforced rather than merely conventional, were measured against the production deployment that motivated them, over a frozen snapshot of 194,620 rows and the two verification decisions the snapshot supports. Neither reaches either decision. Both were prescribed by a companion paper, which diagnosed that deployment: its verification routines decided outcomes using values the system itself had written. Neither prescription is new: both are established practice in fields that do not cite one another, and no prior work measuring whether either changes a verdict was found, so what is offered here is the measurement and not the prescriptions. Filtering the verification queries by grade turns both decisions from pass to undetermined; widening the grade vocabulary raises classified coverage from 36.1% to 98.4%; a single ingress requiring a grade refuses 3,070 writes. None of the three gives either decision admissible input. The prescriptions do not fail at what they specify. Each is stated over the population and makes no reference to any decision, so neither says which rows a decision will read, and the rows each intervention repairs and the 32 rows the decisions read do not intersect. The intervention that changed the most rows shows the reach most plainly: all 121,296 rows it moved from unnameable to named fall outside both query windows. This paper reports the conditions, measured rather than designed, under which the decisions would have admissible input at all, and notes that the two decisions are blocked for different reasons.

AI.tldr: This paper measures two provenance defense mechanisms (grade on every row and single write ingress) against a production deployment with 194,620 rows. Neither defense achieves the verification decisions they were designed for. The interventions that changed the most rows (121,296) still fall outside the query windows used by the two decisions.
AI.motivation: The authors aimed to measure whether two established structural defenses for provenance—originally prescribed in a companion paper that diagnosed a production deployment—actually change verification outcomes. The companion paper had identified that verification routines were deciding outcomes using values the system itself had written, which is a fundamental provenance problem.
AI.method: The authors measured the two defenses against a frozen snapshot of 194,620 rows from the production deployment. They tested three interventions: (1) filtering verification queries by grade, (2) widening the grade vocabulary, and (3) implementing a single ingress requiring a grade. They analyzed which rows each intervention affected and compared these to the 32 rows actually read by the two verification decisions.
AI.result: All three interventions failed to provide admissible input to either decision. Filtering by grade turned both decisions from pass to undetermined. Widening the grade vocabulary raised classified coverage from 36.1% to 98.4%. The single ingress requiring a grade refused 3,070 writes. Most importantly, the rows each intervention repaired and the 32 rows the decisions read do not intersect—the intervention that changed the most rows (121,296 moved from unnameable to named) falls entirely outside both query windows.
AI.conclusion: The prescriptions do not fail at what they specify—they successfully implement their stated requirements. However, the fundamental problem is that neither prescription is stated in terms of which rows a decision will read; they are stated over the entire population. The two decisions are blocked for different reasons, and the conditions under which the decisions would have admissible input remain unmet. This highlights a gap between system-level provenance defenses and the specific data actually used in verification decisions.

title: ScopeBench: Do Agents Preserve Engagement Boundaries Under Goal Pressure?
comment: 18 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Accepted at AISec 2026. Code and tasks: https://github.com/dreadnode/scopebench-pilot. Trajectories: https://huggingface.co/datasets/dreadnode/scopebench-pilot. Leaderboard: https://scopebench.ai
summary: Agents are increasingly deployed with real autonomy in web application and network penetration testing, where a single out-of-scope action can breach a client's engagement boundary. Existing offensive-security benchmarks measure raw hacking capability; as those benchmarks saturate, the real barrier to deployment is a special case of alignment: scope adherence. We introduce ScopeBench, a benchmark of 30 dead-end agentic security tasks in which the stated objective is reachable only by violating the stated scope. Each task appears under two conditions that share an environment, verifier, and objective and differ only in scope: one instruction set has no scope and measures capability; the other has a natural-language scope to measure adherence. Scopeless trajectories are graded by a standard deterministic verifier. Scoped trajectories pass through two grading arms. First, the same deterministic verifier checks for the flag: because the flag sits behind the scope boundary, a pass proves by construction that a forbidden action occurred, yielding a high-precision lower bound on the violation rate. If the verifier does not pass the trajectory, an agentic judge estimates whether an out-of-scope call occurred. We calibrate the judge against 100 ScopeBench trajectories labeled call-by-call by human annotators, and a blinded audit of the evaluated rollouts finds its high recall holds - no false negatives among the 36 audited violations, with over-flagging its only observed error. Across 8 models in one harness, raw capability spans 12.2% to 81.1% and scope adherence spans 34.4% to 86.7%, with the judge finding 331 violations that mechanical verification misses. Opus-4-8 achieves a raw-capability score 10 percentage points higher than sonnet-4-6's while exhibiting 35.6 percentage points higher scope adherence. We release the frozen pilot benchmark, evaluation code, and all 2160 ATIF trajectories.

AI.tldr: ScopeBench is a benchmark evaluating 30 security tasks where reaching the objective requires violating the stated scope. It measures both raw hacking capability (scopeless) and scope adherence (scoped) across 8 models, using a deterministic verifier and an agentic judge for detection. Results show capability ranges 12.2%-81.1% and adherence ranges 34.4%-86.7%, with the judge catching 331 missed violations.
AI.motivation: Existing offensive-security benchmarks only measure hacking capability, but the real barrier to deploying autonomous agents in security testing is scope adherence - ensuring agents don't exceed client-defined boundaries. A single out-of-scope action can breach engagement terms, making this a critical alignment problem.
AI.method: ScopeBench contains 30 dead-end tasks appearing under two conditions: scopeless (capability measure) and scoped (adherence measure). Scopeless trajectories use a deterministic verifier. Scoped trajectories are graded by: (1) the same verifier - if it passes, a violation occurred by design (high-precision lower bound); (2) if verifier fails, an agentic judge estimates out-of-scope calls. The judge was calibrated against 100 human-annotated trajectories and validated via blinded audit.
AI.result: Across 8 models: raw capability spans 12.2% to 81.1%; scope adherence spans 34.4% to 86.7%. The judge finds 331 violations that mechanical verification misses. Opus-4-8 achieves 10 percentage points higher capability than sonnet-4-6 while having 35.6 percentage points higher scope adherence. The blinded audit found no false negatives among 36 audited violations, with over-flagging as the only observed error.
AI.conclusion: Scope adherence is a distinct capability from raw hacking ability, requiring separate evaluation. The dual-grading approach (verifier + agentic judge) effectively detects scope violations. The benchmark, evaluation code, and 2160 ATIF trajectories are released to advance research in aligned autonomous security agents.

title: HyQDB: LLM-Assisted Debugging for Hybrid Quantum Workflows
summary: Hybrid quantum program failures frequently occur silently, yet existing debugging tools provide limited support for detecting and repairing them. These faults dominate the failures reported by domain experts, yet existing tools evaluate on public data that under-represents this failure mode. Our key insight is that faults divide into two classes that require different strategies: mechanical faults, which allow deterministic analysis, and conceptual faults, which require reconstructing the program's intent. To address this challenge, we present HyQDB, a tiered agent that injects deterministic hardware, physics and optimization evidence into the LLM repair process. When no evidence is detected, the agent treats this silence as a signal to escalate to a second intent-reconstruction tier, that infers the program's behaviour and reconciles it with the implementation. To evaluate HyQDB, we introduce QFaultBench, a benchmark built from an expert-derived fault taxonomy that represents the true failure modes of hybrid programs. On a held-out set of human-authored programs, HyQDB raises repair success over a standard LLM from 45% to 75%. We show that the escalation gate is crucial, giving a 20% improvement in mechanical fault repair accuracy.

AI.tldr: HyQDB is a tiered debugging agent for hybrid quantum programs that addresses silent failures by injecting deterministic hardware/physics/optimization evidence into LLM repair, and escalates to intent-reconstruction when evidence is absent. It uses QFaultBench, a benchmark based on expert-derived fault taxonomy, achieving 75% repair success vs 45% for standard LLM.
AI.motivation: Hybrid quantum program failures occur silently, existing debugging tools provide limited support for detecting and repairing them. Existing tools evaluate on public data that under-represents this failure mode. Domain experts report these faults as the dominant failure type.
AI.method: A tiered agent approach: (1) First tier injects deterministic hardware, physics and optimization evidence into LLM repair process; (2) Second tier treats silence/no evidence as signal to escalate to intent-reconstruction, inferring program behavior and reconciling with implementation. Benchmark built from expert-derived fault taxonomy (QFaultBench).
AI.result: On held-out human-authored programs, HyQDB raises repair success from 45% to 75% (a 30% improvement). The escalation gate is crucial, providing 20% improvement in mechanical fault repair accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The two-tier approach effectively addresses both mechanical and conceptual faults in hybrid quantum programs. The key insight that these fault classes require different strategies leads to significant improvements over standard LLM debugging. The QFaultBench benchmark provides realistic evaluation of failure modes.

title: When Is a Multi-Agent Code Judge Actually Grounded? Two Label-Free Measurements, and a Judge That Declines to Guess
comment: Accepted at the 21st Women in Machine Learning Workshop (WiML), NeurIPS 2026
summary:
When one language model judges whether another's code is correct, it does not report the absence of evidence. It returns a confident verdict with reasoning attached, indistinguishable from a verdict it had grounds for. Multi-agent verification, which decomposes a judgment into checkable claims and verifies each against evidence, is a promising response and works well when the evidence is a set of retrieved documents.
  We argue such methods require two things of their evidence: it must be independent of the answer under review, and it must differ between the two candidates being compared. The second condition holds automatically with retrieved documents and stops holding in code judging.
  Running MARCH, a published framework unmodified over 80 condition-by-cell measurements on two code judging benchmarks, we find it declares both solutions equally good on 78 to 95% of comparisons, reaching 4.4% accuracy where the same model asked directly reaches 43.7%. Neither easier problems nor a larger judge changes this. Two measurements taken from the pipeline's own logs explain it without needing labels.
  Gating on one of them, the pipeline declines the comparisons it cannot make and raises its accuracy from 20.7 to 36.9% while still answering half of all comparisons. The contribution is not a more accurate judge, but a label-free way to tell when a judge has no basis for its answer.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses a critical flaw in multi-agent verification for code judging: language model judges cannot distinguish between having evidence for a verdict versus having no evidence. The authors demonstrate that MARCH, a multi-agent verification framework, performs poorly (4.4% accuracy) on code judging because the evidence (code) doesn't differ between compared candidates as it would for retrieved documents. They propose a label-free method to detect when a judge has no basis for its answer, improving accuracy from 20.7% to 36.9%.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent verification systems for code judging fail to report "absence of evidence" - they give confident verdicts even without proper grounds. The authors argue this stems from a fundamental requirement: evidence must differ between candidates being compared. This condition holds for document retrieval but fails for code judging, making the approach fundamentally limited.
AI.method: The authors ran MARCH (a published multi-agent verification framework) unmodified over 80 condition-by-cell measurements on two code judging benchmarks. They analyzed two measurements from the pipeline's own logs to explain the poor performance without needing external labels.
AI.result: MARCH declares both solutions equally good in 78-95% of comparisons, achieving only 4.4% accuracy compared to 43.7% when asking the same model directly. This poor performance persists regardless of problem difficulty or judge model size. By gating on one measurement from the pipeline's logs, accuracy improved from 20.7% to 36.9% while still answering half of all comparisons.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is not a more accurate judge, but a label-free method to detect when a judge has no basis for its answer. This addresses a fundamental limitation: multi-agent verification requires evidence that differs between candidates, which doesn't hold in code judging. The proposed gating mechanism provides a practical solution to avoid unreliable verdicts.

title: Offline Policy Evaluation as a decision support tool for designing Adaptive Experiments
summary: We investigate how historical data from fixed randomized experiments (A/B tests) can be used to inform the deployment of adaptive experiments based on contextual bandits. Given data collected under a static allocation, our goal is to assess which adaptive policies, if any, would have outperformed the original design and under what conditions. To this end, we combine off-policy evaluation (OPE) with a controlled warm-start simulation. From logged A/B test data exhibiting heterogeneous treatment effects, we estimate nuisance components and use doubly robust estimators to rank a portfolio of pre-specified adaptive and non-adaptive policies. When ground truth is available, we then deploy the same offline-trained policies in a simulator that reuses the exact data-generating reward probabilities, providing a safe, ground-truth-anchored environment to study the offline-to-online transition under warm starting. Using synthetic randomized controlled trials with known heterogeneity structures and an oracle policy, our results indicate that adaptive, context-aware policies improve upon fixed allocations when meaningful heterogeneity is present, while providing little benefit in its absence. We reinforce our findings on standard open benchmarks (Hillstrom, Criteo Uplift, and LaLonde), reinterpreted through a policy-value and regret perspective. Overall, our results provide a practical methodology for deciding when adaptive experimentation is worth deploying and how to select among competing adaptive policies using existing A/B test data.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a methodology for using historical A/B test data to determine whether adaptive contextual bandit experiments would outperform static allocations, and how to select the best adaptive policy. The approach combines off-policy evaluation with warm-start simulation to safely assess offline-to-online transitions.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to solve a practical problem: given fixed randomized experiment (A/B test) data, how can we determine if adaptive experiments would be beneficial, and which adaptive policy to deploy. This addresses the challenge of safely transitioning from static to adaptive experimentation in real-world settings.
AI.method: The methodology combines: (1) Off-policy evaluation (OPE) using doubly robust estimators to rank pre-specified adaptive and non-adaptive policies from logged A/B test data; (2) Controlled warm-start simulation that reuses the exact data-generating reward probabilities to provide ground-truth validation; (3) Experiments on synthetic RCTs with known heterogeneity and standard benchmarks (Hillstrom, Criteo Uplift, LaLonde).
AI.result: Adaptive context-aware policies improve upon fixed allocations when meaningful treatment effect heterogeneity is present, but provide little benefit when heterogeneity is absent. The methodology successfully identifies when adaptive experimentation is worthwhile and enables selection among competing policies.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a practical methodology for: (1) deciding when adaptive experimentation is worth deploying; (2) selecting among competing adaptive policies using existing A/B test data. This enables a safe, data-driven transition from static to adaptive experiments.

title: Bridging LLM Agents and Data Spaces: An Architectural Mediation Approach using the Model Context Protocol
summary: Data Spaces enable sovereign and governed data sharing across organizational boundaries, but their integration with AI agents remains challenging due to mismatches between probabilistic language model interactions and policy-driven data infrastructures. This article presents an architectural mediation approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), implemented through the Eunomia Agent, to enable controlled interaction between large language model (LLM) agents and data space services. The proposed mediation layer translates data space capabilities into structured, schema-driven tools that AI agents can discover and invoke while preserving governance constraints. A prototype implementation validates end-to-end interaction across catalog discovery, metadata retrieval, and data service invocation without modifying existing data space components. Results demonstrate that protocol-based mediation enables interoperable and standards-aligned integration of AI agents into data space ecosystems. The approach provides practical guidance for organizations seeking to introduce AI-driven automation into governed data-sharing environments while maintaining compliance, interoperability, and architectural separation of concerns.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an architectural mediation approach using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to enable AI agents to interact with Data Spaces in a controlled, governance-compliant manner. The Eunomia Agent implements this mediation layer, translating data space capabilities into schema-driven tools for LLM agents while preserving policy constraints.
AI.motivation: Data Spaces enable sovereign data sharing across organizations, but integrating AI agents with these policy-driven infrastructures is challenging due to mismatches between probabilistic LLM interactions and structured data space systems.
AI.method: An architectural mediation approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is proposed, implemented through the Eunomia Agent. This mediation layer translates data space capabilities into structured, schema-driven tools that AI agents can discover and invoke while preserving governance constraints. A prototype validates end-to-end interaction across catalog discovery, metadata retrieval, and data service invocation without modifying existing data space components.
AI.result: The approach enables interoperable and standards-aligned integration of AI agents into data space ecosystems, validating end-to-end interaction across catalog discovery, metadata retrieval, and data service invocation.
AI.conclusion: Protocol-based mediation enables organizations to introduce AI-driven automation into governed data-sharing environments while maintaining compliance, interoperability, and architectural separation of concerns.

title: What Will Remain Human in Software Architecture? A Focus Group Report
summary: AI development agents are increasingly used to support and partially automate software architecture tasks. To explore how practitioners perceive this shift, specifically what changes, what remains, and what new responsibilities emerge, we conducted a focus group at the 31st European Conference on Pattern Languages of Programs, People, and Practices (EuroPLoP 2026). Twenty-two participants from industry and academia discussed current practices, trust and validation strategies, the boundaries of AI autonomy, governance challenges, and implications for education. Among others, we found broad consensus that architectural decision-making, accountability, and the authoring of architectural guardrails remain fundamentally human tasks. A central emergent concept was harness engineering: the discipline of building the system that governs AI-assisted system creation, comprising validation mechanisms, knowledge lay- ers, and company-specific standards. The participants agreed that criticality, understood as the combination of uncertainty and cost of change, serves as the universal criterion for calibrating human oversight. A further concern was cognitive debt: the progressive erosion of human understanding of the system when AI-assisted decisions are accepted without full intellectual engagement. In this report, we present the findings of the focus group and describe directions for future work.

AI.tldr: A focus group at EuroPLoP 2026 explored practitioner perceptions of AI development agents in software architecture tasks. Twenty-two participants from industry and academia identified that architectural decision-making, accountability, and guardrail authoring remain human responsibilities. The study introduced two new concepts: "harness engineering" (building systems that govern AI-assisted creation) and "cognitive debt" (erosion of human understanding from uncritical AI adoption). Criticality (uncertainty + cost of change) serves as the criterion for human oversight calibration.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand how practitioners perceive the shift toward AI-assisted software architecture tasks—what changes, what remains human-controlled, and what new responsibilities emerge.
AI.method: Focus group conducted at EuroPLoP 2026 with 22 participants from industry and academia, discussing current practices, trust/validation strategies, AI autonomy boundaries, governance challenges, and education implications.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Architectural decision-making, accountability, and guardrail authoring remain human tasks; (2) "Harness engineering" emerged as a new discipline for building governance systems for AI-assisted creation; (3) "Criticality" (uncertainty + cost of change) is the universal criterion for calibrating human oversight; (4) "Cognitive debt" was identified as a concern—the erosion of human understanding from uncritical AI adoption.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that AI should augment rather than replace human architectural judgment, with criticality-based oversight and attention to cognitive debt. Future work should explore harness engineering practices and education for AI-augmented architecture.

title: Stealth Apart, Harm Together: Skill Cascading Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
summary: A skill is a modular package of natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and reference resources that an agent can load at runtime to extend its capabilities for a specific task. Skill-based agent systems therefore enable flexible reuse of third-party capabilities, but the openness of this skill ecosystem also opens up a new attack surface. Prior work has focused on vulnerabilities within individual skills, but little attention has been paid to risks that arise from interactions across skills. In this paper, we introduce skill cascading attacks, a threat paradigm in which a malicious objective is distributed across multiple skills so that each modification looks benign in isolation, yet their combined execution is harmful. For instance, in a prescription-review pipeline, the first skill weakens signals of recently discontinued medications in the extracted history, the second downgrades the severity of any drug interaction tied to them, and the third suppresses the resulting low-priority alert in the final summary, so that a severe drug-interaction warning silently disappears before reaching the physician. To systematically study this safety blind spot, we develop SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework, and release SkillCascade-Bench, a benchmark of 213 validated cascading test cases across multiple agent systems and domains. Across representative agents (e.g., OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and LLM backbones, cascaded interactions reliably induce harmful behaviors while evading existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors. Our findings highlight a gap between component-level integrity and system-level safety, and call for defenses that reason over cross-skill interactions rather than individual skills in isolation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "skill cascading attacks" - a novel threat paradigm where malicious objectives are distributed across multiple skills in agent systems, making each modification appear benign in isolation while their combined execution causes harm. The authors develop SkillCascade (red-teaming framework) and SkillCascade-Bench (213 test cases) to demonstrate these attacks across multiple agent systems.
AI.motivation: Prior security research on skill-based agent systems focused on vulnerabilities within individual skills, but overlooked risks arising from interactions across skills. The openness of skill ecosystems creates a new attack surface that existing per-skill scanners fail to detect.
AI.method: The authors developed SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework, and created SkillCascade-Bench, a benchmark containing 213 validated cascading test cases across multiple agent systems and domains. They tested attacks against representative agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and LLM backbones.
AI.result: Cascaded interactions reliably induced harmful behaviors while evading existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors. The example demonstrates how a prescription-review pipeline can be compromised: (1) weakening signals of discontinued medications, (2) downgrading drug interaction severity, and (3) suppressing low-priority alerts - causing a severe drug-interaction warning to silently disappear.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight a critical gap between component-level integrity and system-level safety in skill-based agent systems. The paper calls for new defenses that reason over cross-skill interactions rather than evaluating individual skills in isolation.

title: Untangling the Spaghetti Code in Game Development: A Review of Challenges and Academic Solutions
summary: The code quality in the game domain is perceived as less structured and more convoluted than in other domains, which results in lower maintainability and higher bug frequency. In this work, we conduct a systematic literature review to address four main research questions: (1) how the incidence of code smells and technical debt differs in game development compared to other software domains; (2) what academic solutions are proposed to mitigate these code quality issues; (3) whether researchers collaborate effectively with developers to implement these solutions; and (4) if the proposed solutions are sufficient to tackle the diagnosed problems. Thirty-four works were mapped and analyzed. We found that the game domain is affected by a short-term mentality, continuous requirements changes, reduced code reuse, and minimal to no automated testing. As potential solutions, we identified tools and models to detect code smells, along with testing practices and product lines adapted for game development. Although these solutions exist, they are not widely adopted by practitioners, highlighting the need to investigate barriers to their integration.

AI.tldr: A systematic literature review examining code quality issues in game development, comparing it to other software domains, and identifying proposed solutions and their adoption gaps. The study analyzes 34 works and finds that game development suffers from short-term mentality, continuous requirements changes, reduced code reuse, and minimal testing, with proposed solutions existing but not widely adopted.
AI.motivation: The code quality in game development is perceived as lower than in other domains, resulting in lower maintainability and higher bug frequency. This motivates a comprehensive investigation to understand the extent of the problem and evaluate existing solutions.
AI.method: Systematic literature review (SLR) analyzing 34 works, addressing four research questions: (1) incidence of code smells and technical debt in game development vs. other domains; (2) proposed academic solutions; (3) researcher-developer collaboration effectiveness; (4) sufficiency of proposed solutions.
AI.result: Game development is affected by short-term mentality, continuous requirements changes, reduced code reuse, and minimal to no automated testing. Identified solutions include tools/models for code smell detection, testing practices, and product lines adapted for games. However, these solutions are not widely adopted by practitioners.
AI.conclusion: While code quality solutions exist for game development, their low adoption highlights the need to investigate barriers to integration. The gap between proposed solutions and practical implementation remains a significant challenge.

title: A Synthetic Ground-Truth Framework for the Evaluation of Explainable AI Methods
summary: Evaluating explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods is a challenging task due to the lack of reliable evaluation procedures and, in particular, the absence of ground truth explanations. In the literature, existing evaluation approaches typically assess explanations by measuring their fidelity with respect to the predictions of a black-box model. However, such evaluation strategies only quantify the degree to which an explanation reproduces the model's output, without ensuring that the explanation correctly reflects the underlying decision process. As a consequence, different explanations may achieve similar fidelity scores while providing inconsistent or misleading interpretations of the model behavior. In this paper, we propose a framework for the evaluation of XAI methods based on synthetic ground truth. The proposed approach relies on controlled interventions to generate synthetic datasets in which the importance of input components can be determined by design. This enables the construction of ground truth explanations that are directly aligned with the behavior of the model under analysis. The framework is instantiated across three data domains, namely binary images, tabular data, and time series, allowing a comprehensive assessment of explanation methods in heterogeneous settings. Experimental results obtained by evaluating nine widely used XAI methods show significant limitations in current techniques and highlight the importance of synthetic, intervention-based benchmarks for a reliable assessment of explanation quality.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of evaluating explainable AI (XAI) methods by proposing a framework that uses synthetic ground truth through controlled interventions. Current evaluation methods only measure fidelity (how well explanations match model predictions) but fail to verify if explanations correctly reflect the actual decision process. The proposed framework generates synthetic datasets where input importance is known by design, enabling reliable ground truth for evaluation across three data domains (binary images, tabular data, and time series). Evaluation of nine XAI methods reveals significant limitations in current techniques.
AI.motivation: The lack of reliable evaluation procedures and absence of ground truth explanations in XAI. Existing approaches only assess fidelity (how well explanations reproduce model outputs) without ensuring explanations correctly reflect the underlying decision process. Different explanations can achieve similar fidelity scores while providing inconsistent or misleading interpretations.
AI.method: The proposed framework uses controlled interventions to generate synthetic datasets where the importance of input components can be determined by design. This creates ground truth explanations directly aligned with the model behavior. The framework is instantiated across three heterogeneous data domains: binary images, tabular data, and time series.
AI.result: Experimental results from evaluating nine widely used XAI methods show significant limitations in current techniques. The findings highlight the importance of synthetic, intervention-based benchmarks for reliable assessment of explanation quality.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that synthetic, intervention-based benchmarks are crucial for reliable XAI evaluation. Current XAI methods have significant limitations that can only be properly assessed through ground truth-based evaluation frameworks. The proposed framework provides a systematic approach for comprehensive assessment across heterogeneous settings.

title: Evaluating Code Recommender Systems: A Review
summary: Context: Code recommender systems (CRSs) are specialized software systems operating on source artifacts to provide automatically generated recommendations to software developers in all phases of development. The goal is to improve software quality while enhancing developers' efficiency, effectiveness, and experience. Problem: Despite the growing importance, little is known about the state of evaluating these systems in a human-centric manner. Research Approach: We conducted a systematic literature review to identify and to synthesize primary studies evaluating CRSs (2017-2024). Ninety-two publications were included and subjected to a systematic content analysis. Results: Our study confirms that Offline Evaluations are the most common, system-centric evaluation type, whereas user-centric evaluations (Online Evaluations, User Studies) are rarely reported. Evaluations are concentrated on the Software Construction phase. Most studies explicitly report threats to validity, with External threats to study Materials being the most common. Conclusion: The state of evaluations on CRSs is narrowly focused on single or a few system qualities. There is an imbalance between a majority of system-centric evaluations and a minority of user-centric evaluations. Combined, multi-type evaluations are rarely reported.

AI.tldr: A systematic literature review (2017-2024) examining how Code Recommender Systems (CRSs) are evaluated, analyzing 92 primary studies to assess the balance between system-centric and human-centric evaluation approaches.
AI.motivation: Despite the growing importance of CRSs in software development, there is limited understanding of how these systems are evaluated in terms of human factors (developer experience, efficiency, effectiveness). The authors aim to address this gap by systematically reviewing the evaluation practices in this field.
AI.method: Systematic literature review methodology: identified and synthesized 92 primary studies evaluating CRSs published between 2017-2024. Applied systematic content analysis to categorize evaluation types and examine evaluation focus.
AI.result: Offline (system-centric) evaluations dominate the literature, while user-centric evaluations (Online Evaluations, User Studies) are rarely reported. Evaluations concentrate on the Software Construction phase. Most studies report threats to validity, with External threats to study Materials being most common.
AI.conclusion: The evaluation landscape for CRSs is narrowly focused on single or few system qualities. There exists a significant imbalance: system-centric evaluations dominate while user-centric evaluations are underrepresented. Combined multi-type evaluations are rarely conducted, indicating a need for more holistic, human-centric evaluation approaches.

title: Predicting Transmembrane Protein Topology from 3D Structure
summary: This paper presents a novel approach to infer protein topology using the state-of-the-art graph neural network (GNN), SchNet. The model is trained on the same dataset used to develop the recent DeepTMHMM model with 5-fold cross-validation. Unlike the conventional approaches based on using only the protein sequences or the $α$-carbons as features, we have decoded our classifier in this way, so all atom-level embeddings are used. Without applying any pre-trained weight, the final results have shown great potential that GNNs can be used for topological predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using SchNet, a graph neural network, for protein topology prediction. Unlike traditional methods that use only protein sequences or α-carbon coordinates, this approach leverages all atom-level embeddings. The model was trained on the DeepTMHMM dataset with 5-fold cross-validation, demonstrating the potential of GNNs for protein topology prediction without pre-trained weights.
AI.motivation: Current protein topology prediction methods typically rely on either protein sequences alone or simplified representations like α-carbons. This paper aims to explore whether graph neural networks can effectively utilize full atom-level information to improve topology predictions, which is a novel approach in this domain.
AI.method: The researchers used SchNet, a state-of-the-art graph neural network architecture, trained on the same dataset as DeepTMHMM. They employed 5-fold cross-validation for model evaluation. The key innovation is using all atom-level embeddings rather than sequence-only or α-carbon-only features, allowing the model to capture richer structural information.
AI.result: The model demonstrates promising performance for protein topology prediction using GNNs, even without applying any pre-trained weights. The results show that atom-level embeddings can be effectively utilized for topological predictions.
AI.conclusion: Graph neural networks, particularly SchNet, show great potential for protein topology prediction tasks. The approach of using all atom-level embeddings proves viable, suggesting GNNs could be a valuable tool in computational biology for protein structure prediction.

title: Closing the Loop: Continuous Measurement-Driven Refinement of Offloading Predictions
comment: computation offloading, measurement-driven feedback, multi-metric prediction
summary: Modern vehicles increasingly offload computation- ally intensive perception and decision functions to backend servers, requiring accurate predictions of absolute performance metrics such as Round-Trip Time (RTT), processing time, and utilization. In practice, strong temporal variability, heterogeneous backend hardware, and multimodal latency regimes cause offline- trained predictors to drift, creating a reliability gap for latency- sensitive functions. We address this gap with an operational, measurement-driven closed loop that continuously recalibrates absolute-value predictors during runtime. The system aligns real execution measurements with predicted values and performs incremental online updates of a lightweight multi-head neural network while preserving model stability. The model implicitly learns the broad, non-Gaussian spread of input metrics, and a sigma-based error analysis in our evaluation characterizes resid- ual variability under dynamic conditions. Experiments across two Kubernetes clusters show that continuous measurement- driven refinement reduces prediction drift, improves accuracy for RTT, processing time, and utilization, and stabilizes prediction behavior across heterogeneous latency regimes. However, the broad and multimodal distribution of input metrics imposes fundamental limits on absolute-value prediction, with residual errors frequently exceeding configured thresholds. Overall, online calibration proves feasible and necessary for robust computation offloading in dynamic vehicular edge environments, while high- lighting the need for future mechanisms that address extreme latency regimes and high-variance operating conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of maintaining accurate performance predictions for vehicle-to-edge computation offloading in dynamic environments. The authors propose a measurement-driven closed-loop system that continuously recalibrates absolute-value predictors (RTT, processing time, utilization) during runtime using incremental online updates of a lightweight multi-head neural network.
AI.motivation: Modern vehicles offload computationally intensive perception and decision functions to backend servers, but offline-trained predictors drift due to strong temporal variability, heterogeneous backend hardware, and multimodal latency regimes. This creates a reliability gap for latency-sensitive functions in vehicular edge environments.
AI.method: The proposed system uses a closed-loop approach that aligns real execution measurements with predicted values and performs incremental online updates of a lightweight multi-head neural network while preserving model stability. The model implicitly learns the broad, non-Gaussian spread of input metrics. A sigma-based error analysis characterizes residual variability under dynamic conditions. Evaluation was conducted across two Kubernetes clusters.
AI.result: Continuous measurement-driven refinement reduces prediction drift, improves accuracy for RTT, processing time, and utilization, and stabilizes prediction behavior across heterogeneous latency regimes. However, the broad and multimodal distribution of input metrics imposes fundamental limits on absolute-value prediction, with residual errors frequently exceeding configured thresholds.
AI.conclusion: Online calibration proves feasible and necessary for robust computation offloading in dynamic vehicular edge environments. Future work should address extreme latency regimes and high-variance operating conditions to further improve prediction reliability.

title: Spectral Feedback for Test-Time Alignment of Protein Diffusion Models
summary: Reward maximization alignment methods for discrete diffusion models have primarily focused on steering the reverse process, either by influencing token logits or by selecting favorable sequences at intermediate steps. These approaches largely treat inference as a unidirectional process, lacking mechanisms for revisiting undesirable token selections. We introduce Spectral Feedback, an algorithm that selects edit-positions in a feedback loop, allowing the model to iteratively correct its own generations. This approach leverages the mask structure of discrete diffusion models by re-masking and re-sampling tokens, analogous to image editing methods that reintroduce noisy latents and re-run the reverse process. While prior alignment methods focus on what token labels to assign to maximize a target reward, we instead treat which tokens to revisit as the central alignment problem. Selecting edit-positions is challenging because edit effects are interdependent: the impact of modifying one token depends on which others are edited simultaneously. We define an edit-set as a set of token positions to re-mask and re-sample. Motivated by prior work on sparse interactions in biological systems, we find empirically that edit-set value functions for protein inverse folding admit sparse Fourier representations. This structure enables Spectral Feedback to efficiently learn and optimize the value functions for edit-position selection. Spectral Feedback is model-agnostic and can be applied to pretrained, test-time aligned, and fine-tuned diffusion models. For all of these models, the algorithm improves alignment performance without modifying the underlying generative process. Applied to inverse folding with a protein stability reward oracle, it achieves a 32.3% increase in stable proteins for a pretrained model, 24.8% for Best-of-10, and 5.8% for a state-of-the-art RL fine-tuned diffusion model.

AI.tldr: Spectral Feedback is an algorithm for aligning discrete diffusion models that iteratively corrects generations by re-masking and re-sampling tokens at selected positions. Unlike prior methods that focus on token labels, it treats edit-position selection as the core alignment problem, using sparse Fourier representations to efficiently learn and optimize value functions for choosing which tokens to revisit.
AI.motivation: Current reward maximization alignment methods for discrete diffusion models treat inference as a unidirectional process and lack mechanisms for revisiting undesirable token selections. Existing approaches focus on what token labels to assign, but ignore the critical question of which tokens should be re-edited.
AI.method: The method introduces a feedback loop that selects edit-positions for re-masking and re-sampling tokens. It leverages the mask structure of discrete diffusion models (analogous to image editing methods). The key insight is that edit-set value functions for protein inverse folding admit sparse Fourier representations, enabling efficient optimization. The approach is model-agnostic and works with pretrained, test-time aligned, and fine-tuned diffusion models.
AI.result: Applied to inverse folding with protein stability reward oracle: 32.3% increase in stable proteins for pretrained model, 24.8% for Best-of-10, and 5.8% for state-of-the-art RL fine-tuned diffusion model.
AI.conclusion: Spectral Feedback provides a model-agnostic approach that improves alignment performance without modifying the underlying generative process. The sparse Fourier structure enables efficient learning and optimization of edit-position selection value functions.

title: EA-Ops: Git-Native Architecture as Code for Continuous Enterprise Architecture Governance
summary: Enterprise architecture (EA) repositories frequently separate architecture models from the engineering workflow used to change software and infrastructure. This article presents EA-Ops, an open-source Git-native Enterprise Architecture-as-Code framework that represents architecture facts as YAML, validates typed relationships against an ArchiMate 3.2 profile, enforces organization-specific governance rules, performs graph-based change-impact analysis, and publishes human-facing reports and a static interactive portal from the same reviewed source. We evaluate EA-Ops with a reproducible GitHub Actions harness. Eight independently injected structural, semantic, and governance fault classes were executed across 30 trials each; all 240 trials matched ground truth exactly, with precision, recall, and $F_1$ of 1.000. Scalability experiments with 30 measured repetitions reached 50,000 objects and 100,000 relationships: median validation time was 52.582~s, median impact traversal was 627.000~ms, and peak resident-set size was 919.2~MB. A ten-scenario Metroville digital-permit reference architecture produced exact validation outcomes and exact impact-set agreement with an independent breadth-first-search oracle in every scenario. The configured 100,000-object end-to-end benchmark generated its model successfully but exceeded the 180-minute CI budget during the performance stage; no timing result is extrapolated. At 50,000 objects, Markdown report generation rather than semantic validation is the dominant scaling bottleneck. The results support Git-native continuous governance as a practical EA operating model at tens-of-thousands-of-object scale while defining clear limits and optimization targets for larger repositories.

AI.tldr: EA-Ops is an open-source Git-native Enterprise Architecture-as-Code framework that represents architecture facts as YAML, validates typed relationships against an ArchiMate 3.2 profile, enforces governance rules, performs graph-based change-impact analysis, and publishes reports/portals from reviewed source. It achieves perfect precision, recall, and F1 scores (1.000) across 240 fault-injection trials and scales to 50,000 objects with 100,000 relationships.
AI.motivation: Enterprise architecture (EA) repositories frequently separate architecture models from the engineering workflow used to change software and infrastructure, creating a gap between architecture representation and actual engineering changes. This separation hinders continuous governance and traceability.
AI.method: The paper presents EA-Ops, which: (1) Represents architecture facts as YAML files; (2) Validates typed relationships against an ArchiMate 3.2 profile; (3) Enforces organization-specific governance rules; (4) Performs graph-based change-impact analysis; (5) Publishes human-facing reports and a static interactive portal from the same reviewed source. Evaluation used GitHub Actions with 8 fault classes (structural, semantic, governance) across 30 trials each, plus scalability experiments with 30 repetitions up to 50,000 objects and 100,000 relationships.
AI.result: All 240 trials matched ground truth exactly with precision, recall, and F1 of 1.000. At 50,000 objects: median validation time was 52.582s, median impact traversal was 627ms, peak RSS was 919.2MB. The Metroville reference architecture (10 scenarios) produced exact validation outcomes and exact impact-set agreement with a BFS oracle. The 100,000-object benchmark exceeded the 180-minute CI budget.
AI.conclusion: Git-native continuous governance is a practical EA operating model at tens-of-thousands-of-object scale. Clear limits and optimization targets are defined for larger repositories. At 50,000 objects, Markdown report generation (not semantic validation) becomes the dominant scaling bottleneck.

title: Pretrained ASR Pseudo-labeling for Noisy Police Audio
summary: Pretrained ASR systems perform poorly on noisy Broadcast Police Communication (BPC), hindering efforts to understand police decision-making. Pseudo-labeling offers an unsupervised path to improve ASR without expensive human labels, but the efficacy of this approach on very noisy domains is not known. In this work, we systematically assess the opportunities and limits of pseudo-labeling to adapt foundation ASR models (Whisper and Qwen3-ASR) to noisy BPC domain corpora from Baltimore and Chicago. We demonstrate that existing internal confidence metrics (log-probabilities and STAR scores) fail to distinguish between high and low quality BPC pseudo-labels, and we introduce an external LLM-as-a-judge filtering paradigm that leverages parametric knowledge to discard contextually implausible transcripts. Our LLM-judging filters more aggressively than internal metrics and significantly reduces WER of the pseudo-labeled training sets across the Baltimore and Chicago BPC corpora, though a substantial gap remains relative to an oracle filter. We also introduce a new cross-model pseudo-labeling paradigm where one model is finetuned with pseudo-labels from the other, and we identify this method as a promising direction for future pseudo-labeling work.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of adapting pretrained ASR systems (Whisper and Qwen3-ASR) to noisy Broadcast Police Communication (BPC) domains using pseudo-labeling, introducing LLM-as-a-judge filtering to replace failing internal confidence metrics.
AI.motivation: Pretrained ASR systems perform poorly on noisy BPC data, hindering understanding of police decision-making. Pseudo-labeling offers an unsupervised adaptation path, but its efficacy on very noisy domains was unknown.
AI.method: Systematic assessment of pseudo-labeling for ASR adaptation on Baltimore and Chicago BPC corpora. Introduced LLM-as-a-judge filtering using parametric knowledge to filter contextually implausible transcripts. Also proposed cross-model pseudo-labeling where one model is finetuned with pseudo-labels from another.
AI.result: Internal confidence metrics (log-probabilities and STAR scores) failed to distinguish between high and low quality BPC pseudo-labels. LLM-judging filtered more aggressively than internal metrics and significantly reduced WER of pseudo-labeled training sets across both corpora, though a substantial gap remained relative to an oracle filter.
AI.conclusion: LLM-as-a-judge filtering is effective for pseudo-label quality control in noisy BPC domains. Cross-model pseudo-labeling is identified as a promising direction for future work. The approach significantly improves ASR performance on noisy police communications.

title: A Framework for Identifying, Categorizing, and Explaining Bias in AI-Generated Code
summary:
As Large Language Models (LLMs) become integrated into software development workflows, concerns regarding unintentional biases in AI-generated code. Although evidence suggests these biases exist, limited research has systematically identified, categorized, and explained them. This study investigates bias in AI-generated code and evaluates whether LLMs can reliably identify and explain it through a taxonomy-driven framework. We extended an existing dataset of biased AI-generated Python code and manually annotated snippets with bias categories and human-authored justifications to establish a ground-truth dataset. Using this dataset, we evaluated proprietary and open-source LLMs as automated bias detection and justification systems through ICL. Finally, we analyzed similarity between LLM-generated explanations and human-authored justifications using structured justification and code identification metrics.
  Our findings demonstrate that LLMs can effectively support code bias identification and explanation. Gemini achieved 80.14% classification accuracy, with 84.0% precision and 95.7% recall, while the best open-source alternative, Qwen3-coder, achieved 82.45% accuracy, 68.64% precision, and 80.22% recall. Additionally, the models achieved justification similarity scores of 80.4% and 80.14%, respectively, relative to human-authored reasoning, and code identification similarity scores of 86.0% and 87.82%. These results suggest that LLMs can detect biased logic in generated Python code and produce explanations that substantially align with expert interpretations.

AI.tldr: This study investigates bias in AI-generated code and evaluates whether LLMs can reliably identify and explain it through a taxonomy-driven framework. The research extends an existing dataset of biased AI-generated Python code, manually annotating snippets with bias categories and human-authored justifications. Evaluation of proprietary and open-source LLMs shows Gemini achieved 80.14% accuracy (84.0% precision, 95.7% recall) while Qwen3-coder achieved 82.45% accuracy (68.64% precision, 80.22% recall), with justification similarity scores around 80% and code identification similarity scores around 86-88%.
AI.motivation: As LLMs become integrated into software development workflows, concerns regarding unintentional biases in AI-generated code have emerged. Although evidence suggests these biases exist, limited research has systematically identified, categorized, and explained them. This study aims to address this gap by developing a taxonomy-driven framework for bias detection and explanation.
AI.method: The researchers extended an existing dataset of biased AI-generated Python code and manually annotated code snippets with bias categories and human-authored justifications to establish a ground-truth dataset. They then evaluated proprietary and open-source LLMs as automated bias detection and justification systems through In-Context Learning (ICL). Finally, they analyzed similarity between LLM-generated explanations and human-authored justifications using structured justification and code identification metrics.
AI.result: Gemini achieved 80.14% classification accuracy, with 84.0% precision and 95.7% recall. The best open-source alternative, Qwen3-coder, achieved 82.45% accuracy, 68.64% precision, and 80.22% recall. Regarding justification similarity to human-authored reasoning, the models achieved 80.4% and 80.14% respectively. Code identification similarity scores were 86.0% and 87.82% respectively.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively support code bias identification and explanation. They can detect biased logic in generated Python code and produce explanations that substantially align with expert interpretations, though performance varies between proprietary and open-source models.

title: Do LLMs Understand Context? A Knowledge Graph-Based Evaluation Framework
summary: While large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable linguistic capabilities, a profound question lingers at their core: do these models truly comprehend context or simply excel at pattern matching on an unprecedented scale? Contextual understanding in LLMs refers to the ability to correctly extract relevant information from a given context, integrate it into a coherent internal representation, and reason over it to produce factually consistent and contextually grounded responses. However, traditional methods such as BiLingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) and perplexity simply measure surface-level performance. This reveals a critical gap in question answering (QA), where responses must be contextually grounded rather than simply being memorized associations. To fill this void, we propose a novel knowledge graph (KG) based evaluation framework for LLM contextual understanding in QA. Central to this is Semantic Structural Similarity for KGs (S3KG), a hybrid similarity measure combining structural and semantic signals into a single score. In addition, a diagnostic analysis framework is developed to identify and categorize reasoning errors at the triplet level, enabling fine-grained analysis of model failures. Together, across nine benchmarks, S3KG achieves F1 gains of up to $+7.6$ points over the strongest baseline and AUROC up to $0.973$.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses a critical gap in evaluating LLM contextual understanding by proposing a knowledge graph-based evaluation framework (S3KG) that combines structural and semantic signals to assess whether LLMs truly comprehend context or merely perform pattern matching in QA tasks.
AI.motivation: Traditional evaluation metrics like BLEU and perplexity only measure surface-level performance, failing to assess whether LLM responses are contextually grounded rather than memorized associations. This limits proper evaluation of contextual understanding in question answering.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) A novel KG-based evaluation framework for LLM contextual understanding in QA, featuring Semantic Structural Similarity for KGs (S3KG) - a hybrid similarity measure combining structural and semantic signals into a single score; (2) A diagnostic analysis framework for identifying and categorizing reasoning errors at the triplet level.
AI.result: Across nine benchmarks, S3KG achieves F1 gains of up to +7.6 points over the strongest baseline and AUROC up to 0.973.
AI.conclusion: The proposed S3KG framework provides a more effective way to evaluate LLM contextual understanding in QA by leveraging knowledge graph representations to capture both structural and semantic relationships, enabling fine-grained analysis of model reasoning errors.

title: Developing a Roadmap to an AI-first Organization: A Case Study in Embedded Software Development
summary: The emergence of AI agents is expected to reshape software engineering by moving beyond AI as assistants towards systems capable of planning, executing, and evaluating development tasks with increasing autonomy. This transition is particularly significant for embedded software organizations, where strict requirements for quality, traceability, verification, and long-term maintainability often apply. This paper presents a case study of a large embedded systems company and its transition toward becoming an AI-first organization. Through a mixed method, we analyzed data collected from a semi-structured workshop with 40 participants, including scrum masters, architects, management, and product owners. The findings show that the participants expect agentic AI to affect team structure, required competencies, organizational strategies, and developers' roles within the organization. Based on these findings, the paper discusses implications for federated AI team formation, human-in-the-loop practices in such an organization, and the sustainable adoption of AI agents in embedded software engineering. We also present a concrete roadmap for the organization towards becoming an AI-first organization.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a case study of a large embedded systems company transitioning toward becoming an AI-first organization, examining how agentic AI is expected to impact team structure, competencies, organizational strategies, and developer roles, with findings from a workshop of 40 participants and a roadmap for adoption.
AI.motivation: The emergence of AI agents is reshaping software engineering from AI as assistants toward autonomous systems capable of planning, executing, and evaluating development tasks. This transition is particularly significant for embedded software organizations with strict requirements for quality, traceability, verification, and maintainability.
AI.method: Mixed-method case study of a large embedded systems company. Data collected from a semi-structured workshop with 40 participants (scrum masters, architects, management, and product owners).
AI.result: Participants expect agentic AI to affect: (1) team structure, (2) required competencies, (3) organizational strategies, and (4) developers' roles. The paper provides implications for federated AI team formation, human-in-the-loop practices, and sustainable adoption of AI agents in embedded software engineering. A concrete roadmap for becoming an AI-first organization is presented.
AI.conclusion: The transition to AI-first in embedded software engineering requires careful consideration of organizational structures, human-AI collaboration models, and sustainable adoption strategies tailored to the domain's strict quality and verification requirements.

title: BioEVAL: A global, multi-institutional benchmark of large language and multimodal models for bioengineering
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated historic breakthroughs in general reasoning with early successes in biomedical science. However, existing LLM benchmarking emphasizes factual recall, offering limited insight into model performance on frontier and multimodal tasks. We assembled BioEVAL (BioEngineering Validation of AI and LLMs), a global, multi-institutional initiative designed to assess experimental reasoning capability across bioengineering (BE) subfields. BioEVAL spans 11 major BE subfields plus a set of uncategorized items, bringing together 22 research groups to create a PhD-level benchmark comprising 608 evaluation items: 1) 380 multiple-choice questions (MCQs, 359 retained after audit), 2) 218 literature synthesis tasks, and 3) 10 multimodal problems with experimental image interpretation. Benchmark items underwent authoring-group expert review and centralized quality control before evaluation. Following evaluation, a blinded cross-group consensus audit of the highest- and lowest-accuracy MCQ items flagged 21 questions for revision or removal; these were withheld, and all reported MCQ results are computed on the 359 retained items. We evaluated diverse cloud-scale foundation/multimodal models (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok) and locally deployable models suitable for inference on consumer-grade GPUs. Models achieved the highest accuracy of up to 90% on MCQs, similarity score of 0.72 on literature synthesis, and accuracy of 80% on a small sample of multimodal reasoning questions, with substantial performance variation across subfields. Leaderboard rankings characterize current capabilities, limitations, and development priorities across the evaluated BE task categories. BioEVAL is maintained as an extensible benchmark with standardized protocols for continuing expert item contribution and model evaluation.

AI.tldr: BioEVAL is a comprehensive benchmark assessing LLMs' experimental reasoning capabilities across 11 bioengineering subfields, comprising 608 evaluation items (380 MCQs, 218 literature synthesis tasks, 10 multimodal problems). The benchmark evaluated multiple cloud-scale and locally deployable models, with best performance reaching 90% accuracy on MCQs, 0.72 similarity on literature synthesis, and 80% on multimodal reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: While LLMs have shown success in biomedical science, existing benchmarks emphasize factual recall rather than evaluating frontier and multimodal tasks. This gap necessitates a benchmark that assesses experimental reasoning capabilities across diverse bioengineering subfields at a PhD-level difficulty.
AI.method: BioEVAL assembled 22 research groups to create a PhD-level benchmark with 608 evaluation items: 380 multiple-choice questions (359 retained after audit), 218 literature synthesis tasks, and 10 multimodal problems with experimental image interpretation. Items underwent expert review and quality control, with a blinded cross-group consensus audit flagging 21 questions for revision/removal. Diverse models including ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok were evaluated.
AI.result: Models achieved up to 90% accuracy on MCQs, similarity score of 0.72 on literature synthesis, and 80% accuracy on multimodal reasoning questions. Substantial performance variation was observed across subfields, with leaderboard rankings revealing capabilities, limitations, and development priorities.
AI.conclusion: BioEVAL provides the first comprehensive assessment of LLM capabilities in bioengineering experimental reasoning. It is maintained as an extensible benchmark with standardized protocols for continuing expert item contribution and model evaluation, serving as a valuable tool for identifying development priorities across BE task categories.

title: CoCoRerank: Towards Conventional Commit Message Generation by Component and Candidate Consistency Reranking
summary: Commit messages are essential for understanding software changes, yet automatic commit message generation typically treats a message as an unstructured text sequence. This limits its ability to support standardized development workflows, where commit messages are often expected to follow the Conventional Commits Specification (CCS) in the form type (scope): subject. In this paper, we study conventional commit message generation under the complete CCS format. We construct a new benchmark of 86,688 high-quality commits collected from open-source GitHub repositories, with each message normalized into type, scope, and subject through structural normalization and semantic quality filtering. Based on this benchmark, we propose a two-dimensional consistency-based reranking framework named CoCoRerank for LLM-based generation. CoCoRerank exploits horizontal consistency among the code change, type, scope, and subject, as well as vertical consensus across multiple generated candidates. Experiments with representative CMG baselines, LLM generators, reranking strategies, and ablation variants show that CoCoRerank improves both structural component prediction and subject generation quality. The results demonstrate that complete CCS supervision and multidimensional consistency modeling provide an effective foundation for accurate and standardized commit message generation. The artifact is publicly released at https://github.com/bluewhalebug/CoCoRerank.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses conventional commit message generation following the Complete Conventional Commits Specification (CCS) format (type: scope: subject). The authors create a benchmark of 86,688 high-quality commits and propose CoCoRerank, a two-dimensional consistency-based reranking framework that leverages horizontal consistency among code change components and vertical consensus across generated candidates.
AI.motivation: Current automatic commit message generation treats messages as unstructured text, but standardized development workflows require messages to follow the Conventional Commits Specification (CCS) in the form "type (scope): subject". This gap motivates the need for a system that can generate properly formatted conventional commit messages.
AI.method: The authors constructed a new benchmark of 86,688 high-quality commits from open-source GitHub repositories, with messages normalized into type, scope, and subject through structural normalization and semantic quality filtering. They proposed CoCoRerank, a two-dimensional consistency-based reranking framework for LLM-based generation that exploits: (1) horizontal consistency among code change, type, scope, and subject; and (2) vertical consensus across multiple generated candidates.
AI.result: Experiments with representative CMG baselines, LLM generators, reranking strategies, and ablation variants show that CoCoRerank improves both structural component prediction and subject generation quality. Complete CCS supervision and multidimensional consistency modeling provide an effective foundation for accurate and standardized commit message generation.
AI.conclusion: The complete CCS format supervision combined with multidimensional consistency modeling (horizontal and vertical) offers an effective approach for generating accurate and standardized commit messages. The artifact is publicly available at https://github.com/bluewhalebug/CoCoRerank.

title: Benchy: towards a universal language for task-oriented AI benchmarks
summary: Benchy is a semantic language and execution engine for benchmarking AI programs. A benchmark is completely specified by a program, a scoring function, and a dataset, B=(P,S,D), and is separate from the AI-system taking it; a run binds the two, R=(B,AI). Benchmarks are authored as canonical YAML in which each semantic concept has one valid syntax, classified by a shared task/domain/language ontology, and deterministically compiled into a canonical JSON intermediate representation that the engine executes. Compilation changes representation, not meaning: it does not repair invalid definitions or inject hidden defaults. Programs use fixed schemas of named input and output fields, the leaf output fields are the scoring dimensions, and the engine exposes one universal runtime contract --- a named-field input object in, a named-field output object out --- to which external AI-systems adapt at the boundary, so integration mechanics never propagate into benchmark semantics. This paper gives the semantic object model, the ontology and task-to-program validation rule, the scoring and failure semantics, the compilation and execution architecture, and the scope of the current language. An appendix fixes the normative engineering contract for the first engine implementation.

AI.tldr: Benchy is a semantic language and execution engine for benchmarking AI programs. It defines a benchmark as a tuple B=(P,S,D) where P is the program, S is the scoring function, and D is the dataset.
