Benchmarks are authored in canonical YAML and compiled to JSON IR for execution, with the engine providing a universal runtime contract (named-field input/output objects) to which external AI systems adapt at the boundary.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to create a standardized, deterministic benchmark specification system that separates benchmark semantics from AI system integration mechanics. Current benchmarks may have integration mechanics that propagate into benchmark semantics, making comparisons inconsistent. Benchy aims to fix this by providing a canonical representation where compilation changes representation but not meaning.
AI.method: The paper presents: (1) A semantic object model for benchmark specification, (2) A shared task/domain/language ontology with task-to-program validation rules, (3) Scoring and failure semantics, (4) Compilation and execution architecture translating YAML to canonical JSON IR, (5) A universal runtime contract exposing named-field input/output objects to external AI systems.
AI.result: The paper delivers a complete specification for the Benchy language including the semantic object model, ontology, validation rules, scoring/failure semantics, and execution architecture. An appendix provides the normative engineering contract for the first engine implementation.
AI.conclusion: Benchy provides a formal framework for creating deterministic, reproducible AI benchmarks with clear separation between benchmark semantics and AI system integration. The canonical YAML/JSON approach ensures consistency while the universal runtime contract enables external AI systems to adapt at the boundary without affecting benchmark definitions.

title: Rethinking Data Quality for AI-Driven Systems: Evidence from Practitioner Interviews
comment: This is a preprint version and the final version will appear in the proceedings of PROFES 2026
summary: Data quality research has usually treated data as an input that is stored, processed, and validated. In AI-driven software-intensive systems, data also shapes model behavior, evaluation, and lawful use. Empirical evidence remains limited on how practitioners define, assess, and manage quality under these conditions. We interviewed 16 practitioners from nine organizations and analyzed the transcripts using reflexive thematic analysis and developed six themes from participants' accounts. In AI systems, traceability shifted from modular debugging to attributing model behavior, while using models as quality assessors introduced circularity. Agent context and memory became data objects, and synthetic and pseudo-labeled data made authenticity a quality concern. In foundation-model development, lawfulness became a gate for training data, while representativeness was judged through coverage of situations in which the system must behave safely. Prior ML research examines many of these problems separately. Our study provides a practitioner-grounded account of how they are encountered together as an engineering and organizational concern. We also interpret five recurring conditions as helping explain how the themes relate to reduced trust in data and AI outcomes. We synthesize these findings through lifecycle assurance: a conceptual framing focused on producing evidence that data can support a specific AI claim when its influence may be embedded in model behavior, model-based judgments, or agent actions.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how practitioners define, assess, and manage data quality in AI-driven software-intensive systems through interviews with 16 practitioners from 9 organizations. Using reflexive thematic analysis, six themes emerged: traceability shifts to attributing model behavior; using models as quality assessors introduces circularity; agent context/memory become data objects; synthetic/pseudo-labeled data raises authenticity concerns; representativeness is judged by safety coverage; and lawfulness becomes a gate for training data. The study proposes "lifecycle assurance" as a conceptual framing for producing evidence that data can support AI claims when its influence is embedded in model behavior, judgments, or actions.
AI.motivation: Traditional data quality research treats data as stored, processed, and validated input. However, in AI-driven software-intensive systems, data also shapes model behavior, evaluation, and lawful use. Empirical evidence was limited on how practitioners define, assess, and manage quality under these conditions where data's role extends beyond storage to actively influencing AI outcomes.
AI.method: The researchers conducted semi-structured interviews with 16 practitioners from nine organizations across the AI/ML industry. They analyzed the interview transcripts using reflexive thematic analysis, a qualitative method that involves iterative coding and theme development to identify patterns in participants' accounts.
AI.result: Six themes emerged from the data: (1) Traceability shifted from modular debugging to attributing model behavior; (2) Using models as quality assessors introduced circularity; (3) Agent context and memory became data objects; (4) Synthetic and pseudo-labeled data made authenticity a quality concern; (5) In foundation-model development, lawfulness became a gate for training data; (6) Representativeness was judged through coverage of situations in which the system must behave safely. Five recurring conditions were identified that relate to reduced trust in data and AI outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a practitioner-grounded account of how data quality challenges are encountered together as an engineering and organizational concern in AI systems, rather than separately as prior ML research has examined. The researchers propose "lifecycle assurance" as a conceptual framing focused on producing evidence that data can support specific AI claims when its influence may be embedded in model behavior, model-based judgments, or agent actions.

title: Rank-Reliable Teacher-Guided Fitness Approximation for Expensive Evolutionary Optimization: A TinyML Architecture Search Study
summary: Expensive evolutionary search does not always need an exact fitness estimate for every candidate. It often needs a reliable answer to a simpler question: which candidate is better? We address this need through Teacher-Guided Learning NSGA-II (TGL-NSGA-II), a low-fidelity framework for constrained Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) neural architecture search. A pretrained teacher organizes samples into strata defined jointly by difficulty and class. Each candidate then undergoes KD-Lite, a short and capped knowledge-distillation procedure on a compact training set, before being scored on a separate stratified evaluation set. This teacher-guided score is fused with a Gaussian-process surrogate to select candidates for full evaluation. For a fixed candidate population, we analyse evaluation variance, score concentration, pairwise rank inversion, expected Kendall-$τ$, first-front identification, and hypervolume perturbation. We also derive a variance-aware fusion weight and a capacity-adaptive distillation rule. On keyword spotting and bird-call classification, the measured Kendall-$τ$ values are 0.74 and 0.62, exceeding the corresponding predicted lower bounds of 0.60 and 0.46. Joint stratification reduces proxy-score variance by 41% relative to random evaluation. Selective teacher mismatch, in contrast, increases differential bias and reduces Kendall-$τ$ to 0.41. Under a constrained evaluation budget, TGL-NSGA-II achieves the largest mean hypervolume and smallest generational distance on keyword spotting, records the lowest mean false-positive rate on BirdCLEF, and runs 2.2x faster than full NSGA-II. These guarantees apply to population-level low-fidelity evaluation and do not establish convergence of the complete evolutionary trajectory.

AI.tldr: TGL-NSGA-II is a low-fidelity framework for constrained TinyML neural architecture search that uses a pretrained teacher to organize samples into difficulty/class strata, applies short knowledge distillation (KD-Lite), and fuses teacher-guided scores with Gaussian-process surrogates to efficiently select candidates for full evaluation.
AI.motivation: Expensive evolutionary search for neural architecture search doesn't always need exact fitness estimates; it primarily needs reliable ranking of which candidate is better. This work addresses the need for efficient low-fidelity evaluation under constrained computational budgets.
AI.method: 1) Pretrained teacher organizes samples into strata defined by difficulty and class; 2) Each candidate undergoes KD-Lite (short, capped knowledge distillation on compact training set); 3) Candidates scored on separate stratified evaluation set; 4) Teacher-guided score fused with Gaussian-process surrogate for candidate selection; 5) Derivation of variance-aware fusion weight and capacity-adaptive distillation rule.
AI.result: Kendall-τ values of 0.74 (keyword spotting) and 0.62 (bird-call classification) exceed predicted lower bounds (0.60, 0.46). Joint stratification reduces proxy-score variance by 41% vs random evaluation. Selective teacher mismatch increases differential bias, reducing Kendall-τ to 0.41. Under constrained budget: largest mean hypervolume and smallest generational distance on keyword spotting; lowest mean false-positive rate on BirdCLEF; runs 2.2x faster than full NSGA-II.
AI.conclusion: TGL-NSGA-II provides population-level low-fidelity evaluation guarantees for evolutionary search, achieving significant speedup (2.2x) while maintaining ranking quality. The method excels under constrained evaluation budgets, though these guarantees apply to population-level evaluation rather than complete evolutionary trajectory convergence.

title: Joule-Profiler: Profiling the Energy Consumption of Build Automation Tools Made Easy
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures. Submitted to the ICSE 2027 Tool Demonstration and Data Showcase Track
summary: Build pipelines are integral to modern software development, yet their energy footprint remains largely invisible to practitioners. Existing CI energy tools either rely on model-based estimation (due to hardware access restrictions in cloud runners) or report only total pipeline energy without decomposing it into meaningful phases. Joule-Profiler is an open-source command-line tool for Linux that measures hardware energy consumption via Intel RAPL (CPU), NVML (NVIDIA GPU), and attributes it to user-defined program phases by monitoring standard output. In this tool paper, we demonstrate Joule-Profiler in the context of Maven build pipelines using Google Gson as a case study. By applying a token pattern-matching Maven plugin invocations, we analyze builds across the 5 most recent Gson releases into per-phase energy profiles, comparing cold builds (empty local repository) and warm builds (cached dependencies).

AI.tldr: Joule-Profiler is an open-source CLI tool for Linux that measures hardware energy consumption (CPU via Intel RAPL, GPU via NVML) and attributes it to user-defined program phases by monitoring standard output. The tool is demonstrated with Maven build pipelines using Google Gson as a case study, analyzing builds across 5 recent releases with comparison between cold and warm builds.
AI.motivation: Build pipelines have significant energy footprint that remains invisible to practitioners. Existing CI energy tools either rely on model-based estimation (due to hardware access restrictions in cloud runners) or only report total pipeline energy without decomposing it into meaningful phases. There is a need for a tool that can provide fine-grained, hardware-based energy measurement attributed to specific build phases.
AI.method: Joule-Profiler uses hardware energy measurement via Intel RAPL for CPU and NVML for NVIDIA GPU. It monitors standard output and applies token pattern-matching to identify Maven plugin invocations, enabling per-phase energy attribution. The case study analyzes Maven builds across 5 most recent Gson releases, comparing cold builds (empty local repository) versus warm builds (cached dependencies).
AI.result: The abstract indicates the tool provides per-phase energy profiles for Maven build pipelines, enabling comparison between cold and warm builds across multiple Gson releases.
AI.conclusion: Joule-Profiler fills a gap in CI energy measurement by providing hardware-based, phase-level energy profiling for Linux build pipelines, making the energy footprint of software builds visible and actionable for practitioners.

title: Thinking Less to Simulate Better: Intuitive Prompting Improves LLM Agents Simulating Individual Social Media Reactions, Including Unfamiliar Content
summary: Platform policies are increasingly tested on artificial users, making agent fidelity important. Yet convincing fake profiles could also manipulate perceived public opinion before elections. Validation has concentrated on agreement with human behaviour and has paid little attention to whether an agent behaves in line with the profile it was given. The present study profiled eight Serbian participants through a questionnaire, a deep interview, and a written self-presentation, recorded their reactions to sixty-eight social media posts, and asked four language models to predict those reactions under five prompt conditions varying profile content and instruction style. Attitudinal content improved prediction over demographic backstories by a wide margin. Agents matched their stated profiles more closely than participants matched their own survey answers, and consistency proved unrelated to fidelity once profile information was present. Instructing models to respond intuitively and immediately rather than analytically gave the highest fidelity of any condition and cut the compression of individual differences from seven times the human level to three. The advantage held on posts about topics the questionnaire never raised, where that condition reached the highest fidelity of any setup and beat a crowd baseline by a wide margin, which suggests that agents prompted this way could serve as general-purpose simulated users rather than specialists on the topics they were profiled for. Results may bear implications for the development of language models, because intuition-based setups appear better suited to some tasks than reasoning-based ones.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether language model agents can accurately simulate human users on social media, and which prompting strategies produce the most faithful simulations. It profiles 8 Serbian participants and tests 4 language models under 5 different prompt conditions to predict their reactions to 68 social media posts.
AI.motivation: Platform policies are increasingly tested on artificial users, but validation has focused on agreement with human behavior rather than whether agents behave consistently with their given profiles. Additionally, there's concern that convincing fake profiles could manipulate perceived public opinion before elections.
AI.method: Researchers profiled eight Serbian participants through questionnaire, deep interview, and written self-presentation. They recorded participants' reactions to 68 social media posts, then asked four language models to predict those reactions under five prompt conditions varying profile content (demographic vs. attitudinal) and instruction style (intuitive/immediate vs. analytical).
AI.result: Attitudinal content improved prediction over demographic backstories by a wide margin. Agents matched their stated profiles more closely than participants matched their own survey answers. Instructing models to respond intuitively and immediately rather than analytically gave the highest fidelity, reducing compression of individual differences from 7x to 3x human level. This advantage held on posts about topics never covered in the questionnaire, beating crowd baseline.
AI.conclusion: Intuition-based prompting appears better suited for simulating general-purpose users than reasoning-based approaches. Agents prompted intuitively could serve as general-purpose simulated users rather than specialists on profiled topics. Results have implications for language model development, suggesting intuition-based setups may be superior for certain tasks.

title: Parameters vs. Context: TRACE Fine-Tuning for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates knowledge obsolescence and factual hallucination in large language models by introducing external context. However, when retrieved knowledge conflicts with the model's internal parametric knowledge, the model may either blindly follow misleading context or incorrectly rely on parametric knowledge, leading to unreliable responses. To address this issue, this paper proposes TRACE (Debate-TRace and Answer-Completeness rEgularized fine-tuning), a robust fine-tuning framework for RAG under knowledge conflicts. First, we propose a fine-tuning method that leverages multi-agent debate traces to extract correct candidates, incorrect candidates, and answer-shift patterns, providing fine-grained supervision for reliable knowledge-source selection. In addition, we design an answer completeness regularization mechanism to alleviate empty, overly short, and prematurely terminated responses via answer-tail token reinforcement and premature termination suppression. The fine-tuning objective combines correct-answer supervision, incorrect-candidate suppression, answer-tail token reinforcement, and premature termination suppression, enabling the model to use reliable external context, resist misleading or irrelevant retrieved content, and fall back to parametric knowledge when retrieved evidence is unreliable. Experiments across multiple knowledge-conflict scenarios and datasets show that TRACE improves robustness against misleading retrieved knowledge and reduces incomplete answers. These results demonstrate that multi-agent debate traces and answer completeness regularization jointly enhance knowledge-source selection, conflict robustness, and answer quality in RAG models. Our code is available at https://github.com/PHD-lanyu/TRACE.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a fine-tuning framework for RAG systems that addresses knowledge conflicts between retrieved external context and model's internal parametric knowledge. It uses multi-agent debate traces for supervision and answer completeness regularization to improve reliability and response quality.
AI.motivation: When RAG systems encounter knowledge conflicts between retrieved context and parametric knowledge, models may either follow misleading context or incorrectly rely on parametric knowledge, leading to unreliable responses. Existing methods lack effective mechanisms to handle such conflicts and ensure answer completeness.
AI.method: 1) Multi-agent debate traces to extract correct candidates, incorrect candidates, and answer-shift patterns for fine-grained supervision; 2) Answer completeness regularization via answer-tail token reinforcement and premature termination suppression; 3) Combined fine-tuning objective with correct-answer supervision, incorrect-candidate suppression, answer-tail token reinforcement, and premature termination suppression.
AI.result: TRACE improves robustness against misleading retrieved knowledge and reduces incomplete answers across multiple knowledge-conflict scenarios and datasets.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent debate traces and answer completeness regularization jointly enhance knowledge-source selection, conflict robustness, and answer quality in RAG models.

title: Semi-Automatic Quantification of Bayesian Networks for Software Decision Support: Comparing WSA and RNM in a Software R&D Organization
comment: Submitted to Journal of Systems and Software
summary: Expert-driven Bayesian networks can support recurring software decisions when historical data are limited, but quantifying their conditional probability tables (CPTs) requires many probability judgments. Semi-automatic methods reduce direct elicitation, yet practitioners have little comparative evidence from operational decision processes. We report an embedded case study comparing the Weighted Sum Algorithm (WSA) and Ranked Nodes Method (RNM) as complete elicitation-and-quantification pipelines in two contexts within a single software research and development (R&D) organization: feature selection for Internet of Things projects and user interface design selection. Within each context, the pipelines shared the graph, root priors, and decision evidence. We evaluated them through 15 expert-defined model-walkthrough scenarios and retrospective reconstructions of alternatives recorded in decision meetings. WSA matched 7/7 and 6/8 walkthrough expectations, whereas RNM matched 4/7 and 4/8. Both pipelines placed the selected alternatives near the top of the retrospective rankings. Their complete distributions nevertheless differed: the median total variation distance was 0.304 across four distinct feature patterns and 0.340 across seven distinct design patterns, rising to 0.890 for one design pattern. These results concern two ordinal value-estimation models in one organization. They show that similar shortlist behavior does not imply equivalent representations of uncertainty. For comparable software decision-support models, method selection and validation should consider node semantics, the judgments experts can provide, calibration requirements, complete output distributions, and the intended downstream use of the probabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper compares two Bayesian network quantification methods (Weighted Sum Algorithm and Ranked Nodes Method) in a software R&D organization for decision support. The study finds that while both methods produce similar top-ranked alternatives, their complete probability distributions differ substantially (median distance ~0.3-0.34), demonstrating that similar decision outcomes do not imply equivalent uncertainty representations.
AI.motivation: Expert-driven Bayesian networks can support software decisions when historical data is limited, but quantifying conditional probability tables requires extensive expert judgments. While semi-automatic methods exist to reduce elicitation burden, practitioners lack comparative evidence from operational decision processes about which method performs better in practice.
AI.method: Embedded case study in a single software R&D organization comparing WSA and RNM as complete elicitation-and-quantification pipelines across two contexts: IoT feature selection and UI design selection. Both pipelines shared the same graph, root priors, and decision evidence. Evaluation used 15 expert-defined model-walkthrough scenarios and retrospective reconstructions of alternatives from decision meetings.
AI.result: WSA matched 7/7 and 6/8 walkthrough expectations, outperforming RNM (4/7 and 4/8). Both pipelines placed selected alternatives near the top of retrospective rankings. However, their complete distributions differed significantly: median total variation distance was 0.304 across four feature patterns and 0.340 across seven design patterns, rising to 0.890 for one design pattern.
AI.conclusion: Similar shortlist behavior does not imply equivalent representations of uncertainty. For comparable software decision-support models, method selection should consider node semantics, the judgments experts can provide, calibration requirements, complete output distributions, and intended downstream use of probabilities. The study is limited to two ordinal value-estimation models in one organization.

title: Atelier: Learning Local Self-Supervised Features for CryoEM Volumes via Hypernetworks
summary: CryoEM map interpretation requires features that are spatially localized, consistent across samples, and informative across spatial scales. Most deep learning methods for map annotation extract features from fixed voxel grids. However, implicit neural representations (INRs) are able to model volumetric data as scale-agnostic, coordinate-conditioned functions. INRs are therefore attractive for cryoEM, but fitting a separate INR for each map is too expensive for large-scale feature extraction and produces representations that are not aligned across samples. We introduce Atelier, a self-supervised framework that amortizes INR fitting for reconstructed cryoEM maps. Pretrained on 5,439 Electron Microscopy Data Bank maps, Atelier is a transformer-based hypernetwork that generates high-fidelity reconstructions across a wide range of protein structures, including large multi-subunit assemblies. Beyond reconstruction, the INR generated by the pretrained transformer exposes a continuous, local feature field through its intermediate activations at any spatial query point, a property that voxel grid and patch-tokenizer architectures do not naturally provide. Used as auxiliary channels to a 3D nested U-Net annotation head trained from scratch, these coordinate-conditioned features improve performance on eight voxel-level property prediction tasks over a volume-only baseline. Our results demonstrate that amortized implicit neural representations are an effective primitive for geometry-aware analysis of cryoEM data.

AI.tldr: Atelier is a self-supervised framework that uses a transformer-based hypernetwork to amortize implicit neural representation (INR) fitting for cryoEM maps, enabling high-fidelity reconstructions and extracting coordinate-conditioned features that improve voxel-level property prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: CryoEM map interpretation requires spatially localized, consistent, and informative features across scales. Existing deep learning methods use fixed voxel grids, while individual INR fitting is too expensive for large-scale analysis and produces unaligned representations across samples.
AI.method: Transformer-based hypernetwork pretrained on 5,439 EMDB maps; generates INRs that expose continuous, local feature fields through intermediate activations; used as auxiliary channels to 3D nested U-Net annotation head.
AI.result: Achieves high-fidelity reconstructions across diverse protein structures including large multi-subunit assemblies; improves performance on eight voxel-level property prediction tasks over volume-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Amortized implicit neural representations are an effective primitive for geometry-aware analysis of cryoEM data, providing scale-agnostic, coordinate-conditioned features that enhance downstream annotation tasks.

title: When the Model Retires: An Empirical Study of LLM Migration in Open-Source Applications
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Dataset and scripts to be released on Zenodo
summary: Applications built on commercial large language model (LLM) APIs depend on model versions that providers retire on their own schedule, with notice periods ranging from one year to two weeks. We ask what actually happens to applications when a model is retired. We mine GitHub for commits that migrate away from officially deprecated models and endpoints of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, matching each commit to the provider's published announcement and shutdown dates. From 22,555 commits in 17,703 non-fork repositories (2024-2026), 5,139 are matched to an official event; two independent coders validated a stratified sample of 300 (kappa = 0.89-0.95), and we reweight all estimates by their labels. We find that an estimated 82% (95% CI 79-84) of migrations away from retired models were committed after the shutdown date - after the application had started failing - regardless of repository popularity, prior retirement experience, or the presence of a provider-abstraction layer. The share tracks the provider's notice policy: 89% for Anthropic's 60-114-day notices versus 13% for OpenAI's one-year Assistants API notice, and each e-fold increase in notice length reduces the odds of post-shutdown migration by about three quarters. Model identifiers are hard-coded in 94% of migrating applications, migration effort scales from a median of 6 added lines for prompt-only applications to nearly 700 for fine-tuned ones, and only 8% of migrations switch provider. We release the dataset and pipeline and discuss implications for deprecation policy, dependency-risk assessment of LLM products, and tooling.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes GitHub commits to understand what happens when LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) retire model versions. The study finds that 82% of applications only migrate after the shutdown date (i.e., after the application has already started failing), with migration effort ranging from 6 lines for simple apps to 700 for fine-tuned models. Only 8% of migrations switch providers.
AI.motivation: Applications built on commercial LLM APIs depend on model versions that providers retire on their own schedule, with highly variable notice periods (from 2 weeks to 1 year). The authors wanted to understand the real-world impact of these retirements on applications.
AI.method: The authors mined GitHub for commits migrating away from deprecated OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google models/endpoints. From 22,555 commits in 17,703 non-fork repositories (2024-2026), they matched 5,139 to official deprecation events. Two independent coders validated a stratified sample of 300 (kappa = 0.89-0.95), with reweighted estimates.
AI.result: 82% (95% CI 79-84) of migrations occurred after the shutdown date—after applications had already started failing. This share correlates with provider notice policy: 89% for Anthropic's 60-114-day notices vs. 13% for OpenAI's 1-year Assistants API notice. Each e-fold increase in notice length reduces post-shutdown migration odds by ~75%. Model identifiers are hard-coded in 94% of apps. Migration effort ranges from a median of 6 added lines (prompt-only) to ~700 (fine-tuned). Only 8% of migrations switch providers.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals significant dependency risks in LLM-based applications. Most developers procrastinate migrations until after models fail, despite provider notice periods. The findings suggest need for: (1) better deprecation policies from providers, (2) improved dependency-risk assessment for LLM products, and (3) tooling to facilitate model migrations. The dataset and pipeline are released for further research.

title: HARDEN: Constrained Evolutionary Search for Harder, Answer-Preserving Evaluation Cases
summary: Language models are often evaluated on curated benchmarks that underrepresent the complexity of enterprise deployments. We introduce HARDEN, a constrained evolutionary search method to adapt the input of existing evaluation cases into more challenging variants while keeping their expected outputs fixed. HARDEN searches along generated domain-specific complexity axes while enforcing feasibility constraints such as preserving task semantics, realism, and execution validity. Across FinQA, PubMedQA, and ContractNLI and three Qwen3.5 model scales (35B-A3B, 122B-A10B, and 397B-A17B), HARDEN reduces task-model accuracy by 22.7% on average and by up to 49.9% relative to single-pass baselines using the same feasibility checks. These results show that evolutionary search can produce substantially harder valid evaluation cases.

AI.tldr: HARDEN is a constrained evolutionary search method that adapts existing evaluation cases into more challenging variants while preserving expected outputs. It searches along domain-specific complexity axes while enforcing feasibility constraints (task semantics, realism, execution validity).
AI.motivation: Current language model benchmarks underrepresent the complexity of enterprise deployments, creating a gap between evaluation and real-world performance.
AI.method: Constrained evolutionary search method that generates domain-specific complexity axes and enforces feasibility constraints including preserving task semantics, realism, and execution validity. Tested across FinQA, PubMedQA, and ContractNLI datasets with Qwen3.5 models (35B-A3B, 122B-A10B, 397B-A17B).
AI.result: HARDEN reduces task-model accuracy by 22.7% on average and by up to 49.9% relative to single-pass baselines using the same feasibility checks.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary search can produce substantially harder valid evaluation cases, revealing weaknesses in current benchmarks and providing more robust evaluation for enterprise deployment scenarios.

title: Beyond Approved Actions: Runtime Validation of Persistent Outcomes in Agent Workflows
comment: 22 pages including 7 pages of supplementary material. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
summary: Large language model agents increasingly act on software systems, no longer merely generating text but also changing databases and online services. However, an approved database update may succeed yet leave an unapproved notification because execution can produce persistent effects beyond the requested change. Current safeguards can approve an action or record its aftermath, but without checking the persistent result before continuation, an unapproved outcome can be accepted as success and propagated to later steps. We present EffectMatch, a runtime that collects persistent changes within a controlled execution boundary and compares them with what the application approved for the current state and execution. The comparison governs commit and dependent execution. In comparative evaluation on 206 public business tasks, EffectMatch preserved all clean executions and prevented all tested incorrect commits. Six 20-run ablations exposed the failure caused by each removed mechanism, while 80 task-topology cases preserved truthful handoffs and blocked invalid continuation. Together, these results show that EffectMatch blocks the silent acceptance and downstream propagation of persistent outcomes inconsistent with application approval.

AI.tldr: EffectMatch is a runtime system that prevents LLM agents from silently accepting persistent outcomes that differ from what was approved, by collecting and comparing actual persistent changes against approved expectations before committing and allowing continuation to dependent steps.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly modify software systems (databases, online services), but approved actions may succeed while producing additional unapproved persistent effects beyond the requested change. Current safeguards can approve actions or record aftermath but cannot verify the persistent result before continuation, allowing unapproved outcomes to be accepted and propagated to later steps.
AI.method: EffectMatch collects persistent changes within a controlled execution boundary and compares them with what the application approved for the current state and execution. This comparison governs both commit decisions and dependent execution continuation.
AI.result: On 206 public business tasks: EffectMatch preserved all clean executions and prevented all tested incorrect commits. Six 20-run ablations exposed the failure caused by each removed mechanism. 80 task-topology cases preserved truthful handoffs and blocked invalid continuation.
AI.conclusion: EffectMatch effectively blocks the silent acceptance and downstream propagation of persistent outcomes inconsistent with application approval, providing a practical safeguard for LLM agents operating on software systems.

title: T-RoPE: Time-Aware Rotary Position Embedding for Sequential Recommendation
summary: Large-scale recommenders increasingly adopt the sequential generative recipe behind large language models, bringing the Transformer into recommendation along with design choices made for text, including Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE). In language models, RoPE encodes token indices for relative position reasoning, but in recommendation, an interaction index records only event order, saying nothing about elapsed time, behavioral cycles across scales, or calendar phase. We revisit this choice and propose T-RoPE, a time-aware RoPE for sequential generative recommendation that replaces index-only rotation with timestamp-based angles, learnable temporal coefficients, multiscale frequency banks, shifted query alignment, and non-stationary key rotation. We prove that standard RoPE, even on timestamps, remains time-translation invariant and cannot distinguish seasonal contexts, and that T-RoPE breaks this invariance while preserving the RoPE interface. Across five public benchmarks, T-RoPE achieves the best result on every metric on every dataset, improving over the strongest baseline by 78--130\% in HR@10 on the sparse PixelRec data and 8--12\% across metrics on Amazon Books. On an industrial-scale e-commerce dataset with more than 6B interactions, it improves every metric over the HSTU + Time RAB backbone by 13--82\%, with ablations attributing the largest gains to multiscale frequencies ($+56\%$ NDCG@50) and non-stationary keys ($+4\%$). An online A/B test in the Shop app yields positive lifts in conversion rate ($+0.33\%$) and order count ($+0.63\%$). We also provide forward and backward algorithms whose added cost is linear in sequence length and head dimension, keeping time-aware RoPE practical for large generative recommenders.

AI.tldr: T-RoPE is a time-aware Rotary Position Embedding for sequential generative recommendation that replaces index-only position encoding with timestamp-based angles, learnable temporal coefficients, multiscale frequency banks, shifted query alignment, and non-stationary key rotation. It breaks the time-translation invariance of standard RoPE while preserving its interface, achieving state-of-the-art results across five public benchmarks and an industrial e-commerce dataset with 6B+ interactions.
AI.motivation: Large-scale recommenders adopt Transformer architecture with design choices from language models, including RoPE. However, RoPE encodes only interaction indices (event order) without considering elapsed time, behavioral cycles, or calendar phase. This limits the model's ability to capture time-dependent patterns like seasonality, which are critical for recommendation systems.
AI.method: T-RoPE introduces five key modifications to standard RoPE: (1) timestamp-based rotation angles instead of index-based positions, (2) learnable temporal coefficients for adaptive time encoding, (3) multiscale frequency banks to capture periodic patterns at different time scales, (4) shifted query alignment for better query-key interaction, and (5) non-stationary key rotation to handle time-varying user behavior. The method provides forward and backward algorithms with linear complexity in sequence length and head dimension.
AI.result: On five public benchmarks, T-RoPE achieves the best result on every metric on every dataset. Specific improvements include: 78-130% improvement in HR@10 on sparse PixelRec data, 8-12% improvement across metrics on Amazon Books. On an industrial e-commerce dataset with 6B+ interactions, it improves every metric over HSTU + Time RAB backbone by 13-82%. Ablations show multiscale frequencies contribute +56% NDCG@50 and non-stationary keys contribute +4%. Online A/B test in Shop app shows +0.33% conversion rate and +0.63% order count lifts.
AI.conclusion: T-RoPE successfully addresses the limitation of standard RoPE in capturing temporal information for recommendation. By breaking time-translation invariance while preserving the RoPE interface, it enables Transformers to leverage rich temporal signals. The method is theoretically grounded, empirically superior, and computationally practical for large-scale generative recommenders.

title: Compact Documentation for Coding Agents: A Benchmark, an Optimizer, and Why It Does Not Transfer
summary: We investigate whether natural-language documentation helps coding agents resolve software issues, and we build the tools to construct and evaluate it. We introduce a roundtrip benchmark that scores code descriptions by whether code regenerated from them passes the original tests, and show that completeness, not length, drives a description's fidelity. Using the benchmark as an optimization signal, we discover a description-writing prompt that reaches full fidelity and generalizes to unseen files. We then test the hypothesis that motivated the work: that better documentation helps an agent resolve real repository issues. Across two model families and ten repositories, and against a positive control confirming that our evaluation can detect a genuine improvement, we find that it does not. When the source is present, neither static compact documentation nor retrieved context beats the issue alone. We report this negative result together with the benchmark and the optimizer, and we characterize the boundary at which documentation helps.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether natural-language documentation helps coding agents resolve software issues. The authors create a roundtrip benchmark evaluating code descriptions by whether regenerated code passes original tests, discovering that completeness (not length) determines fidelity. Despite achieving full fidelity with an optimized prompt, they find a negative result: documentation does not help agents resolve real repository issues when source code is present.
AI.motivation: The hypothesis motivating this work is that better documentation should help coding agents resolve software issues more effectively. The researchers wanted to test this assumption empirically.
AI.method: The authors: (1) built a roundtrip benchmark scoring code descriptions by whether code regenerated from them passes original tests; (2) used this benchmark as an optimization signal to discover an effective description-writing prompt; (3) tested across two model families and ten repositories with a positive control to confirm evaluation validity.
AI.result: The benchmark achieved full fidelity and generalized to unseen files. However, the main hypothesis test yielded a negative result: documentation does not help agents resolve real repository issues. Neither static compact documentation nor retrieved context outperforms the issue alone when source code is present.
AI.conclusion: Documentation, even when optimized for completeness, does not improve coding agents' performance on resolving software issues when the source code is available. The authors characterize the boundary at which documentation might help (presumably when source is absent or insufficient).

title: Audio LLMs Know When They Can't Hear You
summary: Audio large language models allow users to interact with the model through speech. When an input recording is too degraded, the model may misinterpret the user's query and respond based on an incorrect transcription. In this paper, we study model-conditional transcription reliability: whether an Audio LLM can recognize when its own transcription is unreliable. We first prompt the Audio LLM to assess whether its own transcription would be reliable, and find that the model is a poor judge of its own transcription reliability: in most cases, it predicts that its transcription will be reliable. We find that existing approaches, including speech quality predictors, audio LLM generation uncertainty, and transcript-conditioned WER estimation, provide limited signals for detecting transcription failures. In contrast, we discover that transcription reliability is strongly represented in the model's audio-encoder representations. Based on this observation, we devise a lightweight reliability predictor that operates on representations extracted by the frozen audio encoder and predicts the reliability class before generation. The reliability predictor can trigger a clarification request from the user when their voice query is predicted to be unreliable, while allowing reliable queries to proceed without modifying the underlying Audio LLM. Our predictor achieves 81.10% in-domain and 78.09% cross-domain macro-F1 scores, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.33 and 11.93 points, respectively. Finally, we show that reliability labels can transfer across Audio LLM families, and that transfer performance is closely related to the alignment of their model-specific reliability boundaries.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses whether Audio LLMs can recognize when their own transcription is unreliable, and proposes a lightweight reliability predictor based on the model's audio-encoder representations that outperforms baselines by over 10 percentage points.
AI.motivation: When input audio is degraded, Audio LLMs may misinterpret user queries based on incorrect transcriptions, but the model itself cannot reliably assess its transcription quality.
AI.method: The authors first test whether Audio LLMs can self-assess transcription reliability via prompting. They then evaluate existing approaches (speech quality predictors, generation uncertainty, transcript-conditioned WER estimation) and discover that transcription reliability is strongly encoded in the model's audio-encoder representations. Based on this, they develop a lightweight reliability predictor using frozen audio encoder representations to predict reliability before generation.
AI.result: The proposed predictor achieves 81.10% in-domain and 78.09% cross-domain macro-F1 scores, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.33 and 11.93 points respectively. Reliability labels also transfer across Audio LLM families, with transfer performance correlated to alignment of model-specific reliability boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Audio LLM audio-encoder representations contain strong signals for transcription reliability detection. A lightweight predictor can be built on frozen encoder representations to trigger clarification requests for unreliable queries without modifying the underlying Audio LLM. Cross-model transfer is possible when reliability boundaries are aligned.

title: LLM Parkinsonism: Executive-Control Failure, Token-Inefficient Persistence, and an Uncertainty-Aware Global Executive Control Architecture for Autonomous Language-Model Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can plan, use tools, write code, and execute long-horizon workflows, yet strong local competence does not guarantee project-level executive control. Agents may continue acting after the original objective is satisfied, producing low-value refinements, repeated verification, and repairs to self-created complexity. We use LLM Parkinsonism as a narrowly defined, non-clinical metaphor for this pattern of persistent action despite diminishing task-level value. We argue that the problem is not explained by autoregressive next-token prediction alone, but more directly by concentrating proposal generation, scope interpretation, progress assessment, and stopping authority within the same self-conditioned loop. We therefore introduce Global Executive Control (GEC) v0.2, an uncertainty-aware governance architecture that separates action generation from project-level control. In a 24,000-episode matched-candidate benchmark under a common 40,000-token ceiling, a first-candidate baseline achieved 67.42% hard-goal success, a candidate-set local control achieved 96.53%, and GEC achieved 96.57%. The candidate-set control shows that access to multiple candidate actions explains most of the success gain; relative to that control, GEC preserved success while reducing mean token use from 19,782 to 12,574 (36.4%) and restricted mean tokens to completion at the 40,000-token ceiling from 16,136 to 13,114 (18.7%), while eliminating measured pre-completion drift and sharply reducing gross complexity. Governance-overhead sensitivity remained favorable through an additional 500 synthetic governance tokens per cycle. These mechanistic simulations support explicit governance of scope, evidence, resource use, and stopping, while live-model validation remains necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "LLM Parkinsonism" as a metaphor for LLMs persisting with low-value actions after objectives are met, and proposes Global Executive Control (GEC) v0.2, an architecture that separates action generation from project-level governance. GEC achieved 96.57% success rate while reducing token use by 36.4% compared to candidate-set local control.
AI.motivation: LLMs can execute long-horizon workflows but often continue acting after objectives are satisfied, producing low-value refinements and self-created complexity. This pattern is termed "LLM Parkinsonism" - a non-clinical metaphor for persistent action despite diminishing task-level value.
AI.method: The authors propose Global Executive Control (GEC) v0.2, an uncertainty-aware governance architecture that separates action generation from project-level control. They conducted a 24,000-episode matched-candidate benchmark under a 40,000-token ceiling, comparing three approaches: (1) first-candidate baseline, (2) candidate-set local control, and (3) GEC with explicit governance of scope, evidence, resource use, and stopping.
AI.result: First-candidate baseline achieved 67.42% hard-goal success. Candidate-set local control achieved 96.53%. GEC achieved 96.57%. Relative to candidate-set control, GEC preserved success while reducing mean token use from 19,782 to 12,574 (36.4% reduction) and restricting mean tokens at the 40,000-token ceiling from 16,136 to 13,114 (18.7% reduction). GEC also eliminated measured pre-completion drift and sharply reduced gross complexity. Governance-overhead sensitivity remained favorable through an additional 500 synthetic governance tokens per cycle.
AI.conclusion: The mechanistic simulations support explicit governance of scope, evidence, resource use, and stopping in LLM agents. The key insight is that concentrating proposal generation, scope interpretation, progress assessment, and stopping authority within the same self-conditioned loop causes the problem, not autoregressive next-token prediction alone. Separating action generation from project-level control (GEC) effectively addresses LLM Parkinsonism while maintaining high success rates with significantly reduced resource consumption.

title: Analyzing and Mitigating Cost-Inefficient Behaviors in Coding Agents
summary: Although effective, coding agents often incur substantial monetary costs. Their recurring cost-inefficient behaviors remain underexplored. We conduct the first study of behavioral cost inefficiencies in coding agents, analyzing 1,200 trajectories from Claude Code and Mini-SWE-Agent across four configurations on SWE-bench Verified. We identify three cost-inefficient behaviors: subsumed retrieval, similar script generation, and test re-execution. We then evaluate three mitigation strategies: structure-aware retrieval, agent-synthesized skills, and developer-designed skills, over 10k trajectories on held-out SWE-bench Verified and Pro tasks. Our main findings are: (1) The three behaviors affect 79.00\%--98.00\% of coding tasks and account for up to 22.75\% of task cost. (2) Structure-aware retrieval can introduce retrieval overhead and alter agent delegation, causing inconsistent improvements in retrieval efficiency and cost increases of up to 28.14\%. (3) Agent-synthesized skills tend to produce low-level, trace-specific guidance, limiting their effectiveness and generality. (4) In contrast, developer-designed skills provide high-level, trace-agnostic guidance, reducing cost by up to 41.73\%, roughly twice the maximum gain from agent-synthesized skills.

AI.tldr: First study of behavioral cost inefficiencies in coding agents (Claude Code and Mini-SWE-Agent), identifying three cost-inefficient behaviors (subsumed retrieval, similar script generation, test re-execution) that affect 79-98% of tasks and account for up to 22.75% of task cost. Developer-designed skills provide the most effective mitigation, reducing cost by up to 41.73%.
AI.motivation: While coding agents are effective, they incur substantial monetary costs, and their recurring cost-inefficient behaviors have remained underexplored in existing research.
AI.method: Analyzed 1,200 trajectories from Claude Code and Mini-SWE-Agent across four configurations on SWE-bench Verified. Identified three cost-inefficient behaviors. Evaluated three mitigation strategies (structure-aware retrieval, agent-synthesized skills, developer-designed skills) over 10k trajectories on held-out SWE-bench Verified and Pro tasks.
AI.result: Three cost-inefficient behaviors (subsumed retrieval, similar script generation, test re-execution) affect 79%-98% of coding tasks and account for up to 22.75% of task cost. Structure-aware retrieval can cause inconsistent improvements and cost increases up to 28.14%. Agent-synthesized skills have limited effectiveness. Developer-designed skills reduce cost by up to 41.73%, roughly twice the maximum gain from agent-synthesized skills.
AI.conclusion: Developer-designed skills are the most effective mitigation strategy, providing high-level, trace-agnostic guidance that reduces cost by up to 41.73%, significantly outperforming other tested strategies.

title: The Price of Thought: Does Test-Time Reasoning Pay in LLM Trading?
summary: While inference-time reasoning in large language models (LLMs) promises better decision making, its higher computational cost may not yield better economic outcomes. Yet reasoning controls are rarely evaluated as economic interventions, where changes in model outputs must translate into better portfolios after trading costs. We conduct a controlled study of representative LLMs from the DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini families. We vary reasoning effort while holding information available at each formation date, prompts, output formats, and portfolio construction fixed. Our evaluation covers a full year of U.S. equities under three input conditions: numerical, identifiable news, and masked news. It includes more than 800,000 asset predictions and repeated model generations. Across all three model families, additional reasoning does not produce a reliable improvement in net portfolio returns. For DeepSeek, where we examine the full progression from no reasoning to maximum reasoning, performance is nonmonotonic. Repeated generations also produce unstable treatment effects and portfolio selections, even when overall scores remain similar. These findings show that additional reasoning can change financial decisions without reliably improving their economic value, motivating validation for each task before deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether increasing reasoning effort in LLMs improves financial trading outcomes. Using over 800,000 predictions across DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models on U.S. equities for one year, the study finds that additional reasoning does not reliably improve net portfolio returns after trading costs, even though it changes model decisions.
AI.motivation: While inference-time reasoning in LLMs is believed to improve decision-making, its higher computational cost may not yield better economic outcomes. Reasoning controls are rarely evaluated as economic interventions where changes in outputs must translate into better portfolios after trading costs.
AI.method: Controlled study varying reasoning effort while holding information, prompts, output formats, and portfolio construction fixed. Evaluation covers one year of U.S. equities under three input conditions (numerical, identifiable news, masked news) with more than 800,000 asset predictions and repeated model generations across DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini families.
AI.result: Across all three model families, additional reasoning does not produce reliable improvement in net portfolio returns. For DeepSeek, performance is nonmonotonic from no reasoning to maximum reasoning. Repeated generations produce unstable treatment effects and portfolio selections, even when overall scores remain similar.
AI.conclusion: Additional reasoning can change financial decisions without reliably improving their economic value. This motivates validation for each task before deployment, as reasoning may alter outputs without delivering economic benefits.

title: LAVOIR: Teaching a Single-Pass Decision Encoder When and What to Ask with Amortized Value of Information
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Code: https://github.com/moganai/lavoir ; model: https://huggingface.co/moganai/lavoir
summary: "System One" decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev and its open counterpart Laya answer typed questions about a text in a single forward pass with calibrated probabilities, but they cannot ask for missing information: when a first message does not say what separates two departments, they guess. We present LAVOIR (Laya with Value-Of-Information Routing), which places the candidate pieces of missing information (slots) in the input next to the answer options, so that one forward pass returns both the decision distribution and, for every slot, the expected gain in the probability of the correct decision if the user were asked about it. VOI targets need no human labels: gold decisions come from schema rules, an LLM only verbalizes messages and answers, a model from another family checks every text, and pairing each message with several profiles makes regression on realized gains estimate the expected gain. A Gini-impurity cap bounds the predicted value by what a calibrated model can still gain. In a controlled study, decisions on seen schemas are statistically indistinguishable from the Bayes ceiling. The final model's question policy matches a greedy oracle VOI policy on seen schemas (AUC 0.799 vs. 0.797), and with at most 0.5 questions per conversation it is 14.1 points more accurate than never asking. On real ABCD conversations, one real exchange raises accuracy by 8.3 points where LAVOIR asks and leaves it unchanged where it does not; on SGD the cap lowers the asking rate from 93% to 8.6%. On Laya's twelve benchmarks LAVOIR is above Laya's reported scores on seven, and it answers a question in 31 ms (median, GH200).

AI.tldr: LAVOIR is a decision-making system that extends System One models (like Laya) by adding the ability to ask for missing information. It uses Value-of-Information (VOI) routing to determine which clarifying questions to ask, achieving near-Bayes-optimal accuracy with minimal questions.
AI.motivation: Existing System One decision models (like Jev and Laya) answer typed questions in a single pass but cannot ask for missing information—they simply guess when information is absent. This limitation reduces accuracy in real-world conversations where information is often incomplete.
AI.method: LAVOIR places candidate missing information (slots) in the input alongside answer options, enabling a single forward pass to return both the decision distribution and the expected gain from asking about each slot. VOI targets require no human labels: gold decisions come from schema rules, an LLM verbalizes messages/answers, a model from another family verifies text, and pairing messages with multiple profiles enables regression on realized gains. A Gini-impurity cap bounds predicted value by what a calibrated model can still gain.
AI.result: On seen schemas, decisions are statistically indistinguishable from the Bayes ceiling. The question policy matches a greedy oracle VOI policy (AUC 0.799 vs 0.797). With at most 0.5 questions per conversation, accuracy improves by 14.1 points over never asking. On real ABCD conversations, one real exchange raises accuracy by 8.3 points where LAVOIR asks; on SGD, the cap reduces asking rate from 93% to 8.6%. LAVOIR outperforms Laya on 7 of 12 benchmarks and answers in 31 ms median (GH200).
AI.conclusion: LAVOIR successfully enables System One decision models to ask clarifying questions for missing information using VOI routing, achieving near-oracle performance with minimal questions. The approach requires no human annotations and generalizes well to real conversations while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: CRC-Router: Risk-Constrained Routing for Medical Agentic AI Systems
summary: Agentic AI systems are increasingly being explored in medical imaging to improve throughput and reduce clinician workload; however, safe deployment remains challenging because autonomous errors may propagate into downstream clinical decisions. A central requirement is therefore not only strong predictive performance, but also a reliable routing mechanism that determines when the system should proceed autonomously and when a case should be escalated for further review. To address this gap, we propose CRC-Router, a risk-constrained, uncertainty-aware routing module that is applicable to both conventional medical prediction models and agentic medical AI systems. CRC-Router combines multiple complementary uncertainty signals with the predictive score to construct a per-finding routing feature vector, maps this vector to an estimated wrong-accept risk using a lightweight per-finding risk model, and then applies Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to calibrate acceptance thresholds under a user-specified risk target. Instantiated on chest X-ray multi-finding triage using the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset, CRC-Router achieves the strongest empirical risk--coverage trade-off among the evaluated baselines, both as a standalone routing layer and as a plug-in module integrated with the state-of-the-art MedRAX agent. These results demonstrate both the effectiveness of CRC-Router in selective medical automation and its modular, model-agnostic compatibility with existing predictive and agentic medical pipelines. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/XLIAaron/CRC-Router

AI.tldr: CRC-Router is a risk-constrained, uncertainty-aware routing module for medical imaging AI that determines when to proceed autonomously versus when to escalate to human review. It combines uncertainty signals with predictive scores, maps them to wrong-accept risk, and applies Conformal Risk Control to calibrate acceptance thresholds under user-specified risk targets.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems in medical imaging can improve throughput but autonomous errors may propagate into clinical decisions. Current systems lack reliable routing mechanisms to determine when to proceed autonomously vs. escalate for human review. A central requirement is strong predictive performance combined with a trustworthy routing system that ensures patient safety.
AI.method: CRC-Router combines multiple complementary uncertainty signals with predictive scores to construct per-finding routing feature vectors. It maps this vector to estimated wrong-accept risk using a lightweight per-finding risk model, then applies Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to calibrate acceptance thresholds under user-specified risk targets. Evaluated on chest X-ray multi-finding triage using NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset.
AI.result: CRC-Router achieves the strongest empirical risk-coverage trade-off among evaluated baselines, both as a standalone routing layer and as a plug-in module integrated with the state-of-the-art MedRAX agent.
AI.conclusion: CRC-Router demonstrates effectiveness in selective medical automation and provides modular, model-agnostic compatibility with existing predictive and agentic medical pipelines, enabling safer deployment of AI systems in clinical settings.

title: Learning What to Skip: Counterfactual Credit Assignment for Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows
summary: Multi-agent LLM workflows use planning, execution, verification, and summarization to improve task performance, yet the value of each component depends on the state already produced. Executing every component can waste computation or overwrite a correct intermediate answer. We formulate component omission as counterfactual credit assignment: full-workflow logs reveal the executed trajectory's reward, while controlled skip interventions reveal the consequences of omitting a future step. We introduce Learning What to Skip (LW2S), which learns action-specific safety models from these interventions and combines held-out calibration with domain-native guards to select skips. When an early skip is rejected, the controller can continue execution and reconsider a later component. Across mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice QA, and code generation with two instruction-model families, LW2S reduces recorded token cost while matching or improving aggregate full-workflow accuracy in the evaluated settings. Scale-up and second-topology experiments further examine component redundancy, while shared-error cases reveal why agreement alone is insufficient for skip selection. These findings connect efficient workflow execution to learning the conditional utility of individual components.

AI.tldr: LW2S learns to skip unnecessary components in multi-agent LLM workflows using counterfactual credit assignment, reducing token costs while maintaining or improving accuracy across math reasoning, QA, and code generation tasks.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM workflows execute planning, execution, verification, and summarization components sequentially, but executing every component wastes computation and may overwrite correct intermediate answers. The value of each component depends on the current state, making component selection nontrivial.
AI.method: The paper formulates component omission as counterfactual credit assignment: (1) full-workflow logs provide the executed trajectory's reward, (2) controlled skip interventions reveal consequences of omitting future steps. LW2S learns action-specific safety models from these interventions and combines held-out calibration with domain-native guards to select skips. When an early skip is rejected, the controller can continue and reconsider later components.
AI.result: Across mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice QA, and code generation with two instruction-model families, LW2S reduces recorded token cost while matching or improving aggregate full-workflow accuracy. Scale-up and second-topology experiments examine component redundancy, while shared-error cases reveal why agreement alone is insufficient for skip selection.
AI.conclusion: The findings connect efficient workflow execution to learning the conditional utility of individual components, demonstrating that selective execution can be both computationally cheaper and more accurate than full workflow execution.

title: From S3Q Theory to Implementation: Towards an Architecture for Machine Qualia
summary: A key challenge in machine consciousness research is translating theoretical models into computational-level implementations. In this paper, we address this challenge by proposing a five-layer implementation architecture for the S3Q (Simulated, Situated, Structurally Coherent) theory of consciousness. Rather than introducing novel formalisms, the architecture composes published computational primitives into a single pipeline. S3Q identifies three jointly necessary conditions for qualia: (1) grounded sensorimotor situatedness, (2) internal simulation via a world model, and (3) structural coherence between predictions and observations. No existing computational system implements all three simultaneously. We map each S3Q tenet to specific, compatible computational machinery and specify how these components interface within a single representation pipeline that operates on continuous, differentiable, per-object slot vectors, along with a developmental bootstrap sequence and falsifiable predictions for the composed system that no subset of the architecture produces in isolation. The model suggests that a basic sense of "self" develops by linking actions to their outcomes, and that behavior falls into three patterns (hesitation, curiosity, or avoidance) depending on how unexpected an outcome is and whether it is experienced as positive or negative. Each prediction is individually falsifiable, providing the field with a testable framework to advance our understanding of machine consciousness.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a five-layer implementation architecture for the S3Q (Simulated, Situated, Structurally Coherent) theory of consciousness, which translates theoretical models into computational-level implementations by composing existing computational primitives into a single pipeline.
AI.motivation: A key challenge in machine consciousness research is translating theoretical models into computational implementations. S3Q theory identifies three jointly necessary conditions for qualia (grounded sensorimotor situatedness, internal simulation via world model, and structural coherence), but no existing system implements all three simultaneously.
AI.method: The architecture maps each S3Q tenet to specific compatible computational machinery and specifies component interfaces within a single representation pipeline operating on continuous, differentiable per-object slot vectors, along with a developmental bootstrap sequence.
AI.result: The model suggests that a basic sense of "self" develops by linking actions to their outcomes, and that behavior falls into three patterns (hesitation, curiosity, or avoidance) depending on outcome unexpectedness and positive/negative valence. Each prediction is individually falsifiable.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides the field with a testable, falsifiable framework to advance understanding of machine consciousness, as no subset of the architecture produces these predictions in isolation.

title: ORCA: Evaluating LLMs on Data Science Code Translation
summary: Data Science Code Translation (DSCT) is the process of converting code between data science libraries while preserving functional equivalence and enabling interoperability across data science ecosystems. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable progress in Data Science Code Generation (DSCG), their performance in DSCT remains insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we introduce ORCA, a comprehensive benchmark with two complementary settings: ORCA-MAIN, which comprises 1,600 carefully curated grounding-level tasks across 3 representative domains: Data Querying, Data Manipulation, and Deep Learning; and ORCA-PROJECT, which contains 200 translation tasks over complete data science projects across 7 data science task types. Each task is accompanied by annotated reference translations and test cases for validating functional equivalence. We further incorporate a multi-stage quality verification process that thoroughly verifies task correctness and test case robustness. Experimental results demonstrate challenges in DSCT, with even frontier LLMs showing limited performance. Specifically, Claude-Opus-4.6 achieves a success rate of 56.92% on ORCA-MAIN and 33.67% on ORCA-PROJECT, indicating considerable room for improvement in DSCT. We also observe a clear directional preference in DSCT, where translation is consistently easier when the source code expresses the task through more explicit, fine-grained operations. Motivated by this, we propose an intent-augmented method, in which the model first infers source-code intent and then uses it as additional context for translation, achieving average absolute success-rate gains of 4.80% and 5.33% on ORCA-MAIN and ORCA-PROJECT, respectively.

AI.tldr: ORCA is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating Data Science Code Translation (DSCT) between libraries, featuring 1,600 grounding-level tasks (ORCA-MAIN) and 200 project-level tasks (ORCA-PROJECT). Even frontier LLMs like Claude-Opus-4.6 achieve only 56.92% and 33.67% success rates respectively, indicating significant challenges in DSCT.
AI.motivation: While Large Language Models have shown progress in Data Science Code Generation (DSCG), their performance in Data Science Code Translation (DSCT) - converting code between data science libraries while preserving functionality - remains understudied. There was no comprehensive benchmark to evaluate DSCT capabilities.
AI.method: The authors created ORCA benchmark with two settings: ORCA-MAIN (1,600 tasks across 3 domains: Data Querying, Data Manipulation, Deep Learning) and ORCA-PROJECT (200 tasks across 7 task types). Each task includes annotated reference translations and test cases for functional equivalence verification. They also proposed an intent-augmented method where the model first infers source-code intent and uses it as additional context for translation.
AI.result: Experimental results show significant challenges in DSCT. Claude-Opus-4.6 achieves 56.92% on ORCA-MAIN and 33.67% on ORCA-PROJECT. A directional preference was observed: translation is easier when source code uses more explicit, fine-grained operations. The intent-augmented method improved success rates by 4.80% (ORCA-MAIN) and 5.33% (ORCA-PROJECT).
AI.conclusion: DSCT remains a challenging task for LLMs with considerable room for improvement. The intent-augmented approach shows promise by inferring source-code intent as additional context, demonstrating that understanding the underlying task intent can enhance translation quality. ORCA provides a valuable benchmark for future research in this area.

title: Backbone-Adaptive Evidence Routing for Robust Pairwise LLM Judging
summary: Pairwise language-model judges can gather evidence through direct comparison, reasoning, or reference-based verification, but no single protocol is best across benchmarks and judge backbones. We introduce Backbone-Adaptive Evidence Routing (BAER), which adapts the evidence mechanism while preserving candidate symmetry: swapping the two responses may reverse the preference but cannot change its strength. BAER separates each expert's signed preference from candidate-invariant reliability and builds three symmetric heads: evidence stacking, reliability-based expert routing, and candidate-blind reference verification. Development data select one head for each benchmark--backbone condition, and that choice is frozen before testing. Across four benchmarks and two 8B judge backbones, BAER achieves the highest test accuracy among the compared methods in all eight conditions, with full prediction coverage and gains of 0.87--7.32 points over the strongest external baseline. The results show that adapting how evidence is gathered is more reliable than fixing one judging protocol everywhere.

AI.tldr: BAER (Backbone-Adaptive Evidence Routing) is introduced to address the limitation that no single evidence-gathering protocol works best across all benchmarks and judge backbones for pairwise language model evaluation. The method adapts evidence mechanisms while preserving candidate symmetry (swapping responses reverses preference but not strength).
AI.motivation: The core problem is that pairwise language-model judges use different evidence-gathering approaches (direct comparison, reasoning, or reference-based verification), but no single protocol performs optimally across all benchmarks and judge backbones. There is a need for an adaptive approach that can select the best evidence mechanism for each condition.
AI.method: BAER separates each expert's signed preference from candidate-invariant reliability and builds three symmetric heads: (1) evidence stacking, (2) reliability-based expert routing, and (3) candidate-blind reference verification. Development data is used to select one head for each benchmark-backbone condition, with that choice frozen before testing.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks and two 8B judge backbones, BAER achieves the highest test accuracy among compared methods in all eight conditions, with full prediction coverage and gains of 0.87--7.32 points over the strongest external baseline.
AI.conclusion: Adapting how evidence is gathered is more reliable than fixing one judging protocol everywhere. The results demonstrate that backbone-adaptive evidence routing significantly outperforms固定的单一协议方法.

title: Selective Amortization of Full-Budget Counterfactual Reasoning for Visual Token Communication
comment: Visual token communication, counterfactual evaluation, selective computation, knowledge distillation, resource allocation
summary: Generative image communication transmits compact semantic tokens under a limited packet budget, where token selection directly affects the final reconstruction quality after the complete packet is decoded. However, accurately estimating the terminal value of every candidate token requires repeated receiver-side reconstruction, resulting in substantial encoder-side computation. To address this problem, we propose ACV-Gate, an adaptive candidate evaluation framework that learns to approximate full-budget counterfactual evaluation and selectively assigns exact evaluations to the most informative candidates. Specifically, a set-aware student is trained using terminal advantages and regrets to predict candidate rankings directly, while a selective refinement mechanism evaluates only a bounded candidate set containing both Local-MDL and direct actions; cost-based thresholds further enable explicit control of the average evaluation workload. Experiments on CIFAR-10 show that ACV-Gate consistently improves reconstruction quality while substantially reducing candidate evaluations; at 0.20 bpp, the primary adaptive configuration improves PSNR over LocalMDL by 0.636 dB with only 2.13 candidate evaluations per image, corresponding to 27.60% of the calls required by the Exact-Full expert. Matched-candidate comparisons, synchronized GPU measurements, and evaluations on STL-10 and 384 *384 scale transfer further demonstrate consistent quality computation trade-offs, with particularly pronounced gains at low bit rates. These results show that combining terminal-value learning with selective candidate evaluation provides an effective and controllable mechanism for allocating encoder computation in packet-constrained generative image communication.

AI.tldr: ACV-Gate addresses the computational bottleneck in generative image communication where evaluating candidate semantic tokens requires expensive receiver-side reconstruction. The framework learns to approximate full-budget counterfactual evaluation and selectively evaluates only the most informative candidates using a set-aware student trained on terminal advantages and regrets.
AI.motivation: In generative image communication with limited packet budgets, token selection directly impacts reconstruction quality. However, accurately estimating the terminal value of every candidate token requires repeated receiver-side reconstruction, causing substantial encoder-side computation. This creates a trade-off between evaluation accuracy and computational cost.
AI.method: The proposed ACV-Gate framework consists of: (1) A set-aware student trained using terminal advantages and regrets to predict candidate rankings directly; (2) A selective refinement mechanism that evaluates only a bounded candidate set containing both Local-MDL and direct actions; (3) Cost-based thresholds for explicit control of average evaluation workload.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10 at 0.20 bpp, ACV-Gate improves PSNR by 0.636 dB over LocalMDL with only 2.13 candidate evaluations per image (27.60% of Exact-Full expert calls). Experiments on STL-10 and 384×384 scale transfer demonstrate consistent quality-computation trade-offs, with particularly pronounced gains at low bit rates.
AI.conclusion: Combining terminal-value learning with selective candidate evaluation provides an effective and controllable mechanism for allocating encoder computation in packet-constrained generative image communication, achieving better reconstruction quality with significantly reduced computational cost.

title: HCOE: Hyperbolic Clinical Ontology Embeddings from Biomedical Language Models
comment: Accepted at IEEE BIBM 2026. 7 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables
summary: Biomedical language models (LMs) encode textual semantics but do not explicitly preserve medical code hierarchies.
