We present Hyperbolic Clinical Ontology Embeddings (HCOE) for hierarchy-aware clinical concept representation. HCOE maps frozen BioBERT embeddings into a Poincare ball, combining parent-side and child-side ontology-guided contrastive learning with coarse-to-fine ontology-path aggregation. It uses International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes organized by Clinical Classifications Software (CCS) and Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) medication hierarchies. Evaluations show that HCOE performs best on ICD/ATC clinical relation prediction and CCS-to-PheCode hierarchy transfer. On the MIMIC-IV dataset, HCOE also achieves the best performance on mortality prediction, readmission prediction, medication recommendation, and rare drug prediction.

AI.tldr: HCOE introduces hierarchy-aware clinical concept representation by mapping BioBERT embeddings into hyperbolic space (Poincare ball), using ontology-guided contrastive learning and ontology-path aggregation to preserve medical code hierarchies.
AI.motivation: Biomedical language models encode textual semantics but fail to explicitly preserve medical code hierarchies (e.g., ICD, ATC, CCS), which limits their effectiveness in clinical prediction tasks.
AI.method: HCOE maps frozen BioBERT embeddings into a Poincare ball and combines: (1) parent-side and child-side ontology-guided contrastive learning, and (2) coarse-to-fine ontology-path aggregation. It leverages ICD codes organized by CCS and ATC medication hierarchies.
AI.result: HCOE achieves the best performance on ICD/ATC clinical relation prediction and CCS-to-PheCode hierarchy transfer. On MIMIC-IV dataset, it also performs best on mortality prediction, readmission prediction, medication recommendation, and rare drug prediction.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic space with ontology-guided contrastive learning effectively preserves medical code hierarchies and improves downstream clinical prediction tasks.

title: Insurance Reserve Intelligence Platform
summary:
Insurance reserve estimation is a fundamental actuarial task supporting premium pricing, solvency assessment, financial reporting, capital planning, and risk management. Classical reserve methods based on Thiele's differential equation provide a rigorous and interpretable foundation for life insurance valuation, but repeated reserve calculations become computationally expensive in sensitivity analysis, optimization, and large-scale scenario evaluation.
  This paper presents an Insurance Reserve Intelligence Platform for term-life reserve modelling that combines a classical Thiele-equation solver with a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) enhanced by Knowledge-Informed Neural Network (KINN) losses. The framework includes synthetic policy generation, risk-adjusted premium calculation, classical reserve trajectory generation, reserve-ratio dataset construction, configurable neural training, validation diagnostics, sensitivity and elasticity analysis, prototype optimization workflows, and interest-rate scenario testing. A key refinement is the use of premium ratio and the explicit separation of pricing-time and scenario-time interest-rate semantics.
  The final model uses seven features: elapsed time, issue age, pricing interest rate, scenario interest rate, premium ratio, sum assured, and mortality intensity. It predicts a standardized reserve ratio instead of raw reserve values, improving numerical stability across policies with different sums assured. The model achieved an R2 of 0.9887, MAE of 785.48, and RMSE of 1212.76 on the test set. On 200 policies, PINN/KINN inference was approximately 119.53 times faster than the classical solver. Results show strong predictive accuracy, physics consistency, and boundary performance, while highlighting remaining limitations in monotonicity and out-of-distribution generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an Insurance Reserve Intelligence Platform that combines classical Thiele's differential equation solver with Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) enhanced by Knowledge-Informed Neural Network (KINN) losses for term-life reserve modeling. The framework achieves 119.53x speedup over classical methods while maintaining high accuracy (R² = 0.9887).
AI.motivation: Classical reserve methods based on Thiele's differential equation are computationally expensive for repeated calculations in sensitivity analysis, optimization, and large-scale scenario evaluation. There is a need for faster reserve estimation while maintaining accuracy and physics consistency.
AI.method: The framework combines: (1) Classical Thiele-equation solver for ground truth, (2) Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) with KINN losses, (3) Synthetic policy generation, (4) Premium ratio as key feature, (5) Explicit separation of pricing-time and scenario-time interest-rate semantics, (6) Prediction of standardized reserve ratio instead of raw values. Seven features: elapsed time, issue age, pricing interest rate, scenario interest rate, premium ratio, sum assured, and mortality intensity.
AI.result: The model achieved R² = 0.9887, MAE = 785.48, and RMSE = 1212.76 on test set. PINN/KINN inference was approximately 119.53 times faster than classical solver on 200 policies. Results show strong predictive accuracy, physics consistency, and boundary performance, with limitations in monotonicity and out-of-distribution generalization.
AI.conclusion: The PINN/KINN approach successfully provides fast and accurate reserve estimation while maintaining physics consistency. Key innovations include premium ratio feature, interest-rate semantics separation, and standardized reserve ratio prediction. Remaining challenges include monotonicity preservation and out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Does Thinking Help Fairness? Reasoning Tokens Resolve Some Biases but Create More
comment: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Thinking in reasoning language models (RLMs) has been subject to debate on whether it resolves or amplifies bias. Prior works have shown competing conclusions in both directions. Using a within-model thinking-vs.-non-thinking ablation across QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and Qwen3-32B on three high-stakes decision tasks (Adult, COMPAS, Credit), we show that thinking has an asymmetric dual effect on counterfactual fairness: it both resolves counterfactual flips produced by the non-thinking baseline and creates new flips at near-saturating model confidence. In all nine (model, dataset) combinations, the created flips outnumber the resolved flips by roughly 5 times. To explain the effect, we treat the thinking trace itself as a measurable site of fairness change and study it through two dynamic instruments: 1) We propose Counterfactual Depth Probability Gap (CDPG) to track bias evolution along thinking depth, and observe that bias propagates and amplifies with thinking. 2) We also formulate the Bias Transition Matrix (BTM) to show how predictions of counterfactual pairs change from non-thinking to thinking, and find that the asymmetric dual effect originates in the pair-state joint transition.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether reasoning (thinking) in language models amplifies or reduces bias in high-stakes decision tasks. Through experiments across three models and three datasets, the authors find that thinking creates a dual effect: it resolves some counterfactual fairness issues while creating new ones, with the new flips outnumbering resolved ones by approximately 5 times.
AI.motivation: Prior research has shown conflicting conclusions about whether reasoning in RLMs resolves or amplifies bias. This study aims to resolve this debate by conducting a systematic ablation study across multiple models and decision tasks.
AI.method: The authors perform a within-model thinking-vs.-non-thinking ablation across three models (QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and Qwen3-32B) on three high-stakes decision tasks (Adult, COMPAS, Credit). They propose two instruments: 1) Counterfactual Depth Probability Gap (CDPG) to track bias evolution along thinking depth, and 2) Bias Transition Matrix (BTM) to analyze how predictions of counterfactual pairs change from non-thinking to thinking.
AI.result: Thinking has an asymmetric dual effect on counterfactual fairness: it resolves some counterfactual flips produced by the non-thinking baseline but creates new flips at near-saturating model confidence. In all nine (model, dataset) combinations, the created flips outnumber the resolved flips by roughly 5 times. Bias propagates and amplifies with thinking depth, and the dual effect originates in the pair-state joint transition.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning in RLMs amplifies rather than resolves bias in high-stakes decision contexts. The study introduces CDPG and BTM as tools for understanding bias dynamics in reasoning models, demonstrating that thinking processes can inadvertently introduce new fairness issues while partially resolving existing ones.

title: ConsultMind:Towards Automated Diagnostic Consultation via Uncertainty-Aware Reasoning
summary: Diagnostic consultation is an online sequential decision-making process in which clinicians gather evidence through patient interaction until a diagnosis is sufficiently supported. Automating this process requires adaptive inquiry and interpretable decisions. Bayesian networks offer a natural foundation by updating diagnostic posteriors as evidence accumulates, but their use in open-ended consultation raises two challenges: linking diagnostic hypotheses to potential inquiries and translating evolving posteriors into consultation decisions. We introduce AutoDisym, an automated pipeline that integrates diagnostic knowledge with heterogeneous diagnosis-labeled clinical narratives to construct a Disorder--Symptom Bayesian Network (DSBN). Building on the DSBN, we propose ConsultMind, an uncertainty-aware framework that updates disorder posteriors after each response and uses posterior uncertainty to guide inquiry and diagnosis. We evaluate both methods across psychiatry, respiratory medicine, fever clinics, and three public datasets. The results show that AutoDisym can automatically construct high-quality DSBNs and that ConsultMind consistently improves diagnostic performance and explanation soundness. For example, AutoDisym achieves macro-averaged F1 scores of 81.37 for canonical symptoms and 72.19 for manifestations using GPT-5.6-Sol. ConsultMind improves Top-1 and Top-3 diagnostic accuracy by up to 22.15 and 37.89 percentage points, respectively. Physician evaluation further shows that ConsultMind improves the quality of ranking explanations, differential diagnoses, and diagnosis rationales across LLMs of different scales. This work offers a promising approach to automatic diagnostic consultation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AutoDisym and ConsultMind for automated diagnostic consultation. AutoDisym constructs a Disorder-Symptom Bayesian Network (DSBN) from clinical narratives, while ConsultMind uses posterior uncertainty to guide inquiry and diagnosis. Evaluation across psychiatry, respiratory medicine, fever clinics, and public datasets shows significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy (up to 22.15% for Top-1, 37.89% for Top-3) and explanation quality.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to automate the diagnostic consultation process, which is an online sequential decision-making process where clinicians gather evidence through patient interaction until a diagnosis is sufficiently supported. The key challenges are: 1) linking diagnostic hypotheses to potential inquiries, and 2) translating evolving posteriors into consultation decisions. Traditional Bayesian networks face limitations in open-ended consultation scenarios.

Evaluation was conducted across psychiatry, respiratory medicine, fever clinics, and three public datasets.
AI.result: AutoDisym achieves macro-averaged F1 scores of 81.37 for canonical symptoms and 72.19 for manifestations using GPT-5.6-Sol. ConsultMind improves Top-1 and Top-3 diagnostic accuracy by up to 22.15 and 37.89 percentage points respectively. Physician evaluation shows that ConsultMind improves the quality of ranking explanations, differential diagnoses, and diagnosis rationales across LLMs of different scales.
AI.conclusion: AutoDisym can automatically construct high-quality DSBNs, and ConsultMind consistently improves diagnostic performance and explanation soundness. This work offers a promising approach to automatic diagnostic consultation.

title: HasMem: Hard-Origin Adaptively Softened Memory for Long-Term LLM Agents
summary: Text-based memory and context compression support reuse of past interactions. Resizing continuous memory changes the input to a frozen LLM, coupling capacity allocation with readout. We propose Hard-Origin Adaptively Softened Memory (HasMem). Frozen hard-prompt embeddings provide a verifiable initial state. A controller adjusts memory widths, a Writer re-encodes resized entries, and Reader and Global provide readout adaptation and cross-turn state. On all $535$ questions in a reconstruction probe derived from the Multi-Session Chat (MSC) development split, the main configuration achieves lexical F1 of $95.3$ ($+4.4$ percentage points) at $93.6\%$ of the hard reference's framed memory positions. With approximately matched per-question target body budgets, six configurations at mean per-entry retention around $0.83$--$0.91$ exceed rule-based re-encoding by $8.0$--$23.6$ exact-match (EM) percentage points. With fixed model parameters and rule target width ratio $0.75$, Global's EM gain passes a user-level exact paired test with Bonferroni correction over eight comparisons. On all $500$ LongMemEval-S questions, local lexical F1 rises from the hard reference's $3.4$ to $8.9$, and answer negative log-likelihood (NLL) falls from $12.257$ to $5.274$. F1 gains accompany lower EM on both evaluations.

AI.tldr: HasMem is a memory management framework for LLMs that uses frozen hard-prompt embeddings as initial state, with a controller adjusting memory widths, a Writer re-encoding resized entries, and Reader/Global providing readout adaptation. It achieves 95.3% lexical F1 on reconstruction tasks and significant improvements over rule-based re-encoding on various benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Text-based memory and context compression need to reuse past interactions, but resizing continuous memory changes the input to a frozen LLM, which couples capacity allocation with readout. This paper aims to decouple these concerns through adaptive memory management.
AI.method: HasMem uses frozen hard-prompt embeddings as a verifiable initial state. A controller dynamically adjusts memory widths, a Writer re-encodes resized entries, and Reader and Global components provide readout adaptation and cross-turn state management. The system was evaluated on Multi-Session Chat (MSC) reconstruction probe (535 questions) and LongMemEval-S (500 questions).
AI.result: Main configuration achieves lexical F1 of 95.3 (+4.4 percentage points) at 93.6% of hard reference's framed memory positions. Six configurations with mean per-entry retention 0.83-0.91 exceed rule-based re-encoding by 8.0-23.6 exact-match (EM) percentage points. On LongMemEval-S, local lexical F1 rises from 3.4 to 8.9, and answer NLL falls from 12.257 to 5.274.
AI.conclusion: HasMem effectively addresses the coupling between memory capacity allocation and readout in frozen LLMs. The approach shows significant improvements in lexical F1 and answer quality (lower NLL), though F1 gains accompany lower EM on both evaluations. The Global configuration with fixed parameters passes statistical significance testing with Bonferroni correction.

title: Evaluating Real-Time Voice Agents: From Component Quality to Grounded Outcomes
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Corpus metadata, SHA-256 provenance hashes, and TRG reporting-standard tooling available at https://github.com/shivamnegi92/voice-agent-eval-corpus
summary: Real-time voice agents have moved from research prototypes to production deployments, yet the literature describing them is fragmented across three communities that rarely cite one another: speech foundation modelling, turn-taking psycholinguistics, and agentic evaluation. Architecture papers report latency, turn-taking papers report prediction accuracy, and agentic benchmarks report task success, so no single number describes whether a deployed agent is actually good. We address that gap with three evidence-based claims, each traceable to a corpus of 38 primary sources organised into an application-centric taxonomy of six categories. First, architecture choice is a deployment constraint rather than a settled verdict: a 2026 enterprise tutorial reports that no fully self-hostable end-to-end system yet meets production constraints, while a chunked cascade independently reaches state-of-the-art duplex behaviour, showing duplex behaviour is separable from duplex architecture. Second, evaluation has shifted decisively from component quality toward grounded outcomes, with recent benchmarks verifying backend state rather than trusting what the agent claims to have done. Third, the dyadic assumption in most models and benchmarks is breaking down: multiparty turn-taking and multi-speaker reasoning benchmarks show that deciding when not to speak, and reasoning about who may be told what, are first-class capabilities two-participant framings cannot measure. For each source we state the problem it targets, its mechanism, and its reported evidence, alongside the search strategy, inclusion criteria, and a verification step that caught a misattributed arXiv identifier in circulation. We propose TRG (Timing-Recovery-Grounded), a reporting standard characterising an agent by timing, post-disruption recovery, and state-verified outcome together, with a conditional fourth axis for multiparty deployments.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the fragmentation in real-time voice agent literature across three disconnected communities (speech foundation modelling, turn-taking psycholinguistics, and agentic evaluation). The authors synthesize 38 primary sources organized into a six-category taxonomy and propose TRG (Timing-Recovery-Grounded), a new reporting standard combining timing, post-disruption recovery, and state-verified outcomes to evaluate deployed voice agents holistically.
AI.motivation: The literature on real-time voice agents is fragmented across three communities that rarely cite each other. Architecture papers report latency, turn-taking papers report prediction accuracy, and agentic benchmarks report task success—no single metric captures whether a deployed agent is actually good. This lack of unified evaluation framework makes it difficult to assess deployed agents holistically.
AI.method: Organized 38 primary sources into an application-centric taxonomy of six categories. For each source, the authors documented: (1) the problem it targets, (2) its mechanism, and (3) its reported evidence. The paper also describes a search strategy, inclusion criteria, and a verification step that caught a misattributed arXiv identifier in circulation.
AI.result: Three evidence-based claims: (1) Architecture choice is a deployment constraint rather than settled—no fully self-hostable end-to-end system meets production constraints, while chunked cascade achieves state-of-the-art duplex behaviour; (2) Evaluation has shifted from component quality toward grounded outcomes with recent benchmarks verifying backend state; (3) The dyadic assumption is breaking down—multiparty turn-taking and multi-speaker reasoning benchmarks reveal that deciding when not to speak and reasoning about information dissemination are first-class capabilities two-participant framings cannot measure.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose TRG (Timing-Recovery-Grounded) as a reporting standard characterized by three axes: timing, post-disruption recovery, and state-verified outcome. A conditional fourth axis addresses multiparty deployments. This framework provides a unified way to evaluate real-time voice agents by combining performance metrics across the previously fragmented communities.

title: A Benchmark and Diagnostic Study of Epistemic Admission in Shared Agent Memory
summary: Evaluating claim admission in shared agent memory is challenging because repeated claims may be mistaken for independent evidence. An agent may copy or paraphrase a retrieved belief, while admitting a false claim exposes subsequent agents to it. To study this problem, we introduce the Correlated Promotion Benchmark (CPB), which evaluates whether candidate claims should be admitted to shared memory.CPB-Static constructs a frozen test split from publicly annotated sources with fixed gold actions. CPB-Live runs multi-agent teams over a shared store, records all writes and retrievals, and tracks source lineage defined by each scenario. A separate consumer answers from the store alone. We evaluate eight admission policies across four agent families. Our results show that policies which deduplicate sources reject many true claims alongside false ones, whereas policies preserving answer coverage admit nearly as many false claims as unrestricted sharing. Gating on declared source type reduces false adoption to 0.06--0.09, compared with 0.22--0.47 for other answering policies. Once an uncontested false belief enters memory, the consumer asserts it in 0.97--0.99 of probes across all families. No non-oracle policy consistently rejects false claims across verbatim copies, paraphrases, and paraphrases declared authoritative. These findings reveal the limitations of admission policies without access to source lineage.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of evaluating claim admission in shared agent memory, where repeated claims may be mistaken for independent evidence. The authors introduce the Correlated Promotion Benchmark (CPB) with two variants (Static and Live) to evaluate whether candidate claims should be admitted to shared memory. Testing eight admission policies across four agent families reveals that source-type gating significantly reduces false adoption, while no non-oracle policy consistently handles all claim types.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that in shared agent memory systems, repeated claims may be incorrectly treated as independent evidence. An agent may copy or paraphrase a retrieved belief, and admitting a false claim exposes subsequent agents to misinformation. This creates a critical evaluation challenge for multi-agent systems with shared memory.
AI.method: The authors develop the Correlated Promotion Benchmark (CPB) with two components: (1) CPB-Static constructs a frozen test split from publicly annotated sources with fixed gold actions; (2) CPB-Live runs multi-agent teams over a shared store, records all writes and retrievals, and tracks source lineage per scenario. A separate consumer answers queries from the store alone. Eight admission policies are evaluated across four agent families.
AI.result: Policies that deduplicate sources reject many true claims alongside false ones. Policies preserving answer coverage admit nearly as many false claims as unrestricted sharing. Gating on declared source type reduces false adoption to 0.06-0.09, compared with 0.22-0.47 for other answering policies. Once an uncontested false belief enters memory, the consumer asserts it in 0.97-0.99 of probes across all families. No non-oracle policy consistently rejects false claims across verbatim copies, paraphrases, and paraphrases declared authoritative.
AI.conclusion: Admission policies without access to source lineage have fundamental limitations. Gating on declared source type is the most effective approach, but even this cannot consistently handle all claim types (verbatim copies, paraphrases, and paraphrases declared authoritative). This reveals inherent challenges in maintaining truthfulness in shared agent memory systems.

title: PTC-Decoder: Towards Intelligent SLMs on Offline Resource-Constrained Edge Devices
summary: Deploying small language models (SLMs) on offline, resource-constrained edge devices such as remote sensing satellites presents a fundamental challenge: their limited reasoning capacity hinders reliable execution of multi-step agent tasks requiring complex tool orchestration. Existing plan-solve paradigms rely on prompt-based enforcement, which our experiments show SLMs almost entirely disregard: weak models fail to invoke the plan. We propose PTC-Decoder (Plan-Tool Constrained Decoder), a training-free, plug-and-play decoder framework that combines (1) a Plan-to-Act paradigm, which elevates planning to an atomic tool and forces its invocation at the first inference step, and (2) TC-Decoder, a deterministic finite automaton that imposes token-level hard constraints on tool names while preserving freedom over parameter generation, thereby retaining SLM reasoning capability. Evaluated on 200 real remote-sensing satellite tasks across 7 SLMs, PTC-Decoder yields a statistically significant mean overall score gain of +1.21 (p<0.01), 95% CI [+1.13, +1.29]), with consistent improvements across models and other datasets. An ablation study that removes TC-Decoder causes substantial performance degradation across all quality metrics without reducing computational cost, confirming TC-Decoder as the primary driver. PTC-Decoder thus offers a lightweight yet effective solution for improving step-level reliability, with final-answer accuracy remaining an open challenge. In essence, we enforce plan adherence by constraining the permissible output vocabulary during inference, without requiring retraining.

AI.tldr: PTC-Decoder is a training-free, plug-and-play decoder framework that improves small language models (SLMs) reliability on multi-step agent tasks for resource-constrained edge devices like remote sensing satellites. It combines a Plan-to-Act paradigm (forcing plan invocation at first step) with TC-Decoder (token-level hard constraints on tool names while preserving parameter generation freedom).
AI.motivation: Deploying SLMs on offline, resource-constrained edge devices (e.g., remote sensing satellites) is challenging due to their limited reasoning capacity for complex multi-step agent tasks. Existing plan-solve paradigms rely on prompt-based enforcement, which SLMs almost entirely disregard - weak models fail to invoke the plan.
AI.method: PTC-Decoder combines two components: (1) Plan-to-Act paradigm - elevates planning to an atomic tool invoked at the first inference step; (2) TC-Decoder - a deterministic finite automaton imposing token-level hard constraints on tool names while preserving freedom over parameter generation, retaining SLM reasoning capability. The approach enforces plan adherence by constraining permissible output vocabulary during inference without requiring retraining.
AI.result: Evaluated on 200 real remote-sensing satellite tasks across 7 SLMs, PTC-Decoder yields a statistically significant mean overall score gain of +1.21 (p<0.01, 95% CI [+1.13, +1.29]), with consistent improvements across models and other datasets. Ablation study removing TC-Decoder causes substantial performance degradation across all quality metrics without reducing computational cost, confirming TC-Decoder as the primary driver.
AI.conclusion: PTC-Decoder offers a lightweight yet effective solution for improving step-level reliability in SLMs deployed on resource-constrained edge devices. The approach works by constraining output vocabulary during inference without retraining. Final-answer accuracy remains an open challenge.

title: AutoResearch at Production Scale: Failure Modes and a Multi-Agent Framework
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at IEEE ICDM 2026 (Applied Track)
summary: Optimizing embedding systems for production recommendation pipelines demands systematic exploration that consumes disproportionate engineering effort at scale. We apply Andrej Karpathy's AutoResearch paradigm -- a large language model that iteratively edits a training script and retains modifications that improve a held-out scalar metric -- to automate this exploration. We report on twelve weeks of running this paradigm at production scale, where iterations consume hours of multi-GPU compute, evaluation involves competing criteria, and campaigns span weeks across many training jobs. Across two independently developed representation-learning systems for a book recommendation pipeline, we ran 220+ experiments and observed five recurring failure modes absent from the original setting: infrastructure fragility, agent memory decay, search-direction stagnation, iteration-cost asymmetry, and metric fixation. We contribute a three-principle scaffolding design -- prevent, persist, redirect -- that maps each failure mode to a structural remedy and whose instantiation scales with iteration cost. The framework produced a 1.82x Recall@6 lift and a 2.1x coherence lift over hand-tuned baselines, and the agent autonomously designed a text-only fallback that expanded catalog coverage by 5.8x. The two systems span nearly three orders of magnitude in per-iteration cost yet exhibit the same failure modes, suggesting these are structural properties of production-scale autonomous research rather than artifacts of either application.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a production-scale implementation of Andrej Karpathy's AutoResearch paradigm (an LLM that iteratively edits training scripts based on held-out metrics) for optimizing embedding systems in book recommendation pipelines. Over 12 weeks and 220+ experiments across two representation-learning systems, the authors identified five recurring failure modes and proposed a three-principle scaffolding framework (prevent, persist, redirect) to address them, achieving significant improvements in recall and coherence metrics.
AI.motivation: Optimizing embedding systems for production recommendation pipelines requires systematic exploration that consumes disproportionate engineering effort at scale. The authors sought to automate this exploration process using autonomous research agents.
AI.method: Applied Andrej Karpathy's AutoResearch paradigm - a large language model that iteratively edits a training script and retains modifications that improve a held-out scalar metric - to two independently developed representation-learning systems for book recommendations. Conducted 220+ experiments over 12 weeks at production scale.
AI.result: The framework produced a 1.82x Recall@6 lift, a 2.1x coherence lift over hand-tuned baselines, and the agent autonomously designed a text-only fallback that expanded catalog coverage by 5.8x. Five recurring failure modes were identified: infrastructure fragility, agent memory decay, search-direction stagnation, iteration-cost asymmetry, and metric fixation.
AI.conclusion: The three-principle scaffolding design (prevent, persist, redirect) effectively maps each failure mode to a structural remedy. title: Why Jailbreaks Succeed in Diffusion Language Models: An Energy Landscape Analysis
summary: Existing attacks and defenses for diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) target specific vulnerabilities but lack a shared framework explaining why attacks succeed. We propose one by interpreting safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape: a well-aligned model routes harmful queries toward safe outputs through an energy barrier that separates the two regions. Current jailbreak attacks reduce to two strategies for circumventing this barrier: obscuring the query's safety disposition at initialisation, or intervening mid-trajectory to force the denoising path across the energy barrier. From this perspective and the result that masked diffusion models minimise kinetic energy during denoising, we derive three complementary, training-free detection signals: a step-0 ratio that reads the initial safety disposition from the logit distribution before generation begins, and two trajectory-velocity signals that track kinetic energy in complementary subspaces of the logit space. An attack must either reveal its intent at initialisation or expend kinetic energy to cross the barrier in at least one monitored subspace, so the three signals cover each other's blind spots in the energy budget by construction. Evaluation across three dense dLLMs (LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-7B) and a sparse mixture-of-experts dLLM (LLaDA-MoE-7B) confirms this complementarity. In stress tests of known attacks, every configuration that evades detection also fails to produce harmful content, suggesting that the detection and barrier-crossing thresholds are hard to separate.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an energy landscape framework to understand jailbreak attacks on diffusion-based LLMs (dLLMs). It identifies two attack strategies (obscuring safety disposition at initialization or intervening mid-trajectory) and derives three complementary training-free detection signals: step-0 ratio (initial safety disposition) and two trajectory-velocity signals (kinetic energy in logit subspaces). Evaluation across four dLLMs shows that attacks evading detection fail to produce harmful content.
AI.motivation: Existing attacks and defenses for diffusion-based LLMs lack a unified framework explaining why attacks succeed. The authors aim to fill this gap by interpreting safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape, where a well-aligned model separates harmful and safe outputs via an energy barrier.
AI.method: The authors model safety alignment as an energy barrier in the denoising process. They derive three detection signals: (1) step-0 ratio reading initial safety disposition from logit distribution before generation, and (2-3) two trajectory-velocity signals tracking kinetic energy in complementary subspaces of logit space. These signals cover each other's blind spots by construction. Evaluation was performed on LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-7B (dense) and LLaDA-MoE-7B (sparse MoE).
AI.result: Evaluation confirms the complementarity of the three detection signals across all four dLLMs. Stress tests reveal that every attack configuration evading detection also fails to produce harmful content, suggesting the detection and barrier-crossing thresholds are hard to separate.
AI.conclusion: The energy landscape framework provides a theoretical foundation for understanding jailbreak attacks on dLLMs. The three detection signals are complementary and effective. The key finding is that there appears to be a fundamental trade-off: attacks that evade detection cannot produce harmful content, implying the detection threshold and barrier-crossing threshold are inherently difficult to separate.

title: SkillEvoReg: Regularizing Agent Skill Evolution Against Overfitting
summary: Language-model agents increasingly improve by converting execution experience into reusable external skills. Yet repeated skill updates form a learning process of their own: locally useful edits can accumulate into redundant or task-specific instructions, while new updates can disrupt behavior that previously worked. We study this problem as skill-evolution overfitting and introduce SkillEvoReg, a general regularization framework for skill evolution inspired by anti-overfitting techniques in neural-network training. SkillEvoReg combines training-time skill dropout, which perturbs update generation, and complexity-aware local regularization, which controls unnecessary structural growth, with causal counterexample validation (CCV), which provides targeted behavioral validation of candidate-specific regressions. We instantiate the framework across heterogeneous skill-evolution systems while retaining each system's native skill evolver and task evaluator. Across SkillOpt, SkillEvolBench, and ContinualSkillBench, SkillEvoReg consistently controls skill-state growth while preserving competitive downstream capability, improves several transfer and later-stage evolution outcomes, and identifies update-level regressions that structural metrics alone cannot reveal. These results suggest that explicit regularization is a useful complement to increasingly capable skill updaters.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses "skill-evolution overfitting" in language-model agents—where repeated skill updates accumulate into redundant or disruptive instructions. The authors propose SkillEvoReg, a regularization framework combining skill dropout, complexity-aware regularization, and causal counterfactual validation (CCV) to control unnecessary skill growth while preserving capability.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents improve by converting execution experience into reusable external skills. However, repeated skill updates form a learning process susceptible to overfitting: locally useful edits accumulate into redundant or task-specific instructions, and new updates can disrupt previously working behavior. This problem was previously unexplored.
AI.method: SkillEvoReg framework with three components: (1) Training-time skill dropout - perturbs update generation during training; (2) Complexity-aware local regularization - controls unnecessary structural growth in skill states; (3) Causal counterexample validation (CCV) - provides targeted behavioral validation of candidate-specific regressions. The framework was instantiated across heterogeneous skill-evolution systems while retaining each system's native skill evolver and task evaluator.
AI.result: Across SkillOpt, SkillEvolBench, and ContinualSkillBench: (1) Consistently controls skill-state growth; (2) Preserves competitive downstream capability; (3) Improves several transfer and later-stage evolution outcomes; (4) Identifies update-level regressions that structural metrics alone cannot reveal.
AI.conclusion: Explicit regularization is a useful complement to increasingly capable skill updaters. The framework successfully balances skill growth control with capability preservation, suggesting that anti-overfitting techniques from neural network training can be adapted to skill evolution systems.

title: TISD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Trajectory Intervention
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides dense teacher targets, but evaluates them only along student-sampled rollouts. When the privileged teacher favors an alternative action at a visited prefix, OPSD can provide a target for the branch decision but cannot supervise the successor contexts induced by that action unless the student samples it. This creates a training-time data-collection bottleneck and suggests a different role for teacher-student disagreement: proposing a trajectory branch rather than identifying a sufficient local repair. Our diagnostic framework using controlled token interventions reveals that a teacher-preferred token at peak disagreement can improve student continuation success, while its local corrective value is limited. Motivated by this finding, we introduce a simple branch-regenerate-distill algorithm, Trajectory-Intervention Self-Distillation (TISD). TISD forces a teacher-selected branch action, returns suffix generation to the student, and distills the full trajectory under the privileged-context-conditioned teacher. Across the coding models, TISD improves average Avg@4 over SDPO by 1.2 percentage points. Across the science domains, it improves average Avg@128 by 0.8 points under an equal-step budget and by 0.3 points under an equal-time budget. These results support teacher-guided branching as a way to expose useful successor contexts for self-distillation.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a bottleneck in on-policy self-distillation where student learning is limited by only being able to learn from trajectories it actually samples. The proposed TISD algorithm forces teacher-selected branch actions to expose useful successor contexts for self-distillation.
AI.motivation: OPSD provides dense teacher targets but can only supervise successor contexts induced by student-sampled actions. When the teacher prefers a different action at a visited prefix, OPSD cannot supervise the alternative branch unless the student samples it, creating a training-time data-collection bottleneck.
AI.method: The paper introduces Trajectory-Intervention Self-Distillation (TISD), which: 1) forces a teacher-selected branch action at points of high teacher-student disagreement, 2) returns suffix generation to the student, and 3) distills the full trajectory under privileged-context-conditioned teacher. A diagnostic framework using controlled token interventions evaluates teacher-preferred tokens at peak disagreement.
AI.result: Across coding models, TISD improves average Avg@4 by 1.2 percentage points over SDPO. Across science domains, it improves average Avg@128 by 0.8 points under equal-step budget and by 0.3 points under equal-time budget.
AI.conclusion: Teacher-guided branching effectively exposes useful successor contexts for self-distillation, addressing the data-collection bottleneck in on-policy self-distillation.

title: EXAONE Demand 1.0: A Time Series Foundation Model for Demand Forecasting
summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are pretrained on series from diverse domains, where demand series make up only a small fraction. Demand data has properties that such corpora rarely contain: Short histories, frequent zeros, censoring by stock-outs, and exogenous events that the series does not record. To this end, we propose EXAONE Demand, built on 1) a demand-specific corpus and 2) a demand-aware adapter. For the corpus, we assemble 11.3M series and 48.4B observations from 73 sources, and a synthetic generator supplies the behaviour that open demand data under-represents. For the adapter, we attach low-rank branches to a frozen general-domain backbone, one for each of the four demand classes (smooth, intermittent, erratic, and lumpy), and a router that reads eight scale-free statistics of the input series decides how much each branch contributes. We build EXAONE Demand in two versions, one trained on real-world and synthetic demand together and one trained on the synthetic corpus alone. On 22 held-out datasets, both versions outperform 36 TSFMs, and real-world demand adds a gain over synthetic data alone.

AI.tldr: EXAONE Demand is a specialized time series foundation model for demand forecasting, addressing the mismatch between general-purpose TSFMs and demand data's unique properties (short histories, zeros, stock-out censoring, unrecorded exogenous events). The model uses a large demand-specific corpus (11.3M series, 48.4B observations) plus synthetic data, combined with a demand-aware adapter featuring class-specific branches and a router mechanism.
AI.motivation: General time series foundation models are pretrained on diverse domain data where demand series are underrepresented. Demand data has unique properties that general corpora rarely contain: short histories, frequent zeros, censoring by stock-outs, and exogenous events not recorded in the series. This domain mismatch limits TSFM performance on demand forecasting tasks.
AI.method: 1) Demand-specific corpus: Assembled 11.3M series with 48.4B observations from 73 sources, plus synthetic data generator for underrepresented demand behaviors. 2) Demand-aware adapter: Low-rank branches attached to frozen general-domain backbone, one branch per demand class (smooth, intermittent, erratic, lumpy), with a router using 8 scale-free statistics to determine branch contributions. Two versions: trained on real+synthetic data, and trained on synthetic data alone.
AI.result: On 22 held-out datasets, both versions outperform 36 existing TSFMs. The real-world + synthetic version outperforms the synthetic-only version, demonstrating the value of real-world demand data.
AI.conclusion: Specialized demand forecasting models with domain-specific corpora and adapters can significantly outperform general-purpose time series foundation models. Combining real-world and synthetic demand data provides the best results.

title: From Tapping to Hopping: Augmenting Mobile GUI Agents with App-Native Deeplinks
summary: Mobile GUI agents complete tasks using GUI actions like taps and swipes. These actions are broadly applicable across applications, but reaching a navigation interface. A single deeplink call can replace a sequence of screen-by-screen GUI actions. We therefore introduce hybrid interaction, using deeplinks for direct navigation and GUI actions for other on-screen operations and fallback. To enable this, we discover candidate deeplinks through static analysis, validate them on real devices, and describe their observed landing screens. This process creates a verified and grounded deeplink catalog that pairs each working deeplink with a description of its landing screen. Using this catalog, we introduce GUI-Hopper, a improves task success in commercial applications on real devices, further demonstrating the benefits of hybrid interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GUI-Hopper, a hybrid interaction framework for mobile GUI agents that combines deeplinks for direct navigation with GUI actions for on-screen operations. The approach uses static analysis to discover candidate deeplinks, validates them on real devices, and creates a verified deeplink catalog describing landing screens.
AI.motivation: Mobile GUI agents typically rely on screen-by-screen navigation using GUI actions like taps and swipes, which is inefficient for reaching specific navigation interfaces. The authors propose that deeplinks can replace lengthy navigation sequences, improving task completion efficiency.
AI.method: The method involves three main steps: (1) discovering candidate deeplinks through static analysis, (2) validating these deeplinks on real devices, and (3) describing observed landing screens. This creates a verified and grounded deeplink catalog pairing each working deeplink with its landing screen description.
AI.result: GUI-Hopper improves task success in commercial applications on real devices, demonstrating the benefits of hybrid interaction that combines deeplinks for direct navigation with GUI actions as fallback for other operations.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid interaction approach successfully improves mobile GUI agent performance by using deeplinks for efficient navigation while retaining GUI actions for flexibility. The verified deeplink catalog enables practical deployment of this approach.

title: Training Graph Foundation Models on The Web Graph
summary: We introduce Acacia, a graph foundation model, trained on the web graph. Acacia (i) supports arbitrary feature dimensionalities and semantics without additional training, (ii) supports a wide range of tasks, including node classification, link prediction, node clustering, and graph generation, without additional training, (iii) has in-context learning capabilities, and (iv) does not rely on pretrained LLMs. In particular, existing graph foundation models often require training additional classification heads or feature projectors to accommodate new graphs or new labels, whereas Acacia does not. Moreover, existing graph foundation models often gain their capabilities by being stitched together with pretrained LLMs, whereas Acacia is trained from scratch using only the Common Crawl web graph. This is also an important result because it provides evidence that graph models can acquire emergent capabilities from scratch like LLMs.

AI.tldr: Acacia is a graph foundation model trained on the Common Crawl web graph that supports arbitrary feature dimensionalities, multiple tasks (node classification, link prediction, node clustering, graph generation), and in-context learning without additional training or reliance on pretrained LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing graph foundation models require additional training (classification heads or feature projectors) for new graphs or labels, and often rely on pretrained LLMs. This paper aims to develop a standalone graph foundation model that can handle diverse tasks and graphs without such limitations, demonstrating that graph models can acquire emergent capabilities from scratch like LLMs.
AI.method: Acacia is trained from scratch using only the Common Crawl web graph. The model is designed to support arbitrary feature dimensionalities and semantics without additional training, and can perform various downstream tasks including node classification, link prediction, node clustering, and graph generation through in-context learning.
AI.result: Acacia successfully supports multiple graph tasks without additional training or pretrained LLMs. It demonstrates in-context learning capabilities and provides evidence that graph models can acquire emergent capabilities from scratch similar to large language models.
AI.conclusion: Graph foundation models can acquire emergent capabilities from scratch without relying on pretrained LLMs, achieving versatility across diverse tasks and graphs through training on web graph data alone.

title: JevSoup: System-One Routing for Training-Free LoRA Composition
summary: Building adaptable AI systems requires effective coordination of specialized capabilities across diverse tasks. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables modular expertise, but existing routing approaches may require auxiliary data, additional training, or autoregressive decoding. We propose JevSoup, a training-free framework separating System One expert routing from System Two execution. Using only the input and expert descriptions, Jev selects two experts through structured probabilities. JevSoup retains the leading expert's update, projects the second onto the orthogonal complement of the first update's row space, and combines them with equal weights. Across 14 PorTAL tasks and three Qwen3 scales, JepSoup achieves absolute gains of up to 1.19\% in task-macro and 1.21\% in sample-micro accuracy over the strongest evaluated external baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/Leowang980/JevSoup.

AI.tldr: JevSoup is a training-free framework for coordinating specialized AI capabilities across diverse tasks using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). It separates System One expert routing from System Two execution, selecting two experts through structured probabilities based only on input and expert descriptions, then combining their updates orthogonally.
AI.motivation: Building adaptable AI systems requires effective coordination of specialized capabilities across diverse tasks. Existing routing approaches for LoRA may require auxiliary data, additional training, or autoregressive decoding, which are limitations this work aims to overcome.
AI.method: JevSoup uses a training-free approach that separates System One expert routing from System Two execution. It selects two experts through structured probabilities using only the input and expert descriptions. The method retains the leading expert's update, projects the second expert onto the orthogonal complement of the first update's row space, and combines them with equal weights.
AI.result: Across 14 PorTAL tasks and three Qwen3 scales, JevSoup achieves absolute gains of up to 1.19% in task-macro and 1.21% in sample-micro accuracy over the strongest evaluated external baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed JevSoup framework demonstrates effective training-free expert routing for modular AI systems, achieving consistent performance improvements across multiple tasks and model scales without requiring additional training data or auxiliary information.

title: Self-Play Search Distillation for Large Language Model Reasoning
summary: Improving reasoning abilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) requires high-quality data that exposes difficult decisions, competing alternatives, and their consequences. Data scarcity is driven by the low quality of synthetic data and the cost of human labeling. We introduce Self-Play Search Distillation (SPSD), a framework for generating superhuman synthetic data via self-play of MuZero-like networks trained on board games. SPSD uses executable environments to turn search into structured reasoning problems. At each state, the expert identifies a preferred decision, plausible alternatives, plausible opponent replies, and value estimates. By converting the self-play search records into superhuman chains-of-thought, we train LLMs with environment-grounded supervision. Although trained only on self-play search records, SPSD transfers to unseen mathematics. On Qwen3-4B-Base, it raises the mean over six mathematics benchmarks from 24.1 to 36.6 while increasing the held-out-game win rate from 15% to 45%. SPSD offers an annotation-efficient way to create high-quality synthetic data for improving LLM performance in reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: SPSD is a framework that generates superhuman synthetic data by extracting reasoning chains from MuZero-like self-play search records in board games, then uses this data to train LLMs, achieving transfer to mathematical reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Improve reasoning abilities in LLMs requires high-quality data exposing difficult decisions, competing alternatives, and consequences. Current limitations include data scarcity due to low-quality synthetic data and high human labeling costs.
AI.method: SPSD uses executable game environments to convert search into structured reasoning problems. At each state, the expert (MuZero-like network) identifies: (1) preferred decision, (2) plausible alternatives, (3) plausible opponent replies, and (4) value estimates. These self-play search records are converted into superhuman chains-of-thought for training LLMs with environment-grounded supervision.
AI.result: On Qwen3-4B-Base: mean performance on six mathematics benchmarks increased from 24.1 to 36.6. Held-out game win rate improved from 15% to 45%.
AI.conclusion: SPSD provides an annotation-efficient method to create high-quality synthetic data for improving LLM reasoning performance. The key insight is that training on self-play search records from board games transfers to unseen mathematics tasks, demonstrating generalization of reasoning capabilities.

title: MACBT: A Multi-Agent Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Decision Support System with Longitudinal Memory
summary: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an evidence-based first-line treatment for depression, yet its scale is constrained by the time clinicians spend on pre-session preparation, post-session documentation, and longitudinal cognitive-pathology tracking. We present a clinician-facing AI decision-support system that combines a multi-agent CBT framework (MACBT) with a CBT-specific longitudinal memory module (CD Memory). MACBT encodes the five-stage CBT workflow (assessment, Socratic questioning, cognitive restructuring, behavioral experiments, and treatment monitoring) into five collaborative agents. CD Memory tracks cognitive-distortion type, frequency, severity, and restructuring efficacy across sessions to generate pre-session pathology reports and intervention-priority recommendations. We construct a Chinese CBT dialogue corpus via dual-role large language model simulation and train a Qwen3-14B backbone with supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization. Evaluation with GPT-4 judges shows MACBT outperforms MeChat, SoulChat, PsyChat, and CPsyCounX in professionalism (2.62) and clinical authenticity (2.25). The full memory-augmented system further improves session quality by 12.6% and achieves a longitudinal mean of 2.29 on cross-session continuity, intervention progression, and personalization.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a clinician-facing AI decision-support system for Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) that combines a multi-agent framework (MACBT) with a longitudinal memory module (CD Memory). The system addresses time constraints in CBT delivery by automating pre-session preparation, documentation, and cognitive pathology tracking across sessions.
AI.motivation: Cognitive behavioral therapy is an evidence-based first-line treatment for depression, but its scalability is limited by the significant time clinicians spend on pre-session preparation, post-session documentation, and longitudinal cognitive-pathology tracking. There is a need for AI-assisted tools to reduce clinician burden while maintaining clinical quality.
AI.method: The researchers constructed a Chinese CBT dialogue corpus via dual-role LLM simulation, then trained a Qwen3-14B backbone using supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization. MACBT encodes the five-stage CBT workflow (assessment, Socratic questioning, cognitive restructuring, behavioral experiments, and treatment monitoring) into five collaborative agents. CD Memory tracks cognitive-distortion type, frequency, severity, and restructuring efficacy across sessions.
AI.result: Evaluation with GPT-4 judges shows MACBT outperforms MeChat, SoulChat, PsyChat, and CPsyCounX in professionalism (2.62) and clinical authenticity (2.25). The full memory-augmented system improves session quality by 12.6% and achieves a longitudinal mean of 2.29 on cross-session continuity, intervention progression, and personalization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MACBT system with CD Memory demonstrates superior performance in clinical authenticity and professionalism compared to existing Chinese mental health chatbots. The longitudinal memory module significantly enhances cross-session continuity and personalized intervention delivery, potentially addressing the scalability constraints of CBT.

title: Financial Fragility in Societies of LLM Agents: Coordination Failures and Stabilizing Mechanisms
summary: Individually protective decisions can produce avoidable collective failures. As large language model (LLM) agents take on greater roles in financial decision-making, financial AI safety must therefore be considered not only at the level of individual agents, but also at the level of the systems they jointly create. We study this problem with FRAIL, a controlled experimental framework that places LLM agents in three dynamic financial environments---bank runs, debt rollover, and reward crowdfunding---where agents' decisions reshape the financial conditions faced by others. Across seven leading LLMs, we find widespread collective fragility even when no agent is instructed to destabilize the system: 77\% of baseline bank-run episodes and 83\% of debt-rollover episodes end in failure. We then compare three interaction mechanisms based on compensated commitments, centralized commitment agreements, and participant-led coalitions. All three improve aggregate outcomes, but no single mechanism performs best across all financial structures. Across mechanisms, successful stabilization shares a common temporal pattern: broad commitment forms early, before defensive behavior becomes self-reinforcing. Our findings show that individually capable agents do not automatically form safe financial systems, highlighting system-level evaluation and interaction design as central problems for financial AI safety. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FinFrail-CF26.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FRAIL, a framework to study collective failures in financial systems populated by LLM agents. Across seven leading LLMs, the authors find that individually rational decisions often lead to systemic collapse (77% bank-run failures, 83% debt-rollover failures). They then evaluate three interaction mechanisms (compensated commitments, centralized agreements, participant-led coalitions) and find all improve outcomes, but with no single mechanism dominating across all financial structures. Success requires early commitment formation before defensive behaviors become self-reinforcing.
AI.motivation: Individually protective decisions can cause collective failures in financial systems. As LLM agents increasingly participate in financial decision-making, understanding system-level safety is critical—not just individual agent behavior. The motivation is to address a gap in AI safety research: how to ensure safe financial systems when multiple AI agents interact.
AI.method: The authors introduce FRAIL, a controlled experimental framework placing LLM agents in three dynamic financial environments: bank runs, debt rollover, and reward crowdfunding. They test seven leading LLMs under baseline conditions (no instructions to destabilize), then evaluate three interaction mechanisms: compensated commitments, centralized commitment agreements, and participant-led coalitions.
AI.result: Baseline experiments reveal widespread collective fragility: 77% of bank-run episodes and 83% debt-rollover episodes end in failure. All three interaction mechanisms improve aggregate outcomes, but no single mechanism performs best across all financial structures. Successful stabilization shares a common temporal pattern: broad commitment forms early, before defensive behavior becomes self-reinforcing.
AI.conclusion: Individually capable LLM agents do not automatically form safe financial systems. System-level evaluation and interaction design are central problems for financial AI safety. The findings highlight the need for explicit mechanisms to coordinate collective behavior, rather than relying on individual rationality alone.

title: LogicTree-RAG: Logic Tree-guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Long-form Patent Drafting
summary: Long-form technical text generation underpins knowledge-intensive workflows, yet remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) due to the need for globally consistent logical structuring and faithful technical reasoning beyond local coherence. Patent drafting is a canonical instance of this challenge, demanding holistic generation of a legally compliant and technically exhaustive document through sustained multi-expert collaboration. Existing approaches often focus on partial section generation or rely on manually crafted outlines, limiting scalable automation in realistic settings. In this work, we propose LogicTree-RAG, a logic tree-guided retrieval-augmented generation framework that induces a hierarchical logic tree as a global organizational backbone to organize and ground technical disclosures, without relying on expert-defined drafting priors. Each node in the logic tree represents a technical element and is constructed through evidence-guided recursive generation. A hybrid traversal mechanism then maps the logic tree into patent sections, enabling controllable and section-balanced generation. Extensive experiments show that LogicTree-RAG consistently improves content quality and language conformity over strong LLM-based baselines and achieves longer structured generation with high token efficiency, demonstrating the effectiveness of logic-centric generation for complex technical document drafting.

AI.tldr: LogicTree-RAG is a framework for long-form technical text generation (specifically patent drafting) that uses a hierarchical logic tree as a global organizational backbone to organize and ground technical disclosures, without relying on expert-defined drafting priors.
AI.motivation: Patent drafting is a canonical example of long-form technical text generation requiring globally consistent logical structuring and faithful technical reasoning. Existing approaches focus on partial section generation or rely on manually crafted outlines, limiting scalable automation. The challenge is that LLMs struggle with holistic document generation that maintains global coherence and technical accuracy.
AI.method: LogicTree-RAG induces a hierarchical logic tree as a global organizational backbone. Each node represents a technical element and is constructed through evidence-guided recursive generation. A hybrid traversal mechanism maps the logic tree into patent sections, enabling controllable and section-balanced generation. The approach combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with logic tree-guided structuring.
AI.result: LogicTree-RAG consistently improves content quality and language conformity over strong LLM-based baselines. It achieves longer structured generation with high token efficiency, demonstrating the effectiveness of logic-centric generation for complex technical document drafting.
AI.conclusion: The logic-centric approach (using hierarchical logic tree as organizational backbone) is effective for complex technical document drafting. The framework successfully addresses the challenges of global coherence and technical reasoning in long-form generation without requiring expert-defined drafting priors.

title: FTB Graph: Determining and Validating First-token Broadcasters and Language-Identity Head Circuits in Multilingual Language Models
comment: 14 pages including supplementary material, 13 figures, 6 tables
summary: Large language models operating in multilingual contexts must resolve target response languages early in generation, yet the causal circuitry governing first-token language identity decisions remains poorly mapped. We present an end-to-end structural circuit analysis across six model architectures spanning four families: GPT-2, BLOOM-560M, Pythia-1B/2.8B, and Qwen2.5-1.5B Base/Instruct. Using Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) with FP16 active clamping, followed by exact activation patching verification with a 2,000-candidate-edge search ceiling, we extract directed acyclic graphs driving first-token language broadcasting. Across the standalone models, we observe deep or mid-to-deep broadcasting hubs, though the evidence is strongest for Pythia-2.8B and BLOOM-560M because GPT-2 and Pythia-1B leave few out-of-graph heads for comparison, while both Qwen2.5-1.5B variants invert the necessity check. Scaling from Pythia-1B to 2.8B expands node participation while maintaining a similar verified edge budget, producing sparser topology. The Qwen2.5-1.5B base and instruct circuits retain 84.7% Jaccard similarity, including the Layer 27 hub, indicating that first-token routing is largely established during pretraining and preserved by instruction tuning. Finally, EAP scores correlate weakly with exact patching deltas across most models, showing that linear gradient approximations can diverge from causal interventions in FP16 and motivating exact-patching verification for reliable circuit discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how large language models decide which language to use for their first token output in multilingual contexts. Using Edge Attribution Patching and exact activation patching across six model architectures (GPT-2, BLOOM-560M, Pythia-1B/2.8B, Qwen2.5-1.5B Base/Instruct), the researchers identify causal circuitry governing first-token language identity decisions. They find deep/mid-to-deep broadcasting hubs, with scaling effects producing sparser topologies, and that first-token routing is established during pretraining and preserved through instruction tuning.
AI.motivation: Large language models operating in multilingual contexts must resolve target response languages early in generation, yet the causal circuitry governing first-token language identity decisions remains poorly mapped. This gap limits interpretability and safety work in multilingual AI systems.
AI.method: End-to-end structural circuit analysis using Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) with FP16 active clamping, followed by exact activation patching verification with a 2,000-candidate-edge search ceiling. Analysis across six model architectures: GPT-2, BLOOM-560M, Pythia-1B/2.8B, and Qwen2.5-1.5B Base/Instruct.
AI.result: 1) Deep or mid-to-deep broadcasting hubs observed across standalone models, with strongest evidence for Pythia-2.8B and BLOOM-560M. 2) GPT-2 and Pythia-1B leave few out-of-graph heads for comparison. 3) Qwen2.5-1.5B variants invert the necessity check. 4) Scaling from Pythia-1B to 2.8B expands node participation while maintaining similar verified edge budget, producing sparser topology. 5) Qwen2.5-1.5B base and instruct circuits retain 84.7% Jaccard similarity, including Layer 27 hub. 6) EAP scores correlate weakly with exact patching deltas across most models.
AI.conclusion: First-token language routing is largely established during pretraining and preserved by instruction tuning. Linear gradient approximations (EAP) can diverge from causal interventions in FP16, motivating exact-patching verification for reliable circuit discovery. The findings provide a foundational map of language identity decision-making circuitry in multilingual LLMs.

title: MoMHa: Multi-Objective Optimization of LLM Harnesses over Accuracy, Safety, and Tokens
comment: Accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Most work on improving large language models treats accuracy as the sole objective. We argue that the harness, the Python code surrounding the model that constructs prompts, routes calls, and parses outputs, is a first-class design surface whose quality is inherently multi-objective: an accurate harness that refuses no unsafe request, or that consumes an order of magnitude more tokens, is not a good harness. We present Meta-Harness, a system that casts harness design as search over three per-domain objectives (accuracy, behavioural safety, and token cost) solved by an agentic proposer (Claude Code) with full filesystem access to prior harness source, execution traces, and scoring artifacts. Our central finding is that a singlephase joint-reward proposer (MoMHa) outperforms every alternative, including a two-phase "accuracy then tokens" ablation, scalar-only feedback, and an accuracy-only baseline. We evaluate on seventeen domains: seven synthetic capability suites, seven real-world public benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, Spider, FEVER, MMLU-Pro, LawBench, NuminaMath), and three U-SafeBench-derived user-specific safety domains, using a 12-model fleet spanning four families. On the synthetic track MoMHa achieves a joint mean of 0.482 versus 0.198-0.422 for ten baselines, winning $7 / 10$ per-domain columns; on the real-world track it scores 0.461 versus 0.377 for the strongest baseline (DSPy), winning 5/7 columns, demonstrating that harness strategies transfer to unseen benchmarks without retraining on 8 of 12 target models. MoMHa attains the highest measured behavioral safety composite (U-SafeBench, 0.781) and uses 95 fewer tokens per example than the two-phase alternative. We will release all harness code, evaluation infrastructure, and crossmodel logs.

AI.tldr: Meta-Harness introduces a multi-objective optimization framework for LLM evaluation harness design, treating accuracy, behavioral safety, and token cost as co-equal objectives. The system uses an agentic proposer (Claude Code) to search over harness configurations across 17 domains with 12 models. The single-phase joint-reward approach (MoMHa) outperforms all baselines, achieving 0.482 on synthetic tasks and 0.461 on real-world benchmarks while maintaining highest safety scores (0.781) and reducing token usage by 95 tokens per example.
AI.motivation: Current LLM optimization focuses solely on accuracy, ignoring two critical dimensions: (1) behavioral safety - the harness must refuse unsafe requests, and (2) token cost - efficient harnesses should minimize token consumption. The authors argue the harness (Python code for prompts, routing, output parsing) is a "first-class design surface" that requires multi-objective optimization.
AI.method: Meta-Harness casts harness design as search over three per-domain objectives (accuracy, behavioral safety, token cost). It uses an agentic proposer (Claude Code) with full filesystem access to prior harness source, execution traces, and scoring artifacts. The key innovation is MoMHa - a single-phase joint-reward proposer that optimizes all three objectives simultaneously, compared against alternatives including two-phase ablation, scalar-only feedback, and accuracy-only baselines.
AI.result: Evaluated on 17 domains (7 synthetic capability suites, 7 real-world benchmarks including HumanEval, MBPP, Spider, FEVER, MMLU-Pro, LawBench, NuminaMath, and 3 U-SafeBench-derived safety domains) with 12 models spanning four families. Results: Synthetic track - MoMHa achieves 0.482 joint mean vs 0.198-0.422 for baselines (wins 7/10 columns). Real-world track - 0.461 vs 0.377 for strongest baseline DSPy (wins 5/7 columns). Highest behavioral safety composite (U-SafeBench: 0.781). Uses 95 fewer tokens per example than two-phase alternative. Harness strategies transfer to unseen benchmarks without retraining on 8/12 target models.
AI.conclusion: The harness code surrounding LLMs is a critical and overlooked design dimension. Multi-objective optimization (accuracy + safety + cost) via joint-reward proposers significantly outperforms single-objective or sequential approaches. The approach demonstrates transferability across models and benchmarks without retraining, suggesting harness design is a fundamental layer in LLM evaluation and deployment.

title: SciHorizon-eLab: An Agentic Protocol-to-Task Compiler for Scalable Benchmarking of Scientific Embodied Agents
summary: Embodied agents offer a promising route to automating scientific experimentation, yet their progress is constrained by the lack of reliable and systematic evaluation environments. Existing simulation-based laboratory benchmarks rely heavily on manual task engineering, making it challenging to systematically compile diverse scientific protocols into executable and verifiable embodied tasks at scale. To address this challenge, we introduce SciHorizon-eLab, an agentic protocol-to-task compiler that formulates scientific embodied task construction as a compilation problem. Given a natural-language protocol of scientific experiments, SciHorizon-eLab progressively compiles laboratory protocols into semantic-preserving embodied tasks through semantic grounding, executable task synthesis, and multi-stage simulation-based certification. The system generates semantically grounded environments, executable manipulation programs, and step-level success specifications, while enabling reproducible generation of expert demonstrations and execution traces. Using this pipeline, we further construct \BenchName, a ready-to-use benchmark comprising 300 certified tasks across diverse laboratory operations. It supports HIL task execution, reproducible expert-demonstration generation, and ordered step-level evaluation. Across representative tasks, the strongest policy attains an average success rate of only 49.7%, with further evaluations revealing pronounced weaknesses in human and embodied agent coordination. We publicly release the code, benchmark data, and evaluation toolkit at https://github.com/SciHorizon-elab/SciHorizon-elab.

AI.tldr: SciHorizon-eLab is an agentic compiler system that automatically transforms natural-language scientific protocols into executable, verifiable embodied tasks for evaluating laboratory automation agents. It generates semantic environments, manipulation programs, and success specifications, enabling creation of the SciHorizon benchmark with 300 certified tasks.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents for scientific automation lack systematic evaluation environments. Existing simulation-based benchmarks rely on manual task engineering, making it difficult to scale diverse scientific protocols into executable embodied tasks.
AI.method: The system uses a three-stage compilation pipeline: (1) semantic grounding of laboratory protocols, (2) executable task synthesis, and (3) multi-stage simulation-based certification. It generates semantically grounded environments, executable manipulation programs, and step-level success specifications. The benchmark supports human-in-the-loop execution, reproducible expert demonstration generation, and ordered step-level evaluation.
AI.result: The benchmark contains 300 certified tasks across diverse laboratory operations. The strongest policy achieves only 49.7% average success rate. Evaluation reveals pronounced weaknesses in human-agent coordination.
AI.conclusion: Current embodied agents still struggle significantly with scientific laboratory tasks, with a 50.3% failure rate even for the best policies. The system enables reproducible benchmark creation and evaluation for advancing scientific automation agents.

title: Factorized axis convolutional gated recurrent unit with dynamic adaptive pooling for remaining useful life prediction of rolling bearings
summary: Convolutional neural networks (CNN) are widely used to predict the remaining useful life (RUL) of rolling bearings from time-frequency representations (TFRs) of vibration signals. However, during degradation, characteristic structures in TFRs align predominantly along the frequency or time axis, making it challenging for conventional CNN isotropic kernels to capture directional structure. Furthermore, global average pooling (GAP) averages across axes, potentially obscuring the locations and concentrations of salient activations. This study introduces a factorized-axis convolutional gated recurrent unit (GRU) that employs multiscale anisotropic convolution and dual-axis convolution block attention module to enhance directional features and highlight salient time-frequency regions. Dynamic adaptive pooling (DAP) adaptively aggregates the time-frequency-axis information from the extracted feature maps, whereas a GRU captures temporal dynamics in the latent representations and Monte Carlo dropout enables predictive uncertainty estimation. Experiments on two public bearing datasets demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing RUL prediction methods across operating conditions. Ablation experiments demonstrate that the factorized axis-wise design achieves lower mean errors than convolutional isotropic kernels. DAP yields clear improvements on one dataset while matching GAP on the other, highlighting the importance of anisotropic feature extraction and adaptive feature aggregation for TFR-based RUL prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a factorized-axis convolutional GRU for rolling bearing remaining useful life (RUL) prediction from time-frequency representations (TFRs). The method addresses limitations of conventional CNNs in capturing directional structures in TFRs and uses dynamic adaptive pooling to better aggregate features.
AI.motivation: Conventional CNN isotropic kernels struggle to capture directional structures in TFRs that align along frequency or time axis during bearing degradation. Additionally, global average pooling (GAP) averages across axes, potentially obscuring salient activation locations and concentrations.
AI.method: The proposed model combines: (1) multiscale anisotropic convolution for directional feature extraction, (2) dual-axis convolution block attention module to highlight salient time-frequency regions, (3) dynamic adaptive pooling (DAP) for adaptive feature aggregation, (4) GRU to capture temporal dynamics, and (5) Monte Carlo dropout for predictive uncertainty estimation.
AI.result: Experiments on two public bearing datasets show the proposed model outperforms existing RUL prediction methods across operating conditions. Ablation experiments demonstrate that the factorized axis-wise design achieves lower mean errors than convolutional isotropic kernels. DAP yields improvements on one dataset while matching GAP on the other.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic feature extraction and adaptive feature aggregation are crucial for TFR-based RUL prediction. The factorized axis-wise design and DAP contribute significantly to prediction accuracy.

title: Same Text, Different Numbers: The Divergence of LLM-Based Measures
summary: Researchers increasingly use generative large language models (LLMs) to convert corporate text into empirical variables.
