Batching is the most impactful energy optimization. Neural OCR should be avoided. Concrete guidelines provided for energy-efficient, privacy-compliant local information extraction.

title: Mutable Transcripts: Mitigating Context Pollution through Editable Conversation State
summary: Contemporary large language model (LLM) chat systems treat conversation history as an immutable sequence of turns that defines the model's working context. However, user intent in real interactions is not static: it evolves through correction, refinement, and shifting constraints. This mismatch between dynamic intent and static transcripts can result in context pollution, where outdated or irrelevant information persists and continues to influence subsequent responses. We introduce mutable transcripts, a new interaction paradigm that enables users to revise prior turns through natural language edit requests, allowing the conversation history itself to be updated rather than appended. This reframes the transcript from a passive record into an editable representation of conversational state. We present a working prototype that integrates transcript-level revision into a standard chat interface and evaluate its feasibility through a controlled user study (n=17) and an illustrative transcript analysis of representative interaction scenarios. Participants significantly preferred mutable transcripts over standard chat across measures of clarity, confidence, and ease of use, with reduced intent to restart conversations. Transcript analysis of representative user study conversations shows that mutable transcripts can reduce conversation length and eliminate obsolete retained context. These findings provide initial evidence that user-driven revision of conversational history can improve interaction quality and help maintain a more current representation of user intent. The source code and prototype can be accessed at https://github.com/QxLabIreland/ReChat

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "mutable transcripts," a new interaction paradigm for LLM chat systems that allows users to revise prior conversation turns through natural language edit requests. Unlike traditional chat systems that treat conversation history as immutable, this approach enables the conversation history itself to be updated rather than merely appended, addressing the problem of context pollution from outdated or irrelevant information.
AI.motivation: The core problem addressed is the mismatch between dynamic user intent and static conversation transcripts in LLM chat systems. In real interactions, user intent evolves through correction, refinement, and shifting constraints, but current systems treat conversation history as an immutable sequence. This leads to "context pollution" where outdated or irrelevant information persists and continues to influence subsequent responses.
AI.method: The researchers developed a working prototype that integrates transcript-level revision into a standard chat interface. They evaluated feasibility through two approaches: (1) a controlled user study (n=17) and (2) an illustrative transcript analysis of representative interaction scenarios.
AI.result: Participants significantly preferred mutable transcripts over standard chat across measures of clarity, confidence, and ease of use, with reduced intent to restart conversations. Transcript analysis showed that mutable transcripts can reduce conversation length and eliminate obsolete retained context.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide initial evidence that user-driven revision of conversational history can improve interaction quality and help maintain a more current representation of user intent. The source code and prototype are available at https://github.com/QxLabIreland/ReChat.

title: Programs-of-Layers in LLMs through the Lens of Cortical Areas
summary: Inference in LLMs is conventionally a fixed-depth, fixed-order forward pass through every layer, regardless of how difficult the input is. The human brain does not work this way: using the thalamus as a central hub, it routes information flexibly to all regions of the cortex according to demand. Li et al. (2026) recently showed, with a system they call program-of-layers (PoLar), that transformers can be given an analogous flexibility if their layers are treated as a library of functions rather than a fixed sequence. Performance improves over the standard forward pass when each input is dynamically routed through an adaptive sequence of skipped or repeated contiguous layer blocks. We reconstructed PoLar's diagnostic MCTS in more detail than the original paper and applied it across 5 models. We reproduced several of PoLar's findings: skipping outperformed the standard pass, repeating outperformed skipping, and combining both outperformed either alone. Shorter programs sufficed for easier questions, while harder questions required more layer repeats. However, we failed to replicate the main claim regarding their learned router for single-shot inference: its top-ranked prediction consistently collapsed back to the standard pass, even though its top-k predicted programs, taken together, did show a real accuracy gain. Beyond reproduction, we find that a small number of generic programs are enough to solve most of the questions. We also provide a much deeper analysis of these programs' structure and robustness: for example, we found that programs that correct errors are highly brittle: undoing even a single edit inside a program typically breaks the correction. Connecting this to the brain's routing mechanisms, PoLar mirrors principles of thalamo-cortical coordination between cortical-area-like transformer layers. We publicly release the code at https://datexis.github.io/RE-PoLar/

AI.tldr: This paper reproduces and extends PoLar, a system that gives transformers brain-like flexible inference by treating layers as a library of functions. The authors confirmed most findings (skipping/repeating improve performance) but failed to replicate the learned router's single-shot prediction claim. They also discovered that error-correcting programs are brittle and that a small number of generic programs solve most questions.
AI.motivation: The conventional LLM inference uses fixed-depth, fixed-order passes through all layers, unlike the human brain which uses the thalamus as a hub to flexibly route information to cortical regions. This work aims to replicate and extend PoLar, which gives transformers analogous flexibility by treating layers as a library of functions with adaptive routing.
AI.method: The authors reconstructed PoLar's diagnostic Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) in greater detail than the original paper and applied it across 5 different models. They tested dynamic routing through adaptive sequences of skipped or repeated contiguous layer blocks, and analyzed program structure and robustness.
AI.result: Reproduced findings: (1) Skipping outperformed standard pass, (2) Repeating outperformed skipping, (3) Combining both outperformed either alone, (4) Easier questions used shorter programs, harder questions needed more repeats. New findings: (1) Failed to replicate main claim - learned router's top prediction collapsed to standard pass, though top-k predictions together showed gains; (2) Small number of generic programs solve most questions; (3) Error-correcting programs are highly brittle - single edits typically break correction.
AI.conclusion: Most PoLar findings are robust and reproducible. However, the learned router for single-shot inference claim does not hold. The work reveals that adaptive layer routing follows similar principles to brain thalamo-cortical coordination. Key limitation: error-correcting programs lack robustness, suggesting practical deployment challenges.

title: Completed Pairs Hide Capped Failures: A ReVerPi Case Study of Selective Context Projection
comment: 15 pages, 12 tables, 5 figures. Project code: https://github.com/timwhitez/ReVer_Pi. Source archive includes anc/ analysis data and reproduction scripts
summary: Context projection replaces older tool observations with compact, addressable excerpts, reducing repeated input while potentially adding evidence-retrieval turns. We study this trade-off in ReVerPi, a Pi extension with archived observations and matched full/projected continuations. In an 86-run source-reading campaign with 641 model requests, the 15 completed pairs show identical success: 12/15 per arm. Twelve further boundary runs stop, with the runner suppressing the companion whenever the first arm fails to complete. Restoring all 27 boundary runs bounds projected-minus-full success between $-$9 and +1 tasks. One omitted, selector-chosen projected continuation successfully retrieves archive text yet exhausts twelve requests; its full counterpart answers in three. The eleven jointly correct pairs form a fully observed success stratum within this recorded frame: projection reduces aggregate logical tokens by 25%, while increasing the median pair's tokens by 29% and total suffix requests from 35 to 55. Separating fitting from evaluation changes the selector's apparent tie: outside its four fitting pairs, it incurs one extra failure and 8.6% more logical tokens over thirteen comparable runs. This methodological case study connects stopping rules, known bounded failures, unexecuted companions, and resource aggregation. Its findings concern the recorded campaign, rather than population noninferiority or superiority over unrestricted Pi. Evaluations should retain every intervention boundary, execute both allocated arms independently of the first arm's completion, and report completion alongside interaction and token expenditure.

AI.tldr: This paper studies context projection in ReVerPi (a Pi extension), comparing full vs. projected continuations in an 86-run source-reading campaign. Results show identical success rates (12/15) in completed pairs, with projection reducing aggregate logical tokens by 25% but increasing median tokens by 29% and total suffix requests from 35 to 55.
AI.motivation: To investigate the trade-off in context projection: replacing older tool observations with compact, addressable excerpts reduces repeated input but may add evidence-retrieval turns. The study aims to quantify this trade-off in terms of success rates and resource usage.
AI.method: An 86-run source-reading campaign with 641 model requests was conducted using ReVerPi with archived observations. The study compared matched full/projected continuations across 15 completed pairs, supplemented by 12 boundary runs where the companion was suppressed after the first arm failed.
AI.result: 15 completed pairs showed identical success: 12/15 per arm. Twelve boundary runs stopped when the first arm failed, bounding projected-minus-full success between -9 and +1 tasks. One omitted case showed projected used 12 requests vs full's 3. The 11 jointly correct pairs showed projection reduced aggregate logical tokens by 25% but increased median pair's tokens by 29%. Total suffix requests increased from 35 to 55. Outside fitting pairs, the selector incurred one extra failure and 8.6% more logical tokens.
AI.conclusion: The study provides methodological recommendations: evaluations should retain every intervention boundary, execute both allocated arms independently of the first arm's completion, and report completion alongside interaction and token expenditure. Findings are specific to this recorded campaign and do not generalize to population noninferiority or superiority over unrestricted Pi.

title: Compress What You See, Not What You Say: Anchored Context Distillation for Latent-Observation Software Engineering Agents
summary: Tool observations dominate the context of software-engineering agents, making long interaction histories costly to maintain. Existing context compression methods can discard information needed by later actions, while adapting agents to soft-token representations can compromise their original behavior. To reduce context while preserving action-critical information and agent behavior, we combine Latent Observations, Hard Actions (LOHA), a context layout that separates compressed history from text needed for exact reference, with Anchored Context Distillation (ACD), a training method that enables latent reading while constraining behavioral drift. LOHA compresses older tool observations into soft tokens while retaining the agent's own turns and the last K observations in text, providing compact access to historical information and exact access to recent content. To enable the agent to use this representation, ACD distills the base model's full-text predictions into the latent view while anchoring its behavior on plain-text inputs to the same base model. On SWE-bench Verified, K=3 reduces context per call by 43% for Qwen3-4B and 57% for SWE-Master-4B-RL, with resolve rates of 12.1% and 21.8% versus 14.5% and 27.5% for their uncompressed bases. A single-run recency sweep reaches 14.4% and 23.0% at K=8, with larger windows generally favoring task performance over compression. Under a 32K-token limit, Qwen3 with K=3 resolves 21.1% of a 199-instance subset versus 11.1% for the same adapted agent using full text. In concurrent single-GPU serving, it achieves 1.9 times that full-text agent's instance throughput.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the context length problem in software-engineering agents by proposing LOHA (Latent Observations, Hard Actions), a context layout that compresses older tool observations into soft tokens while retaining recent observations in text, combined with ACD (Anchored Context Distillation), a training method that enables latent reading while preserving the agent's original behavior.
AI.motivation: Tool observations dominate the context of software-engineering agents, making long interaction histories costly to maintain. Existing context compression methods can discard information needed by later actions, while adapting agents to soft-token representations can compromise their original behavior.
AI.method: The authors propose two components: (1) LOHA, a context layout that separates compressed history from text needed for exact reference by compressing older tool observations into soft tokens while retaining the agent's own turns and the last K observations in text; (2) ACD, a training method that distills the base model's full-text predictions into the latent view while anchoring its behavior on plain-text inputs to the same base model.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, K=3 reduces context per call by 43% for Qwen3-4B and 57% for SWE-Master-4B-RL, with resolve rates of 12.1% and 21.8% versus 14.5% and 27.5% for their uncompressed bases. A single-run recency sweep reaches 14.4% and 23.0% at K=8. Under a 32K-token limit, Qwen3 with K=3 resolves 21.1% of a 199-instance subset versus 11.1% for the same adapted agent using full text. In concurrent single-GPU serving, it achieves 1.9 times that full-text agent's instance throughput.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LOHA+ACD approach successfully reduces context length while preserving action-critical information and agent behavior. It achieves significant context compression (43-57%) with minimal performance degradation, and under token limits, it can even outperform full-text approaches due to better context utilization. The method also enables 1.9x throughput in single-GPU serving scenarios.

title: Segment-Level Agentic Topic Modeling for Improved Data Exploration and Resource Efficiency
summary: Topic modeling is an effective technique for discovering hidden themes within documents and is widely used in text mining and data analysis across a variety of industry sectors. Recently, large language model (LLM)-based topic models have been emerged that prompt LLMs to generate topics then assign the topics to documents, producing more natural and human-readable topics than conventional topic modeling algorithms. However, the nature of topic assignment process causes certain drawbacks, such as the incapability to produce topic distributions over a document, too broad or narrow topics, and high resource consumption, which increases with the number and length of of documents being assigned topics. These issues are particularly critical for industrial applications, which require high-quality, in-depth analysis and the processing of large volumes of documents. In this context, this paper introduces a framework called SeLATM, which addresses these concerns by employing segment-level topic generation and topic refinement through agentic feedback loops. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that SeLATM significantly reduces the LLM resources compared to methods based on topic assignment process, while maintaining superior performance.

AI.tldr: SeLATM is a framework that addresses limitations of LLM-based topic modeling by using segment-level topic generation and agentic feedback loops for topic refinement, significantly reducing LLM resource consumption while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based topic models suffer from three critical issues: inability to produce topic distributions over documents, topics that are too broad or narrow, and high resource consumption that scales with document number and length. These are particularly problematic for industrial applications requiring high-quality analysis of large document volumes.
AI.method: SeLATM employs segment-level topic generation combined with topic refinement through agentic feedback loops to address the limitations of traditional LLM-based topic assignment approaches.
AI.result: Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that SeLATM significantly reduces LLM resources compared to methods based on topic assignment process, while maintaining superior performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SeLATM framework successfully addresses the resource consumption and quality issues of LLM-based topic modeling, making it more suitable for industrial applications requiring large-scale document analysis.

title: Game Arena: Strategic LLM Evaluation in Competitive Environments
comment: 31 pages, 15 figures. Technical report. Project page: https://www.kaggle.com/game-arena
summary: We introduce Kaggle Game Arena, an open and ever-expanding platform to evaluate large language models (LLMs) through competitive games. Different from static benchmarks, game arena enables models to play head-to-head matchups in structured environments where the gameplay strength naturally increases as models evolve, preventing performance saturation. This technical report details the infrastructure behind Game Arena and describes the three pilot game environments: Chess, Poker, and Werewolf. These environments span perfect information, imperfect information, and multiplayer game settings, enabling a systematic study of models' strategic planning, adaptation, and robustness under uncertainty. For each game, we provide a detailed description of the environment, evaluation metrics, and results from running full competitions across models. Through robust infrastructure and large-scale ground-truth based evaluation, Game Arena ensures reproducibility, transparency and generalizability to new games and variants over time.

AI.tldr: Kaggle Game Arena is an open platform for evaluating large language models (LLMs) through competitive games, featuring three pilot environments (Chess, Poker, and Werewolf) that span perfect information, imperfect information, and multiplayer settings. The platform addresses benchmark saturation by providing dynamic gameplay that scales with model evolution.
AI.motivation: Static benchmarks suffer from performance saturation as models evolve, creating a need for dynamic evaluation environments where gameplay difficulty naturally increases. The authors aim to create a systematic framework for studying LLMs' strategic planning, adaptation, and robustness under uncertainty across diverse game conditions.
AI.method: The paper details the infrastructure design and describes three pilot game environments: (1) Chess - perfect information game, (2) Poker - imperfect information game, (3) Werewolf - multiplayer social deduction game. Each environment includes specific evaluation metrics, and full competitions were run across multiple models to generate comparative results.
AI.result: The paper presents results from running full competitions across models in each of the three game environments, though specific numerical results are not detailed in the abstract. The infrastructure enables large-scale ground-truth based evaluation with reproducibility and transparency.
AI.conclusion: Game Arena provides a scalable, extensible platform for LLM evaluation through competitive games. Its robust infrastructure ensures reproducibility, transparency, and generalizability to new games and variants over time, offering a sustainable alternative to static benchmarks for assessing evolving LLM capabilities.

title: "AI is (not) the new...": A Diagnostic Analogy Framework for Generative AI's Cultural Impacts
summary: Generative AI is reshaping the cultural infrastructures through which knowledge is found, synthesized, and held accountable. To make sense of this shift, scholars and policymakers reach for historical analogies of technologies such as the printing press, steam power or electricity. But these comparisons are typically imprecise about which property of the technology carries the comparison, and imprecise analogies produce imprecise governance by designing interventions against the wrong property of the system. This paper offers a diagnostic framework for analyzing how generative AI can transform epistemic and cultural practice. This paper offers a diagnostic framework for analyzing how generative AI can transform epistemic and cultural practice. We decompose each intervention into three coordinates: the epistemic site at which a technology acts, the governing logic by which it organizes its object, and the technical mechanism through which the logic is instantiated. This framework allows us to distinguish between structural cultural consequences, which follow from the mechanism itself, from contingent ones, which remain open to design and institutional choice. Applying the framework to information discovery and knowledge synthesis, we show how the shift from indexicality to inference and from editorial authority to statistical consensus produces specific, traceable cultural effects and reveals governance levers that gestalt analogy obscures.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a diagnostic framework to analyze how generative AI transforms epistemic and cultural practices, addressing the problem of imprecise historical analogies in AI governance by decomposing technological interventions into three coordinates: epistemic site, governing logic, and technical mechanism.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from a critical observation: scholars and policymakers frequently use historical analogies (printing press, steam power, electricity) to understand generative AI's impact, but these analogies are imprecise because they fail to specify which property of the technology is being compared. This imprecision leads to flawed governance that targets the wrong properties of the system.
AI.method: The authors develop a diagnostic framework with three analytical coordinates: (1) Epistemic site - the location where technology acts on knowledge/culture; (2) Governing logic - the organizational principle by which technology structures its object; (3) Technical mechanism - the specific instantiation of that logic. This framework is applied to analyze information discovery and knowledge synthesis, examining the shift from indexicality to inference and from editorial authority to statistical consensus.
AI.result: The framework reveals specific, traceable cultural effects of generative AI and identifies governance levers that gestalt historical analogies obscure. It distinguishes between structural cultural consequences (which follow inevitably from the mechanism itself) and contingent ones (which remain open to design and institutional choice).
AI.conclusion: The diagnostic framework provides a more precise analytical tool for understanding AI's cultural transformation than historical analogies. By decomposing interventions into epistemic site, governing logic, and technical mechanism, policymakers and scholars can better target governance efforts at the appropriate level and distinguish which effects are structurally inevitable versus designable.

title: UQ-LOB: Uncertainty-Aware Limit Order Book Mid-Price Forecasting
summary: Forecasting short-horizon mid-price movements from limit order book (LOB) data is central to algorithmic trading, yet most deep LOB forecasters are point predictors: they output a direction or a displacement, but never indicate which of their forecasts can be trusted. We introduce UQ-LOB, a lightweight, encoder-agnostic uncertainty quantification module that attaches to any pretrained LOB encoder and, in the spirit of attentive neural processes, conditions each forecast on a context set of recently completed windows whose outcomes are already realised. The UQ-regression variant outputs a calibrated Gaussian over the future tick displacement, while the UQ-classification variant outputs a categorical distribution over down/up/stationary. Both expose a scalar confidence (predicted signal-to-noise ratio or class probability) that supports selective prediction. On 5.2 billion LOB events across seven cryptocurrency assets and horizons of 5, 10 and 15 seconds, UQ-regression attains near-nominal 68% interval coverage, and restricting to the most confident 10% of predictions raises directional macro F1 by 0.11-0.15 for UQ-regression and 0.05-0.11 for UQ-classification, at every horizon. On large, economically meaningful moves, the tightest confidence tier reaches a directional F1 of 0.88 (down) and 0.83 (up) at the 5-second horizon.

AI.tldr: UQ-LOB is a lightweight, encoder-agnostic uncertainty quantification module for limit order book (LOB) forecasting that attaches to any pretrained LOB encoder. It uses an attentive neural process approach to condition forecasts on a context set of recently completed windows. Two variants are proposed: UQ-regression (calibrated Gaussian output) and UQ-classification (categorical distribution over down/up/stationary), both exposing scalar confidence measures for selective prediction.
AI.motivation: Most deep LOB forecasters are point predictors that output only direction or displacement without indicating forecast reliability. This limits their practical utility in algorithmic trading where knowing which predictions to trust is crucial. The paper addresses this gap by introducing uncertainty quantification to LOB forecasting.
AI.method: UQ-LOB attaches to any pretrained LOB encoder and conditions each forecast on a context set of recently completed windows (whose outcomes are already realized), in the spirit of attentive neural processes. The UQ-regression variant outputs a calibrated Gaussian over future tick displacement, while UQ-classification outputs a categorical distribution over down/up/stationary classes. Both expose a scalar confidence measure (predicted signal-to-noise ratio or class probability) that supports selective prediction.
AI.result: On 5.2 billion LOB events across seven cryptocurrency assets and horizons of 5, 10 and 15 seconds: (1) UQ-regression achieves near-nominal 68% interval coverage; (2) restricting to the most confident 10% of predictions raises directional macro F1 by 0.11-0.15 for UQ-regression and 0.05-0.11 for UQ-classification at every horizon; (3) on large, economically meaningful moves, the tightest confidence tier reaches directional F1 of 0.88 (down) and 0.83 (up) at the 5-second horizon.
AI.conclusion: The proposed UQ-LOB module successfully adds uncertainty quantification to LOB forecasting with minimal architectural overhead. The confidence measures enable selective prediction, significantly improving accuracy for high-confidence predictions. The approach is encoder-agnostic, making it broadly applicable to existing LOB forecasting models.

title: Prompt Minimization: Reducing Input Redundancy Without Sacrificing Output Fidelity
summary: Despite the growing capabilities of large language models (LLMs), prompt design remains largely heuristic and ad hoc. This project will explore $\textit{prompt minimization}$, the process of reducing prompts to their smallest, most information-dense form while preserving output fidelity. Practically, shorter prompts reduce computational overhead and inference latency, especially when large contexts, such as entire documents or codebases, are included unnecessarily. Further, longer prompts can damage LLM reasoning and accuracy. Theoretically, the existence of multiple prompts yielding equivalent outputs suggests a high degree of redundancy in the input space, raising fundamental questions about what information is essential to elicit specific model behaviors. We propose three variant frameworks to identify and evaluate minimal prompts and demonstrate that minimal prompts often produce outputs comparable to those of their longer counterparts. These findings suggest new directions for efficient prompt engineering and deepen our understanding of input compression in LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper explores "prompt minimization" - the process of reducing prompts to their smallest information-dense form while preserving output quality. The authors propose three frameworks to identify minimal prompts and demonstrate that shorter prompts can produce outputs comparable to longer ones.
AI.motivation: Prompt design is currently heuristic and ad hoc. Longer prompts increase computational overhead and inference latency, especially when large contexts are unnecessarily included. Additionally, longer prompts can damage LLM reasoning and accuracy. The existence of multiple prompts yielding equivalent outputs suggests redundancy in the input space, raising fundamental questions about what information is essential to elicit specific model behaviors.
AI.method: The authors propose three variant frameworks to identify and evaluate minimal prompts.
AI.result: Minimal prompts often produce outputs comparable to those of their longer counterparts.
AI.conclusion: These findings suggest new directions for efficient prompt engineering and deepen understanding of input compression in LLMs.

title: A Flow Matching Framework for Neural Representational Dissimilarity
summary: Neural representational dissimilarity quantifies differences between neural response distributions, and is essential for comparing neural codes across stimuli, brain areas, tasks, and models. Commonly used distance metrics involve different assumptions and are estimated with separate methods. Here, we show that a variety of distance metrics can be unified under a flow matching framework developed in deep generative models. That is, these distances arise as Jeffreys divergences under different velocity constraints. We find that flow matching has advantages for estimating distances involving complicated distributions and continuous variables. Furthermore, this framework enables the design of new distance metrics in a principled way. Together, flow matching provides a unified approach for understanding, estimating, and designing neural representational dissimilarity metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified framework for neural representational dissimilarity metrics using flow matching from deep generative models. The approach shows that various distance metrics can be understood as Jeffreys divergences under different velocity constraints, enabling better estimation for complex distributions and principled design of new metrics.
AI.motivation: Neural representational dissimilarity is essential for comparing neural codes across stimuli, brain areas, tasks, and models. However, commonly used distance metrics involve different assumptions and are estimated with separate methods, creating fragmentation in the field. This lack of unification makes it difficult to compare results across studies and choose appropriate metrics.
AI.method: The authors propose using flow matching, a framework developed in deep generative models, to unify various distance metrics. They demonstrate that these distances arise as Jeffreys divergences under different velocity constraints. Flow matching is applied to estimate distances involving complicated distributions and continuous variables.
AI.result: The study finds that flow matching provides advantages for estimating distances involving complicated distributions and continuous variables. Additionally, the framework enables the principled design of new distance metrics, which was not previously possible in a systematic way.
AI.conclusion: Flow matching provides a unified approach for understanding, estimating, and designing neural representational dissimilarity metrics. This framework bridges neuroscience and deep learning methodologies, offering a principled way to compare neural representations across different conditions and enabling innovation in metric design.

title: Multi-agent Scaling Across Disjunctive and Compensatory Tasks
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are often expected to improve as team size increases, yet the scaling behavior may depend on task structure. Our central contribution is to introduce Steiner's taxonomy of group tasks as a framework for analyzing multi-agent LLM scaling and focusing the analysis on disjunctive and compensatory tasks. We model independently sampled agents as conditionally independent given the item, which yields their large-team limits: plurality voting converges to the model's modal answer, and averaging converges to the model's item-level bias. Across selected representative benchmarks, 13 open-weight models, and teams of up to 30 agents, we find qualitatively different scaling behavior. On disjunctive tasks, the probability that at least one agent is correct grows by 5-20 points with team size, but plurality voting over agents that answer directly realises almost none of this potential, as the model predicts to within 0.5 points on average. Multi-round revision raises accuracy considerably, yet the gain is nearly the same with one peer as with 29. In contrast, scaling provides little benefit on Fermi estimation, despite its natural suitability for aggregation: item-level biases shared across the samples of a model account for about 87% of the squared error, so averaging reduces error by only about 6%. Combining model families helps on Fermi estimation but does not surpass the strongest member on disjunctive tasks. These results show that task structure, together with the mechanism combining member outputs, is a fundamental determinant of team scaling.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Steiner's taxonomy of group tasks to analyze how multi-agent LLM systems scale with team size, finding that task structure fundamentally determines scaling outcomes - disjunctive tasks show significant potential gains (5-20 points) that are largely unrealized by direct voting, while compensatory tasks like Fermi estimation show minimal benefit due to shared item-level biases.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems are expected to improve with team size, but the scaling behavior may depend on task structure. The authors seek to understand how different task types affect scaling outcomes and which aggregation mechanisms realize the potential benefits.
AI.method: The authors model independently sampled agents as conditionally independent given the item, deriving large-team limits for plurality voting (converges to modal answer) and averaging (converges to item-level bias). They tested 13 open-weight models across teams of up to 30 agents on selected representative benchmarks, focusing on disjunctive and compensatory tasks.
AI.result: On disjunctive tasks, the probability that at least one agent is correct grows by 5-20 points with team size, but plurality voting realizes almost none of this potential (predicts within 0.5 points). Multi-round revision helps but gains are nearly the same with one peer as with 29. On Fermi estimation, scaling provides little benefit despite natural suitability for aggregation - item-level biases account for ~87% of squared error, so averaging reduces error by only ~6%. Combining model families helps on Fermi estimation but doesn't surpass the strongest member on disjunctive tasks.
AI.conclusion: Task structure, together with the mechanism combining member outputs, is a fundamental determinant of team scaling in multi-agent LLM systems. The potential benefits of scaling are heavily dependent on whether the task is disjunctive or compensatory, and simple aggregation methods may fail to realize the theoretical benefits.

title: FuseReg: Regularizing Layer Fusion Mitigates the Reconstruction-Generation Gap in Representation Autoencoders
summary: Representation autoencoders (RAEs) reuse features from a pretrained visual encoder as reconstruction and diffusion latents, integrating strong visual representations into image generation. However, RAEs still need to decide which encoder layers form the shared latent space for the generator and pixel decoder. This choice involves a trade-off. Shallower layers tend to preserve fine pixel details better, while deeper layers tend to yield better generation metrics. A fixed heuristic layer fusion therefore couples two stages that benefit from different information. We introduce FuseReg, which replaces heuristic feature selection with training over random subsets of encoder layers. We theoretically analyze the underlying mechanism: subset sampling explicitly penalizes sensitivity to cross-layer disagreement. On ImageNet-256 with DINOv3-L, a single FuseReg decoder reconstructs from full, sparse, and single-layer fusions without retraining, achieving higher PSNR than decoders specialized to fixed fusions. This flexibility also benefits generation: decoder replacement alone reduces unguided gFID by 27% with an unchanged RAEv2 DiT-XL generator. The same regularization principle extends to diffusion training, with joint regularization of both stages reducing unguided gFID by 29% on DiT-Base. These results show that training downstream models for layer-fusion robustness narrows the reconstruction-generation gap without modifying the pretrained encoder.

AI.tldr: FuseReg introduces a method to address the layer selection trade-off in Representation Autoencoders (RAEs) by training decoders over random subsets of encoder layers instead of using heuristic feature selection. This approach achieves higher reconstruction quality and improves generation metrics (27-29% gFID reduction) without modifying the pretrained encoder.
AI.motivation: RAEs face a fundamental trade-off when choosing encoder layers for the shared latent space: shallower layers preserve fine pixel details while deeper layers yield better generation metrics. Current approaches use fixed heuristic layer fusion, which couples two stages that benefit from different information. The authors aim to find a more flexible solution that doesn't require choosing between these competing objectives.
AI.method: FuseReg trains the decoder over random subsets of encoder layers rather than using a fixed layer fusion heuristic. The theoretical analysis shows that subset sampling explicitly penalizes sensitivity to cross-layer disagreement, effectively regularizing the model to be robust to different layer combinations.
AI.result: On ImageNet-256 with DINOv3-L: (1) A single FuseReg decoder achieves higher PSNR than decoders specialized to fixed fusions when tested on full, sparse, and single-layer fusions without retraining. (2) Decoder replacement alone reduces unguided gFID by 27% with unchanged RAEv2 DiT-XL generator. (3) Joint regularization of both stages reduces unguided gFID by 29% on DiT-Base.
AI.conclusion: Training downstream models for layer-fusion robustness effectively narrows the reconstruction-generation gap without modifying the pretrained encoder. This approach provides flexibility to handle various layer fusion configurations while improving both reconstruction quality and generation metrics.

title: DeepEdu-v1: Efficient and Scalable Agentic LLMs for Vietnamese Education
summary: AI tutoring could markedly improve learning outcomes for students in developing regions such as Vietnam, yet the two obvious paths both fall short. Cloud assistants such as ChatGPT route sensitive student data to foreign servers---violating data-sovereignty laws such as Vietnam's Decree 53---and, pre-trained on Western-centric corpora, are not organized around the national textbook curriculum, so their knowledge of local content is unsystematic and frequently hallucinated. Self-hosting an open model keeps data on-premise but hits a two-fold wall: post-training quantization (AWQ, GPTQ) tames the static weight footprint, yet the dynamic KV cache and prefill latency of long tutoring contexts still cause out-of-memory failures and slow responses on consumer GPUs, while the model keeps hallucinating on region-specific material. We present DeepEdu-v1, an AI-tutoring system for Vietnamese education built on SCALE (Self-improving Context-Aware Learning Engine), a framework with two innovations. First, a long-context inference engine amortizes token selection from per-sub-chunk to per-cluster granularity; on long-context retrieval it issues x7.7 fewer retrieval calls than a state-of-the-art selective-attention baseline, cutting prefill latency (TTFT) by roughly 35% while matching or improving task accuracy. Second, a self-improving agentic layer continuously curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of fine-tuning, a design intended to progressively reduce reliance on dominant-language priors as trustworthy local knowledge accumulates. In its deployed configuration, DeepEdu achieves a nearly x2 TTFT speedup over standard vLLM serving and lifts agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5% on complex tasks, with the strongest per-track gains across financial-reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks.

AI.tldr: DeepEdu-v1 is an AI tutoring system for Vietnamese education built on SCALE framework, featuring a long-context inference engine that reduces retrieval calls by 7.7x and TTFT by 35%, and a self-improving agentic layer that increases accuracy from 70% to 79.5%, achieving 2x speedup over standard vLLM serving.
AI.motivation: AI tutoring could improve learning in developing regions like Vietnam, but cloud assistants violate data-sovereignty laws (Decree 53) and lack systematic local content knowledge, while self-hosted models face memory issues with long contexts and hallucination problems on region-specific material.
AI.method: Two innovations: (1) Long-context inference engine that amortizes token selection from per-sub-chunk to per-granularity, reducing retrieval calls and prefill latency; (2) Self-improving agentic layer that continuously curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of fine-tuning to reduce reliance on dominant-language priors.
AI.result: DeepEdu achieves 7.7x fewer retrieval calls on long-context retrieval, ~35% reduction in TTFT (time to first token), nearly 2x TTFT speedup over standard vLLM serving, and lifts agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5% on complex tasks, with strongest gains in financial-reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The SCALE framework successfully addresses both data sovereignty and performance challenges in deploying AI tutoring systems for Vietnamese education, with the self-improving agentic layer progressively reducing reliance on dominant-language priors as trustworthy local knowledge accumulates.

title: Learning to Stop without Learning to Stop: Self-Supervised Confidence Training Improves Reasoning Efficiency
summary: Reasoning models often generate very long reasoning traces, making inference computationally expensive. Existing approaches typically improve efficiency either through inference-time early-stopping mechanisms or by explicitly encouraging shorter reasoning during training, for example through reinforcement learning with length penalties. We show that substantial efficiency gains can instead emerge from a different kind of supervision: \textit{confidence}. Using a self-supervised procedure, we fine-tune reasoning models to predict their confidence in the answer at intermediate points along their own reasoning trajectories using only 600 training problems. Confidence is used only as a training target: the loss contains no objective for reasoning length, efficiency, or stopping. At inference, the fine-tuned models use the standard generation procedure, with no confidence elicitation or early-stopping mechanism. Despite this, self-supervised confidence fine-tuning makes reasoning more efficient, reducing generated tokens by up to 25\% at matched accuracy across Gemma, Qwen, Nemotron, and GPT-OSS models on mathematical, scientific, and coding reasoning benchmarks, with efficiency gains comparable to methods that explicitly optimize for shorter reasoning. Analysis of reasoning episodes further shows that confidence supervision largely preserves the base models' high-level reasoning composition rather than selectively suppressing particular behaviors. Our results suggest that efficient reasoning may emerge as a downstream consequence of learning metacognitive signals, without being directly optimized.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a self-supervised method to fine-tune reasoning models to predict their confidence at intermediate reasoning points, achieving up to 25% token reduction without explicit length optimization or inference-time mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Reasoning models generate extremely long reasoning traces, making inference computationally expensive. Existing approaches either use early-stopping at inference time or explicitly optimize for shorter reasoning during training. The authors propose that efficiency can emerge from a different kind of supervision: confidence.
AI.method: Self-supervised confidence fine-tuning: Models are fine-tuned to predict their confidence in the answer at intermediate points along their own reasoning trajectories using only 600 training problems. Confidence is used only as a training target with no objective for reasoning length, efficiency, or stopping. At inference, the model uses standard generation procedure with no confidence elicitation or early-stopping mechanism.
AI.result: Reduces generated tokens by up to 25% at matched accuracy across Gemma, Qwen, Nemotron, and GPT-OSS models on mathematical, scientific, and coding reasoning benchmarks. Efficiency gains are comparable to methods that explicitly optimize for shorter reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Efficient reasoning can emerge as a downstream consequence of learning metacognitive signals (confidence) without directly optimizing for it. This suggests that confidence supervision largely preserves the base models' high-level reasoning composition rather than selectively suppressing particular behaviors.

title: ENAS: An Efficient Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search Framework for TinyML on Resource-Constrained Microcontrollers
summary: We present \textbf{ENAS}, a hardware-aware Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework that combines a static feasibility check, a cell-based search space supporting standard, depthwise-separable, and bottleneck blocks with optional skip connections, and a three-stage hybrid search strategy (random $\rightarrow$ top-$K$ $\rightarrow$ mutation) with persistent cross-run caching. Unlike many existing NAS frameworks that rely on GPU acceleration, ENAS is designed to operate efficiently without requiring GPUs, making it suitable for resource-constrained development environments. We evaluate ENAS on two TinyML benchmarks, Visual Wake Words and Melanoma Cancer, across eight microcontrollers with memory footprints ranging from 20\,KB to 1\,MB SRAM and nine input image resolutions. Our experimental results show that ENAS achieves mean search-time speedups of $2.41{\times}$ and $1.70{\times}$ on the Visual Wake Words and Melanoma Cancer datasets, respectively, while maintaining competitive test accuracy compared with the recent NanoNAS framework. A measured resource analysis further shows that ENAS-selected models use substantially lower peak activation RAM, the binding constraint for microcontroller deployment at matched accuracy. Additionally, ENAS achieves $79.4\%$ test accuracy on an STM32H743-based microcontroller, outperforming the greedy CPU-only baseline by $2.6$ percentage points. We release the ENAS framework as open-source at: https://github.com/EdgeIntelligenceLab/ENAS

AI.tldr: ENAS is a hardware-aware Neural Architecture Search framework designed to operate efficiently without GPUs, suitable for resource-constrained TinyML environments. It combines static feasibility checking, a cell-based search space with multiple block types, and a three-stage hybrid search strategy with persistent caching.
AI.motivation: Many existing NAS frameworks rely on GPU acceleration, making them unsuitable for resource-constrained development environments. Microcontroller deployment requires careful consideration of memory constraints (particularly SRAM), and there is a need for efficient architecture search that can run on CPU-only systems while still producing competitive accuracy.
AI.method: ENAS employs: (1) static feasibility check for rapid filtering, (2) cell-based search space supporting standard, depthwise-separable, and bottleneck blocks with optional skip connections, (3) three-stage hybrid search strategy (random → top-K → mutation) with persistent cross-run caching. Evaluation was performed on Visual Wake Words and Melanoma Cancer datasets across eight microcontrollers (20KB-1MB SRAM) and nine input image resolutions.
AI.result: ENAS achieves mean search-time speedups of 2.41x and 1.70x on Visual Wake Words and Melanoma Cancer datasets respectively, while maintaining competitive test accuracy compared to NanoNAS. ENAS-selected models use substantially lower peak activation RAM. On STM32H743 microcontroller, ENAS achieves 79.4% test accuracy, outperforming the greedy CPU-only baseline by 2.6 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: ENAS successfully enables efficient neural architecture search on CPU-only systems for TinyML applications. It delivers significant search-time speedups while producing models with competitive accuracy and lower memory footprint, making it particularly suitable for microcontroller deployment where SRAM is the binding constraint.

title: When Does Advection-Aware Graph Nowcasting Help? A Controlled Study of Distributed Solar Ramp Forecasting with a Self-Supervised Cloud-Motion Estimator
summary: Short-term forecasting of cloud-induced power ramps across a network of distributed photovoltaic (PV) or irradiance sensors is a recognised pain point for grid operators. A natural idea is to make the graph neural network (GNN) advection-aware: connect each site to the sites upwind of it, with edge time-lags set by the cloud-motion vector (CMV), so that a ramp is propagated forward before it physically arrives. Using a controlled synthetic testbed with a known wind field, we show that (i) with a realistic cross-correlation CMV estimate, an explicit advection graph does not beat a plain static or learned-adjacency spatiotemporal GNN; (ii) roughly half of the benefit available from a perfect CMV comes simply from providing an accurate motion vector as an input feature, not from graph structure; and (iii) advection helps only when the advective displacement over the forecast horizon, v*H, fits inside the sensor network. Motivated by (ii), we introduce a small self-supervised cloud-motion estimator -- a position-aware encoder trained only on a multi-lag optical-flow reconstruction objective with an annealed kernel -- that recovers the true wind vector to 2-4 degrees median angular error, 2-4x better than the classical cross-correlation method across every wind regime. Freezing this estimator and feeding its vector to the forecaster closes about 60% of the oracle-CMV RMSE gap at moderate wind (8-15% RMSE reduction over no advection), with no external wind data. We also report a negative result for a spatially-coherent probabilistic head. All claims are established on a single synthetic simulator; we discuss why real-network validation is the necessary next step and outline it.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using advection-aware graph neural networks (GNNs) for short-term forecasting of cloud-induced power ramps across distributed PV sensors. Using a synthetic testbed with known wind field, the authors find that explicit advection graphs don't outperform simpler spatiotemporal GNNs with realistic CMV estimates, but providing accurate motion vectors as input features captures ~50% of the benefit. They introduce a self-supervised cloud-motion estimator that achieves 2-4x better accuracy than cross-correlation methods, closing ~60% of the oracle-CMV gap.
AI.motivation: Grid operators struggle with short-term forecasting of cloud-induced power ramps across distributed PV or irradiance sensors. This is a critical pain point for grid stability and renewable energy integration.
AI.method: The authors used a controlled synthetic testbed with a known wind field to test three hypotheses: (i) comparing explicit advection graphs vs plain static/learned-adjacency spatiotemporal GNNs; (ii) testing whether motion vector input features alone capture advection benefits; (iii) verifying that advective displacement fits within the sensor network. They introduced a self-supervised cloud-motion estimator (position-aware encoder with annealed kernel) trained on multi-lag optical-flow reconstruction objectives, requiring no external wind data.
AI.result: Key findings: (i) With realistic CMV estimates, explicit advection graphs don't outperform simpler GNN architectures; (ii) ~50% of perfect-CMV benefits come from providing motion vectors as input features, not graph structure; (iii) Advection helps only when v*H fits within the sensor network. The self-supervised estimator recovers wind vectors with 2-4° median angular error (2-4x better than cross-correlation). This closes ~60% of the oracle-CMV RMSE gap (8-15% RMSE reduction over no advection). A spatially-coherent probabilistic head showed negative results.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that explicit advection graph structure provides limited additional benefit over providing accurate motion vectors as input features. The proposed self-supervised cloud-motion estimator effectively closes most of the oracle-CMV gap without external wind data. Real-network validation is identified as the necessary next step. All claims are established on a single synthetic simulator.

title: Strategic Self-Consistency
summary: Self-consistency has become a popular technique for enhancing the reasoning abilities of large language models by generating multiple reasoning paths and selecting the final answer through a majority vote. However, because model providers typically charge users in proportion to the number of reasoning paths generated, they have a financial incentive to artificially increase the path count. In this work, we show that an unfaithful provider can exploit this incentive using a simple, efficient algorithm while avoiding detection by an auditor: by generating and strategically reordering additional reasoning paths, the algorithm makes every path appear necessary to reach the majority. To validate our algorithm, we conduct experiments with multiple instruct models from the Llama and Qwen families, as well as reasoning models distilled from DeepSeek-R1, on benchmark datasets spanning mathematics, science, and question answering. Our results suggest that the distribution of additional reasoning paths generated by our algorithm is heavy-tailed and that substantial capacity to overcharge remains even under the best possible audit designed to keep the false-positive rate below $α= 0.1$.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a financial exploitation vulnerability in LLM self-consistency reasoning: providers can artificially inflate reasoning path counts to charge users more, using an algorithm that strategically generates and reorders paths to appear necessary for majority voting, while evading detection audits.
AI.motivation: Model providers charge users based on the number of reasoning paths generated in self-consistency techniques, creating a financial incentive for providers to artificially inflate path counts and overcharge users.
AI.method: The authors propose an algorithm that generates additional reasoning paths and strategically reorders them to make every path appear necessary for achieving the majority vote, while avoiding detection by auditors.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple instruct models (Llama, Qwen families) and reasoning models distilled from DeepSeek-R1 across math, science, and QA benchmarks show the distribution of additional paths is heavy-tailed, with substantial overcharging capacity remaining even under the optimal audit with false-positive rate below α=0.1.
AI.conclusion: Unfaithful providers can exploit self-consistency pricing mechanisms to significantly overcharge users by generating strategically reordered reasoning paths, and this exploitation is difficult to detect even with stringent audit controls.

title: Cost-Aware Best-LLM Identification using Dueling Feedback
comment: We propose a cost-aware dueling bandit algorithm for best arm identification, prove its asymptotic optimality, and demonstrate its effectiveness in reliably identifying the best LLM with a minimum cost Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Inspired by the problem of identifying the best model from a collection of large language models (LLMs) with heterogeneous querying costs, we formulate and analyse a variant of the multi-armed bandit (MAB) with (i) dueling feedback, where pairwise comparisons between model responses provide robust preference signals, and (ii) heterogeneous sampling costs, reflecting the differing costs of querying different LLMs. Assuming the existence of a Condorcet winner, a condition we empirically validate across multiple real-world datasets, we propose a Track-and-Stop style algorithm for best-arm identification with prescribed confidence. We prove that the algorithm almost surely achieves the asymptotically optimal cost as the error tends to zero. Finally, we extensively evaluate our approach on both synthetic and real-world instances, demonstrating consistent improvements over classical cost-unaware algorithms and their cost-aware extensions.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses best-arm identification in a multi-armed bandit setting where large language models (LLMs) have heterogeneous querying costs and provide dueling feedback (pairwise comparisons). The proposed Track-and-Stop style algorithm achieves asymptotically optimal cost under the Condorcet winner assumption.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to identify the best model from a collection of large language models with heterogeneous querying costs, using pairwise comparisons to provide robust preference signals.
AI.method: The paper proposes a Track-and-Stop style algorithm for best-arm identification with prescribed confidence, assuming the existence of a Condorcet winner (empirically validated across multiple real-world datasets).
AI.result: The algorithm almost surely achieves the asymptotically optimal cost as the error tends to zero. Empirical evaluation shows consistent improvements over classical cost-unaware algorithms and their cost-aware extensions on both synthetic and real-world instances.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively handles the trade-off between sampling costs and duel-based preference feedback, achieving optimal cost efficiency while maintaining prescribed confidence in best-arm identification.

title: DanLing NestedTensor: Composable Multi-Ragged Tensors for Deep Learning
summary: Variable-size inputs are common in deep learning, but dense batching allocates a shared envelope and spends computation on padding. The cost multiplies across varying axes: an explicit pair state allocates $BN_{\max}^2$ positions instead of $\sum_i N_i^2$. Packing removes that waste, but composing packed operations still requires the logical axes and sample boundaries a flat buffer no longer exposes. We present DanLing NestedTensor, a PyTorch tensor abstraction that makes multi-ragged structure a property of the tensor itself. Packed values carry tensor-backed partitions and logical dimension order, so broadcasting creates ragged axes, feature transformations retain them, and reductions consume them. The same representation carries through autograd and both eager and compiled execution. On an A100, the geometric-mean speedup over same-mode padding is 2.74$\times$ eager and 3.39$\times$ compiled across four BERT scales, and 1.97$\times$ eager across four FCN backbones. A four-block Pairformer-style workload runs 2.40-4.32$\times$ faster than a padded reference using native PyTorch kernels across square length regimes in eager execution, with peak allocation falling from 38.08 to 5.41 GiB on its high-variation batch. The tensor interface lets model code built from its supported operators compose efficient variable-size computation without managing offsets at any call site. Code will be released publicly upon publication.

AI.tldr: DanLing NestedTensor is a PyTorch tensor abstraction that eliminates padding waste in variable-size input processing by making multi-ragged structure an intrinsic property of tensors, enabling efficient computation without manual offset management.
AI.motivation: Dense batching with padding wastes computation and memory by allocating a shared envelope and spending computation on padding. This is especially costly for operations like explicit pair states where cost scales as BN_max² instead of ΣN_i². While packing removes waste, composing packed operations requires managing logical axes and sample boundaries that flat buffers don't expose.
AI.method: DanLing NestedTensor represents packed values with tensor-backed partitions and logical dimension order. This enables: (1) broadcasting to create ragged axes, (2) feature transformations to retain ragged structure, and (3) reductions to consume ragged axes. The representation persists through autograd and both eager and compiled execution modes.
AI.result: On A100 GPU: 2.74× geometric-mean speedup in eager mode and 3.39× in compiled mode across four BERT scales; 1.97× speedup in eager mode across four FCN backbones. Four-block Pairformer-style workload runs 2.40-4.32× faster than padded reference. Peak memory allocation reduced from 38.08 to 5.41 GiB on high-variation batch.
AI.conclusion: DanLing NestedTensor enables efficient variable-size computation through a clean tensor interface without managing offsets at call sites, achieving significant speedups (2.40-4.32×) and memory reductions (38.08→5.41 GiB) across BERT, FCN, and Pairformer workloads while maintaining compatibility with PyTorch's autograd and execution modes.

title: What Improves Multimodal Misinformation Detection? Answers from a Large-Scale Empirical Study
comment: Accepted at the Tenth Widening NLP Workshop (WiNLP), co-located with EMNLP 2026
summary: Multimodal misinformation is increasingly crafted to look convincing by pairing a textual claim with an image that appears to "prove" it. Yet in practice, building effective detectors often hinges on a small set of design choices that are rarely examined in a controlled way. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale study of multimodal design choices for misinformation detection with over 3,375 experiments- spanning three benchmark datasets and a broad range of pre-trained vision and language backbones. Through systematic comparisons and targeted robustness analyses, we distill practical guidance on which design choices help, when do they fail silently, and what aspects of the pipeline most strongly shape model behavior, answering 4 key Research Questions (RQs). We aim to provide a reliable foundation for designing stronger and more dependable multimodal misinformation detection systems, thus contributing to the broader research community.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a large-scale empirical study (3,375 experiments) examining design choices for multimodal misinformation detection, comparing multiple vision-language backbones across three benchmark datasets to provide practical guidance for building more effective detection systems.
AI.motivation: Multimodal misinformation is increasingly convincing as it pairs textual claims with seemingly supporting images. However, effective detection systems depend on design choices that are rarely systematically examined or evaluated in controlled settings.
AI.method: Large-scale study with 3,375 experiments spanning three benchmark datasets and multiple pre-trained vision and language backbones, with systematic comparisons and targeted robustness analyses.
AI.result: The paper answers 4 key Research Questions (RQs) regarding: (1) which design choices help, (2) when they fail silently, (3) what pipeline aspects most strongly shape model behavior, and (4) practical guidance for stronger detection systems.
AI.conclusion: Provides a reliable foundation for designing stronger and more dependable multimodal misinformation detection systems through empirical evidence and practical guidance.

title: New LoRA Skills Should Read but Never Write
summary: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) make it cheap to fine-tune a large language model once per task, but combining several independently trained adapters into one model remains difficult: merging the updates in weight space causes interference, retraining on all task data is expensive, and routing between separate adapters gives up the goal of a single combined model. We trace the difficulty to two choices that every composition method makes implicitly. A LoRA update admits infinitely many equivalent factorizations; the choice among them is invisible while an adapter serves alone, but it determines what a learned interaction between adapters can see. A coupling between an old skill and a new one can likewise point in either direction, and the direction decides whether the old skills keep computing what they computed before. We introduce READ (Read-only Expansion of Adapter Deltas), which fixes both choices: each adapter is rewritten into a balanced canonical form that preserves its update exactly, and the coupling grows in one direction only, so a new skill can read the input subspaces of old skills but cannot write into their output subspaces. The only trainable object at each append is the new skill's row of the coupling matrix, and the composed update folds into the base weights with no inference cost, routing, or task-specific rules. We evaluate READ across four benchmark suites and two model families, adding skills one at a time. Across several families, READ improves every suite average over the strongest published baselines built from the same adapters---by more than twenty points on SuperGLUE and more than seven points on the domain suite---and nearly all complete addition sequences end above every direct baseline. Factor coordinates and coupling direction, which a lone adapter never exposes, are what decide whether composed skills survive.

AI.tldr: READ addresses the challenge of combining multiple LoRA adapters into a single model by fixing two implicit choices: the factorization of LoRA updates and the coupling direction between skills. The method rewrites each adapter into a balanced canonical form and uses unidirectional coupling so new skills can read old skills' input subspaces but not write to their output subspaces.
AI.motivation: Combining independently trained LoRA adapters causes interference because: (1) LoRA updates admit infinitely many equivalent factorizations that are invisible when adapters work alone but determine learned interactions between adapters, and (2) the direction of coupling between old and new skills determines whether old skills retain their original functionality. Current solutions (weight merging, retraining on all data, or routing) are either ineffective or sacrifice the goal of a single combined model.
AI.method: READ introduces two key fixes: (1) Canonical form transformation - each adapter is rewritten into a balanced canonical form that preserves its update exactly, making the factorization choice visible and controllable. (2) Unidirectional coupling - the coupling grows in one direction only, allowing new skills to read input subspaces of old skills but preventing them from writing to old skills' output subspaces. The only trainable parameter at each skill addition is the new skill's row of the coupling matrix, and the composed update folds into base weights with no inference cost, routing, or task-specific rules.
AI.result: READ improves every suite average over the strongest published baselines built from the same adapters—by more than 20 points on SuperGLUE and more than 7 points on the domain suite. Nearly all complete addition sequences end above every direct baseline across four benchmark suites and two model families.
AI.conclusion: Factor coordinates and coupling direction, which are invisible for a lone adapter, are the critical factors that determine whether composed skills survive. The canonical form and unidirectional coupling in READ solve the adapter composition problem by making these previously hidden choices explicit and controllable.
